Identifiers, keywords, constants, dollar quoting and operator structure of PostgreSQL statements.
Column references, positional parameters, operator invocation, row constructors and expression evaluation.
Projection items, *, expressions in the select list and output column naming.
Sorting result rows with ORDER BY, NULLS FIRST/LAST and collation-aware ordering.
Bounded result retrieval with LIMIT/OFFSET and the standard FETCH syntax.
Duplicate removal with DISTINCT and PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON.
UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT and their ALL variants over compatible queries.
WITH clauses that define auxiliary statements for a larger query.
WITH RECURSIVE iteration, termination, search order and cycle handling.
OVER, PARTITION BY, window frames and ranking/offset window functions.
CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF, GREATEST and LEAST.
NULL semantics, IS NULL/IS DISTINCT FROM and how AND/OR/NOT treat unknown.
Set-valued aggregates, FILTER, ORDER BY inside aggregates and grouping sets.
Inner, outer, cross, natural and LATERAL join semantics.
Integer, arbitrary-precision numeric and floating-point types, serial and arithmetic behavior.
character varying, character and text, padding and length semantics.
boolean storage, accepted literals and NULL truth values.
date, time, timestamp with/without time zone and interval.
json versus jsonb storage semantics, containment, indexing and subscripting.
Array declaration, literals, indexing, slicing and searching.
Enumerated types, UUID, XML, network and bit-string types.
Built-in ranges, bounds, overlap and construction.
Cast syntax, implicit/assignment/explicit casts and union type resolution.
Collation-aware ordering and comparison, COLLATE clauses and ICU.
Domains as base types with reusable CHECK constraints.
String operators and functions such as concatenation, substring and trim.
Numeric operators and functions such as round, trunc, mod and random.
current_date/now, extract, date_trunc, age and interval arithmetic.
LIKE, ILIKE, SIMILAR TO and POSIX regular expressions.
tsvector/tsquery, matching @@, ranking and FTS indexing.
CREATE TABLE, column defaults, temporary and unlogged tables.
GENERATED ALWAYS/BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY versus serial.
Stored generated columns, expression rules and restrictions.
CHECK, NOT NULL and UNIQUE constraint semantics.
Key declaration, referential actions and deferred enforcement.
ALTER TABLE operations and their effects.
Schema organization, name resolution and the public schema.
View semantics, updatable views and CHECK OPTION.
Materialized view storage, refresh and when to prefer them.
Declarative range/list/hash partitioning, pruning and defaults.
Data modification statements, ON CONFLICT and RETURNING.
Conditional merge of a source table into a target.
BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, atomicity, savepoints and transaction properties.
Read committed, repeatable read and serializable behavior in PostgreSQL.
Multiversion snapshots, visibility and their consequences.
Table/row locks, FOR UPDATE/SHARE, deadlocks and advisory locks.
Index purpose, cost, unique/partial/expression and multicolumn indexes.
B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN selection.
Reading plan trees, cost estimates, EXPLAIN ANALYZE and scan types.
ANALYZE statistics, selectivity and statistics targets.
Role attributes, INHERIT, group roles and SET ROLE.
GRANT/REVOKE, object privileges and grant options.
Policies, USING/WITH CHECK, permissive vs restrictive and bypass rules.
CREATE FUNCTION, arguments, volatility categories and SETOF results.
Blocks, declarations, control structures, statements and exceptions.
CREATE PROCEDURE, CALL and transaction control in procedures.
Trigger timing, row/statement granularity, NEW/OLD and trigger functions.
postgresql.conf, ALTER SYSTEM and key resource settings.
VACUUM variants, autovacuum, visibility map and wraparound.
SQL dump, file-system backup, PITR and their tradeoffs.
WAL purpose, durability and archiving basics.
Physical vs logical replication, streaming and slots.
Cumulative statistics views and activity monitoring.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters rows in a SELECT statement?
Which join returns only matching rows from both tables?
Write a query that returns all customer names from the customers table.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name FROM customers

questions.prompt: Explain why indexes speed up reads but slow down writes.
Which SELECT clause chooses the returned attributes?
Which condition excludes a row whose amount is NULL?
What does an INNER JOIN return when a row has no matching key?
What does GROUP BY region_id establish for SUM(amount)?
When is HAVING evaluated relative to grouping?
What happens when a scalar aggregate subquery computes AVG on no non-NULL values?
How is a many-to-many relationship mapped to relational tables?
Which change addresses a repeating multivalued attribute?
What does the dependency student_id -> email mean?
Which representation satisfies atomic attribute values?
Which dependency violates 2NF for a non-prime attribute with composite key (student_id, course_id)?
Which decomposition addresses student_id -> dept_id -> dept_name?
Return the id and amount of every sale.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, amount FROM sales

questions.prompt: Return IDs of sales with an amount of at least 20.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id FROM sales WHERE amount >= 20

questions.prompt: Return each sale ID and its matching region label using a JOIN.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT s.id, r.label FROM sales s JOIN regions r ON r.id=s.region_id

questions.prompt: Return each region_id and the total non-NULL sale amount using GROUP BY.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT region_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region_id

questions.prompt: Return grouped region IDs with a total sale amount of at least 30 using HAVING.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT region_id FROM sales GROUP BY region_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 30

questions.prompt: Return IDs of sales above the overall average amount, using a subquery.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id FROM sales WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM sales)

questions.prompt: For Enrollment(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, dept_id, dept_name, grade), assume (student_id, course_id) is the key and student_id -> student_name, course_id -> course_title, student_id -> dept_id, dept_id -> dept_name. Explain the ER relationships, functional dependencies and a decomposition from 1NF through 2NF to 3NF. Justify lossless joins and dependency preservation.
questions.reference_answer: Separate Student(student_id, student_name, dept_id), Department(dept_id, dept_name), Course(course_id, course_title), and Enrollment(student_id, course_id, grade). Identify partial dependencies on student_id and course_id and the transitive department dependency. Enrollment represents the many-to-many association. Key-based joins reconstruct enrollment facts without spurious tuples and each specified dependency is enforced in a relation.

questions.prompt: Which command changes values in existing rows while preserving the table definition?
Which statement defines a table and its referential integrity constraint?

For Department(dept_id, name) and Employee(employee_id, dept_id, salary), explain how DDL defines keys and referential integrity and how INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE modify data. Describe a targeted salary update, the risk of a missing WHERE clause, and how foreign keys constrain deleting a department. Explain why these statements are described here rather than executed in this read-only assessment sandbox.
questions.reference_answer: CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE defines structure, primary keys and a foreign key from Employee.dept_id to Department.dept_id. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing values and DELETE removes rows. A salary update uses a predicate identifying intended employees; omitting WHERE can update every row. A referenced department deletion is rejected unless its declared referential action permits it; do not assume cascading deletion. These are conceptual answers: learner sandbox execution accepts only read-only SELECT and rolls back, so it cannot run DML/DDL.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which statement about unquoted identifiers is correct?
questions.explanation: Unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive because PostgreSQL folds them to lower case. Quoting an identifier preserves case and makes it case-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid way to write a string literal containing an apostrophe in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Inside a standard string literal an apostrophe is escaped by doubling it (''). Double quotes delimit identifiers, not strings.

questions.prompt: What does PostgreSQL's dollar quoting ($$...$$) provide?
questions.explanation: Dollar-quoted strings let a function body or long literal contain quote characters directly, avoiding '' escaping.

questions.prompt: A column was created with CREATE TABLE t ("Total" numeric). Why does SELECT total FROM t fail?
questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE with the quoted identifier "Total" stores the name with its case preserved. Unquoted total folds to lower case total, which does not match; the query needs "Total".

questions.prompt: In a PostgreSQL expression like 3 + 4 * 2, what determines the result 11?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL applies standard operator precedence: * binds tighter than +, so 4 * 2 is evaluated first, giving 11.

questions.prompt: What does the row constructor expression ROW(1, 'a') = ROW(1, 'a') evaluate to?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL compares row constructors element-by-element; equal fields make the whole comparison true.

questions.prompt: SELECT 1 = NULL; returns which value in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Comparison with NULL yields NULL (unknown) rather than true or false; this is standard three-valued logic.

questions.prompt: Which expression selects rows where a is between 5 and 10 inclusive on both ends?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN x AND y is equivalent to a >= x AND a <= y — both bounds are inclusive.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT * FROM t return?
questions.explanation: * expands to every column of the table(s) in FROM, in declared order.

questions.prompt: In SELECT price * qty AS amount, what does AS amount do?
questions.explanation: AS assigns an output column label; the label exists only in the result and can be referenced by ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: A query uses SELECT a + b total FROM t ORDER BY total. Why is this valid?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY can reference output column labels assigned with AS in the same SELECT.

questions.prompt: Where can an output column label assigned by AS NOT be used directly?
questions.explanation: WHERE is logically evaluated before the select list, so select-list labels are not in scope there; a WHERE must repeat the expression.

questions.prompt: By default, where do NULL values sort in PostgreSQL ORDER BY ... ASC?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL sorts NULLs as larger than any non-null value, so they come last for ASC and first for DESC unless NULLS FIRST/LAST says otherwise.

questions.prompt: Which clause forces NULL values to sort before non-NULL values in ascending order?
questions.explanation: NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST explicitly control null placement, overriding the default (nulls sort larger than non-nulls).

questions.prompt: ORDER BY 2 refers to what?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY accepts output column numbers; 2 means the second select-list item.

questions.prompt: A query orders employees by name. Two installations return different orderings for accented names. What most likely explains this?
questions.explanation: Text ordering follows the column's collation; different collation settings produce different orderings for non-ASCII text.

questions.prompt: Which pair returns at most 5 rows, skipping the first 10?
questions.explanation: LIMIT n caps the row count; OFFSET m skips m rows first. PostgreSQL also supports the SQL-standard FETCH FIRST ... ROWS ONLY form.

questions.prompt: Why should a LIMIT query almost always include ORDER BY?
questions.explanation: LIMIT only bounds how many rows are returned; which rows arrive is arbitrary unless ORDER BY fixes an ordering.

questions.prompt: What does LIMIT ALL mean in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: LIMIT ALL (or LIMIT NULL) explicitly requests no limit, which PostgreSQL accepts for compatibility.

questions.prompt: SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM employees does what?
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows; SELECT DISTINCT dept keeps one row per distinct dept value.

questions.prompt: How does DISTINCT treat NULL values?
questions.explanation: For DISTINCT, NULLs are treated as duplicates of one another — a column of only NULLs yields one row.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT DISTINCT ON (dept) dept, name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY dept, salary DESC return?
questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group defined by its expressions; ORDER BY must lead with those expressions to determine which row is 'first'.

questions.prompt: For DISTINCT ON (dept) to predictably return the newest row per dept, the ORDER BY must start with:
questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON requires the leftmost ORDER BY expressions to match the DISTINCT ON expressions; remaining keys pick which row survives.

questions.prompt: UNION (without ALL) of two SELECTs produces:
questions.explanation: UNION computes the set union and eliminates duplicates; UNION ALL keeps duplicates.

questions.prompt: When might UNION ALL be preferable to UNION?
questions.explanation: UNION must sort or hash rows to deduplicate; UNION ALL just concatenates results, which is cheaper.

questions.prompt: INTERSECT returns rows that are:
questions.explanation: INTERSECT is the set intersection; EXCEPT is the set difference (first minus second).

questions.prompt: For two SELECTs combined with UNION to be valid, they must:
questions.explanation: Set operations require equal column counts and compatible (coercible) data types in each position.

questions.prompt: In q1 UNION q2 INTERSECT q3, which operation binds first in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: INTERSECT has higher precedence; UNION and EXCEPT have equal precedence and associate left-to-right. Parentheses override.

questions.prompt: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 1 returns how many rows?
questions.explanation: UNION ALL preserves duplicates, so the three identical rows all survive.

questions.prompt: How do you test whether a column is NULL in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: = NULL is never true (it yields NULL); the correct test is IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL).

questions.prompt: Given x = 5 and y = NULL, what does x = y OR NOT (x = y) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: x = y is NULL; NOT NULL is still NULL; NULL OR NULL is NULL — the law of excluded middle fails under three-valued logic.

questions.prompt: true OR NULL evaluates to:
questions.explanation: OR returns true when either operand is true regardless of the other — true OR NULL is true.

questions.prompt: A NOT IN list contains a NULL: WHERE a NOT IN (1, 2, NULL). For a = 3 the result is:
questions.explanation: a NOT IN (...) compares against every element; comparing against NULL yields NULL, and NULL AND NULL collapses to NULL — a classic NOT IN/NULL trap.

questions.prompt: IS DISTINCT FROM differs from <> how?
questions.explanation: IS DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe inequality; it never returns NULL.

questions.prompt: A table has col values {1, 2, NULL}. SELECT count(col) and count(*) return respectively:
questions.explanation: count(col) skips NULL inputs; count(*) counts all rows regardless of nulls.

questions.prompt: COALESCE(a, b, c) returns:
questions.explanation: COALESCE evaluates arguments left to right and returns the first non-NULL one.

questions.prompt: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when:
questions.explanation: NULLIF is shorthand for CASE WHEN a = b THEN NULL ELSE a END — commonly used to avoid division by zero.

questions.prompt: SELECT CASE WHEN qty > 10 THEN 'bulk' WHEN qty > 0 THEN 'normal' ELSE 'none' END — for qty = 15 the result is:
questions.explanation: CASE evaluates WHEN branches in order and returns the first true one, so qty = 15 stops at 'bulk'.

questions.prompt: Which CASE form compares one expression to several candidate values: CASE x WHEN 1 THEN ... WHEN 2 THEN ...?
questions.explanation: Simple CASE compares the operand to each WHEN value; searched CASE evaluates independent boolean conditions.

questions.prompt: What happens to CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 'two' END in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: CASE must resolve to one type via type-unification rules; an unknown-type literal is forced to the branch type and 'two' cannot become an integer.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate returns the number of input rows for which the expression is not NULL?
questions.explanation: count(expr) counts non-NULL inputs; count(*) counts all rows.

questions.prompt: What does avg(salary) FILTER (WHERE dept = 'eng') compute?
questions.explanation: FILTER restricts an aggregate's input rows without filtering the query's output rows.

questions.prompt: GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((dept), ()) produces:
questions.explanation: Grouping sets let multiple groupings (here dept, and the empty set = grand total) be computed together.

questions.prompt: ROLLUP(a, b) is equivalent to which grouping sets?
questions.explanation: ROLLUP produces the prefix chain: full grouping, then progressively dropping rightmost columns, ending at the grand total.

questions.prompt: string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) does what?
questions.explanation: string_agg aggregates text inputs into a delimited string; ORDER BY inside the aggregate controls concatenation order.

questions.prompt: Why is SELECT dept, name, max(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept an error in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Every select-list column must be grouped, aggregated, or functionally dependent on a grouped primary key. name is none of these here.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL allows SELECT id, name FROM emp GROUP BY id when id is the primary key because:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL implements the SQL rule: columns functionally dependent on a grouped unique key need no aggregate.

questions.prompt: LEFT JOIN returns which rows?
questions.explanation: LEFT [OUTER] JOIN keeps unmatched left rows, padding right-side columns with NULL.

questions.prompt: To find employees with NO matching department row, the classic pattern is:
questions.explanation: Unmatched left rows get NULL right columns, so the IS NULL filter isolates them — the anti-join pattern.

questions.prompt: CROSS JOIN between a 5-row and a 3-row table returns:
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN is the Cartesian product: 5 × 3 = 15 rows.

questions.prompt: In a LEFT JOIN, adding a right-table predicate to WHERE (e.g. WHERE r.x > 0) typically:
questions.explanation: Padded NULLs fail the right-table predicate, removing the very rows LEFT JOIN was meant to preserve — a common bug.

questions.prompt: FULL OUTER JOIN between A (with unmatched a-rows) and B (with unmatched b-rows) returns:
questions.explanation: FULL JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both tables, NULL-padding whichever side lacks a match.

questions.prompt: NATURAL JOIN joins on:
questions.explanation: NATURAL JOIN equates every same-named column pair — convenient but fragile when schemas evolve.

questions.prompt: What does a LATERAL join allow that a regular FROM item does not?
questions.explanation: LATERAL lets a FROM subquery or set-returning function reference earlier FROM items — evaluated per-row like a foreach.

questions.prompt: A WITH clause (common table expression) primarily provides:
questions.explanation: WITH defines temporary named relations for the statement — improving readability of complex queries.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 12+, a non-recursive CTE referenced once is by default:
questions.explanation: Since v12, singly-referenced non-recursive CTEs are folded into the query; MATERIALIZED/NOT MATERIALIZED hints and multiple references change this.

questions.prompt: To force a CTE to be computed once regardless of references, write:
questions.explanation: AS MATERIALIZED forces materialization (the pre-v12 behavior); NOT MATERIALIZED requests inlining.

questions.prompt: Data-modifying CTEs (WITH x AS (DELETE ... RETURNING *) SELECT ...) are notable because:
questions.explanation: WITH may contain DML; its RETURNING output becomes visible to the main statement — all in one statement.

questions.prompt: A working WITH RECURSIVE query must contain:
questions.explanation: Recursive CTEs evaluate a base term, then repeatedly evaluate the recursive term feeding its output back until no new rows appear.

questions.prompt: Choosing UNION instead of UNION ALL inside a recursive CTE:
questions.explanation: UNION removes duplicates — on cyclic graphs this termination property is essential, at the cost of dedup work.

questions.prompt: The SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY ... SET col clause in a recursive CTE provides:
questions.explanation: SEARCH (and CYCLE) clauses generate synthetic columns marking traversal order/cycle detection per the standard.

questions.prompt: For recursive CTEs over graphs that may contain cycles, PostgreSQL supports which built-in safeguard besides UNION?
questions.explanation: The CYCLE clause marks repeated rows and suppresses their re-expansion — the standard mechanism for cyclic data.

questions.prompt: The key difference between a window function and a regular aggregate is:
questions.explanation: Aggregates collapse groups to one row; window functions compute per-row over a window of related rows via OVER.

questions.prompt: row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) computes:
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY splits rows into groups; row_number numbers each partition's rows by the given ordering.

questions.prompt: rank() versus dense_rank() differ when ties exist because:
questions.explanation: With two rows tied at rank 1, next rank() is 3 but next dense_rank() is 2.

questions.prompt: lag(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) returns, for each row:
questions.explanation: lag/lead access rows before/after the current row within the window ordering; missing positions yield NULL.

questions.prompt: Why can't a window function call appear in a WHERE clause?
questions.explanation: Windows operate on the virtual table produced by FROM/WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING; they are only legal in SELECT and ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: In sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY ts), the default frame is:
questions.explanation: With ORDER BY present, the default frame runs from partition start through the current row including peers (equal sort keys).

questions.prompt: Which PostgreSQL type stores exact arbitrary-precision decimal numbers like monetary amounts?
questions.explanation: numeric stores exact decimal precision up to the declared precision/scale; float types are inexact binary approximations.

questions.prompt: What is the result type of SELECT 7 / 2 in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Dividing two integers performs integer division (7/2 = 3). Cast an operand to numeric/real for fractional results.

questions.prompt: serial primarily provides:
questions.explanation: serial is notational convenience: integer + NOT NULL + a sequence + DEFAULT nextval(...). Identity columns are the SQL-standard alternative.

questions.prompt: Which is a documented caveat of real / double precision types?
questions.explanation: Floating-point types store binary approximations; equality and financial arithmetic should use numeric.

questions.prompt: smallint, integer, bigint use how much storage respectively?
questions.explanation: The integer family is smallint (2 bytes), integer (4 bytes), bigint (8 bytes) with corresponding ranges.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, the practical difference between varchar(n) and text is:
questions.explanation: Both types share storage/performance characteristics; the only difference is that varchar(n) validates maximum length.

questions.prompt: char(5) storing 'ab' produces:
questions.explanation: character(n) is blank-padded to its declared length; the padding is semantically insignificant in comparisons but visible in length-sensitive operations.

questions.prompt: Inserting a 6-character string into varchar(5) with no explicit cast:
questions.explanation: varchar(n) rejects over-length input (unless explicit truncation is requested via cast).

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT accepted as a boolean literal input in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Boolean accepts true/false, t/f, yes/no, on/off, 1/0 (as quoted strings or keywords) — not arbitrary numbers like 2.

questions.prompt: A boolean column can hold how many distinct states?
questions.explanation: SQL booleans are three-valued: TRUE, FALSE, or NULL representing unknown.

questions.prompt: IS TRUE differs from = true in that:
questions.explanation: The IS boolean tests normalize NULL to false; col IS TRUE on a NULL row yields false, while col = true yields NULL.

questions.prompt: timestamp with time zone (timestamptz) stores:
questions.explanation: timestamptz stores an absolute UTC instant; display is rendered in the session TimeZone. The zone itself is not retained.

questions.prompt: The interval type represents:
questions.explanation: interval stores a quantity of time for arithmetic like now() + interval '1 week'.

questions.prompt: Subtracting two timestamp values (ts2 - ts1) yields:
questions.explanation: timestamp - timestamp produces an interval; timestamp - interval produces a timestamp.

questions.prompt: CURRENT_DATE inside a transaction returns:
questions.explanation: CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and now() are transaction-start times — stable within one transaction; clock_timestamp() gives actual wall clock.

questions.prompt: The core storage difference between json and jsonb is:
questions.explanation: json stores raw input text (preserving whitespace, key order, duplicate keys); jsonb stores a binary decomposition enabling fast access and indexing.

questions.prompt: When a jsonb document contains duplicate object keys:
questions.explanation: jsonb normalizes on input — later duplicate keys win; json text preserves them verbatim.

questions.prompt: doc -> 'name' versus doc ->> 'name' differ in that:
questions.explanation: -> yields a JSON value (still typed json), while ->> extracts the textual representation — e.g. for comparisons to plain text.

questions.prompt: Which jsonb-only capability enables efficient key/containment lookups at scale?
questions.explanation: jsonb supports GIN indexes (jsonb_ops/jsonb_path_ops) for containment ?, ?|, ?& and @> queries; json cannot.

questions.prompt: The containment operator data @> '{"a":1}'::jsonb tests whether:
questions.explanation: @> checks jsonb containment — left contains right at the top level; combined with GIN it is the idiomatic document query.

questions.prompt: Querying jsonb_path_ops vs jsonb_ops GIN indexes differ mainly in:
questions.explanation: jsonb_path_ops produces a smaller index and supports @>, @?, @@; unlike jsonb_ops, it does not support the ?, ?|, and ?& key-existence operators.

questions.prompt: The literal '{1,2,3}'::integer[] represents:
questions.explanation: Curly-brace literals with a cast denote array values; ARRAY[1,2,3] is equivalent.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL array subscripting (arr[1]) is:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL arrays default to lower bound 1; arr[1] returns the first element.

questions.prompt: unnest(ARRAY[1,2,3]) used in FROM produces:
questions.explanation: unnest expands an array into a set of rows — the standard way to turn array elements into queryable rows.

questions.prompt: The containment operator tags @> ARRAY['sql'] on an array column checks:
questions.explanation: @> on arrays tests left-contains-right elements; indexable via GIN.

questions.prompt: val = ANY(arr) versus val = ALL(arr):
questions.explanation: = ANY is the array equivalent of IN; = ALL requires equality with every element (and = ANY is what IN expands to).

questions.prompt: int4range(1, 10) by default includes which bounds?
questions.explanation: Range constructors default to [) — lower inclusive, upper exclusive; explicit '[1,10]' notation overrides.

questions.prompt: The && operator on ranges tests:
questions.explanation: && returns true when ranges overlap; @> and <@ test containment, and -|- tests adjacency.

questions.prompt: A multirange (e.g. int4multirange) is:
questions.explanation: Multiranges hold multiple disjoint ranges, automatically sorted and merged — e.g. several booking windows in one value.

questions.prompt: The two cast syntaxes PostgreSQL supports are:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL accepts the SQL-standard CAST and its native :: shorthand.

questions.prompt: An implicit cast in PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: Casts have three contexts — implicit (automatic), assignment (on insert/update), explicit (CAST/::); safe conversions like int→numeric are implicit.

questions.prompt: SELECT '10' + 5 evaluates to:
questions.explanation: Unknown-type literals take the type required by context; + forces integer, so '10' is parsed as 10.

questions.prompt: SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 'a' fails because:
questions.explanation: Set-operation columns are resolved like CASE branches; unknown 'a' takes the sibling type and fails integer parsing.

questions.prompt: A column's collation in PostgreSQL determines:
questions.explanation: Collation defines sort order and comparison rules (per the OS/ICU provider); it is separate from encoding.

questions.prompt: To make ORDER BY use a different collation than the column default for one query:
questions.explanation: A COLLATE clause on an expression overrides the collation used for that comparison/sort.

questions.prompt: A nondeterministic collation is one where:
questions.explanation: E.g. a case-insensitive collation treats 'a' = 'A' — comparisons are nondeterministic w.r.t. bytes, which affects uniqueness and pattern ops.

questions.prompt: CREATE DOMAIN email AS text CHECK (VALUE ~ '.+@.+') creates:
questions.explanation: Domains wrap a base type with constraints; every column using the domain inherits the checks — a central rule for e.g. email validation.

questions.prompt: Which is a documented caveat of domains vs plain columns?
questions.explanation: Domain checks fire on assignment, but the optimizer largely treats the value as the base type; NOT NULL and CHECK propagate at DDL.

questions.prompt: 'Hello' || ' ' || 'World' returns:
questions.explanation: || concatenates strings (and arrays); non-string operands get cast under the operator rules.

questions.prompt: substring('PostgreSQL' from 1 for 6) returns:
questions.explanation: substring(x from start for len) is the SQL form; position is 1-based, giving the first 6 characters.

questions.prompt: position('SQL' in 'PostgreSQL') returns:
questions.explanation: position is 1-based: 'PostgreSQL' = P1 o2 s3 t4 g5 r6 e7 S8 Q9 L10, so 'SQL' begins at position 8.

questions.prompt: upper('abc'), lower('ABC') and initcap('hello world') return respectively:
questions.explanation: upper/lower convert case of the whole string; initcap capitalizes the first letter of each word.

questions.prompt: trim(both 'x' from 'xxhelloxx') returns:
questions.explanation: trim(both chars from string) strips the given characters from both ends; btrim is the function form.

questions.prompt: left('PostgreSQL', 4) and right('PostgreSQL', 3) return:
questions.explanation: left(str,n) takes the first n chars; right(str,n) the last n. Negative n drops |n| from the opposite end.

questions.prompt: round(2.5) and trunc(2.5) return:
questions.explanation: round performs nearest-integer rounding (ties away from zero on numeric); trunc drops the fraction toward zero.

questions.prompt: mod(10, 3) returns:
questions.explanation: mod(n,m) returns the remainder of n divided by m — equivalent to the % operator.

questions.prompt: floor(2.7), ceil(2.1) and sign(-5) return:
questions.explanation: floor rounds down, ceil rounds up, sign returns -1/0/1 by the value's sign.

questions.prompt: div(9, 2) versus 9 / 2 in PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: div truncates toward zero like integer division; numeric / on two integers also truncates.

questions.prompt: extract(year from date '2024-03-15') returns:
questions.explanation: extract(field from value) pulls a numeric date/time component; year gives 2024.

questions.prompt: date_trunc('month', timestamp '2024-03-15 14:30:00') returns:
questions.explanation: date_trunc zeroes out fields below the given precision — month truncates to the first of the month at midnight.

questions.prompt: age(timestamp '2000-01-01', timestamp '1990-06-15') conceptually returns:
questions.explanation: age(ts1, ts2) returns ts1 minus ts2 as a years/months/days interval; single-argument age() measures from current_date.

questions.prompt: now() versus clock_timestamp() inside one transaction:
questions.explanation: Transaction-time functions (now, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, transaction_timestamp) are stable; clock_timestamp and statement_timestamp track real time.

questions.prompt: name LIKE 'Jo%' matches which of these?
questions.explanation: % matches any sequence of zero or more characters; _ matches exactly one. 'Jo%' anchors the start.

questions.prompt: ILIKE differs from LIKE in that ILIKE:
questions.explanation: ILIKE is PostgreSQL's case-insensitive LIKE — a non-standard extension that respects the active collation.

questions.prompt: name ~ '^A[0-9]+$' uses which matching facility?
questions.explanation: ~ applies a POSIX regex match; ^ and $ anchor, [0-9]+ matches one or more digits.

questions.prompt: How do you escape a literal % inside a LIKE pattern?
questions.explanation: Backslash escapes the wildcard meaning; ESCAPE 'x' designates another escape character.

questions.prompt: Under the pattern 'a_%', which value does NOT LIKE 'a_%' keep (i.e., which value fails to match)?
questions.explanation: The pattern requires literal 'a', then exactly one arbitrary character, then any tail. 'ba_' fails the leading 'a'; 'ab' and 'a1b' and 'a_b' all match.

questions.prompt: tsvector and tsquery represent:
questions.explanation: tsvector stores a sorted set of normalized lexemes from a document; tsquery encodes the search terms/boolean ops.

questions.prompt: doc @@ to_tsquery('sql & database') is true when:
questions.explanation: @@ is the match operator; & is AND, | is OR, ! is NOT, <-> is followed-by (phrase).

questions.prompt: For searching 'rates' and matching 'rate', 'rated' etc., tsvector normalization matters because:
questions.explanation: to_tsvector normalizes words to lexemes (e.g. stemming 'rates'→'rate') so inflected forms match — the language config drives this.

questions.prompt: To make @@ queries on a tsvector column fast at scale, the recommended index is:
questions.explanation: GIN indexes are designed for tsvector @@ lookups (and jsonb/array containment); a B-tree on text doesn't help lexeme matching.

questions.prompt: CREATE TABLE t (a int) then DROP TABLE t does what?
questions.explanation: DROP TABLE removes the table, its data, indexes, and dependent objects (subject to CASCADE/RESTRICT).

questions.prompt: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE creates a table that:
questions.explanation: TEMP tables are session-private, auto-dropped at session end (or earlier with ON COMMIT options), and use a temp schema.

questions.prompt: An UNLOGGED table trades what for speed?
questions.explanation: UNLOGGED skips WAL writing (faster loads) but the table is reset after a crash — suitable for cache/staging data.

questions.prompt: A column declared price numeric DEFAULT 9.99 means:
questions.explanation: DEFAULT supplies the value used when INSERT omits the column (or uses DEFAULT keyword).

questions.prompt: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY versus GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY differ in:
questions.explanation: ALWAYS enforces sequence-generated values (overridable only via OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE); BY DEFAULT permits explicit values.

questions.prompt: Why is GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY preferred over serial in modern PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Identity is standard SQL, uses sequences under the hood, and distinguishes ALWAYS vs BY DEFAULT behavior; serial predates it.

questions.prompt: A stored generated column total int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * price) STORED:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports STORED generated columns computed on write; they cannot be assigned in INSERT/UPDATE.

questions.prompt: The generation expression of a generated column must be:
questions.explanation: Generation expressions must be immutable and may only use the row's own non-generated columns.

questions.prompt: A NOT NULL constraint enforces:
questions.explanation: NOT NULL rejects NULL on insert/update — distinct from UNIQUE, which permits NULLs (multiple, by default).

questions.prompt: CHECK (price > 0) on a column:
questions.explanation: CHECK requires the expression be true or NULL (unknown passes); it is evaluated on each write.

questions.prompt: Under default PostgreSQL semantics, a UNIQUE column allows:
questions.explanation: Standard SQL treats NULLs as distinct for uniqueness; PostgreSQL 15+ offers UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT to change this.

questions.prompt: CHECK constraints that reference other rows or subqueries:
questions.explanation: CHECK expressions must be immutable and per-row; cross-row rules need triggers or exclusion constraints.

questions.prompt: A PRIMARY KEY in PostgreSQL implicitly creates:
questions.explanation: PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL enforced by a unique index.

questions.prompt: FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept(id) ON DELETE CASCADE means:
questions.explanation: ON DELETE actions: CASCADE deletes children; SET NULL/DEFAULT resets them; RESTRICT/NO ACTION forbid it.

questions.prompt: ON UPDATE CASCADE on a foreign key does what when the parent's key changes?
questions.explanation: CASCADE updates children to follow the parent's changed key — one of the referential actions.

questions.prompt: A DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED foreign key is checked:
questions.explanation: Deferrable constraints postpone enforcement to COMMIT — essential for cyclic references and bulk loads.

questions.prompt: Why must a referenced column set be UNIQUE (or PRIMARY KEY) for a FOREIGN KEY?
questions.explanation: An FK must reference a unique column combination so every child maps to at most one parent.

questions.prompt: ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c int DEFAULT 0 on a large existing table:
questions.explanation: Constant/immutable defaults avoid a table rewrite in modern PostgreSQL — existing rows read the catalog default.

questions.prompt: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN TYPE on a big table generally:
questions.explanation: Type changes that alter storage force a rewrite and block concurrent access — a classic migration hazard.

questions.prompt: search_path controls:
questions.explanation: Unqualified names resolve against search_path schemas in order; objects may be created in the first listed schema.

questions.prompt: Two tables can share the same name orders if:
questions.explanation: Schemas are namespaces; sales.orders and audit.orders can coexist.

questions.prompt: Since PostgreSQL 15, default public-schema privileges changed so that:
questions.explanation: v15 tightened defaults: public schema creation rights were removed from PUBLIC to reduce surprise writes.

questions.prompt: A view in PostgreSQL is:
questions.explanation: Views store a query, not data. Materialized views are the stored-result counterpart.

questions.prompt: A simple updatable view (one table, no aggregates) supports INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE because:
questions.explanation: Automatically-updatable views translate DML to the base relation when rules are met; otherwise INSTEAD OF triggers are needed.

questions.prompt: WITH CHECK OPTION on an updatable view enforces:
questions.explanation: CHECK OPTION prevents INSERT/UPDATE through the view from producing rows invisible to the view itself.

questions.prompt: A materialized view differs from a regular view in that it:
questions.explanation: Materialized views cache results for fast reads at the cost of staleness; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW recomputes.

source_refs.title: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW
source_refs.section: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW

questions.prompt: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY:
questions.explanation: CONCURRENTLY keeps the view readable during refresh (using a unique index for diff application).

source_refs.title: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW
source_refs.section: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW

questions.prompt: Declarative partitioning in PostgreSQL is declared via:
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY creates a partitioned parent; children are created AS PARTITION OF with bounds.

questions.prompt: Partition pruning means:
questions.explanation: When the partition key appears in the WHERE clause, the planner eliminates non-matching partitions from the scan.

questions.prompt: A DEFAULT partition exists to:
questions.explanation: Without a default partition, rows outside all defined bounds fail at insert; the default partition absorbs them.

questions.prompt: For declaratively partitioned tables, a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint must:
questions.explanation: Uniqueness is enforced per-partition, so the key must cover the partition columns to guarantee global uniqueness.

questions.prompt: INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (1, 2), (3, 4) inserts:
questions.explanation: INSERT accepts a comma-separated list of row values.

questions.prompt: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name means:
questions.explanation: EXCLUDED is the row that would have been inserted; ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE applies it to the conflicting existing row (upsert).

questions.prompt: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING:
questions.explanation: DO NOTHING makes an otherwise-failing insert a no-op — the idempotent insert pattern.

questions.prompt: DELETE FROM t RETURNING id gives back:
questions.explanation: RETURNING works on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE, exposing the affected rows' values (old for DELETE, new for UPDATE).

questions.prompt: UPDATE t SET a = a + 1 FROM other WHERE t.id = other.id uses:
questions.explanation: UPDATE ... FROM lets another table's columns feed the SET and match rows — PostgreSQL's join-update syntax.

questions.prompt: DELETE FROM t USING u WHERE t.id = u.id does:
questions.explanation: USING is to DELETE what FROM is to UPDATE — auxiliary relations for matching.

questions.prompt: MERGE INTO target USING source ON cond WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT:
questions.explanation: MERGE (SQL standard, PG 15+) performs matched/not-matched actions combining insert, update, delete in one pass.

questions.prompt: A documented MERGE caveat versus ON CONFLICT upsert is:
questions.explanation: MERGE's source-driven WHEN clauses differ from ON CONFLICT's speculative-insert path; concurrent workloads can still see unique violations.

questions.prompt: A transaction's atomicity guarantee means:
questions.explanation: COMMIT applies everything; ROLLBACK or failure undoes everything — the 'all or nothing' property.

questions.prompt: SAVEPOINT inside a transaction allows:
questions.explanation: SAVEPOINT marks a point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes later work without aborting the whole transaction.

questions.prompt: In autocommit mode (no explicit BEGIN), each statement:
questions.explanation: Absent BEGIN, PostgreSQL wraps each statement in an implicit transaction.

questions.prompt: After an error mid-transaction (e.g. constraint violation), PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: An error poisons the transaction ('current transaction is aborted'); only rollback-to-savepoint or full rollback recovers.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is:
questions.explanation: Read Committed is the default; PostgreSQL treats Read Uncommitted as Read Committed internally.

questions.prompt: Under Read Committed in PostgreSQL, two identical SELECTs in one transaction can return different rows because:
questions.explanation: Read Committed takes a per-statement snapshot — committed changes between statements become visible (non-repeatable read allowed).

questions.prompt: Which phenomena does PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevent?
questions.explanation: PG Repeatable Read uses a transaction-long snapshot, preventing dirty/non-repeatable/phantom; serialization anomalies remain possible.

questions.prompt: Requesting SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED in PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL implements no dirty reads; the standard's minimum guarantee is Read Committed, so it maps to that.

questions.prompt: Serializable isolation in PostgreSQL is implemented by:
questions.explanation: Serializable Snapshot Isolation tracks rw-antidependencies; transactions forming dangerous structures get serialization failures.

questions.prompt: Under MVCC, readers in PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: MVCC keeps multiple row versions so each transaction sees a snapshot — reads never wait on row writes and vice versa.

questions.prompt: An UPDATE in PostgreSQL physically:
questions.explanation: MVCC updates write new tuples; dead tuples accumulate until VACUUM reclaims them — the reason vacuum exists.

questions.prompt: Which statement about visibility is correct?
questions.explanation: Visibility = snapshot at begin (per-transaction or per-statement) + own writes; others' in-flight work stays invisible.

questions.prompt: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE does what?
questions.explanation: FOR UPDATE takes row-level write locks (like a DELETE would) — the read-modify-write pattern's locking primitive.

questions.prompt: A deadlock occurs when:
questions.explanation: Deadlock detector (deadlock_timeout) finds lock cycles and cancels one participant with a deadlock error.

questions.prompt: SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE versus FOR UPDATE:
questions.explanation: Lock strengths: FOR KEY SHARE < FOR SHARE < FOR NO KEY UPDATE < FOR UPDATE — finer modes reduce contention.

questions.prompt: Advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock) differ from row/table locks in that they:
questions.explanation: Advisory locks are cooperative semaphores keyed by app-defined numbers — useful for app-level mutual exclusion.

questions.prompt: An index primarily helps by:
questions.explanation: Indexes map keys to row locations; selective predicates avoid full scans — at the cost of write/space overhead.

questions.prompt: A multicolumn B-tree index on (a, b) most directly supports:
questions.explanation: B-tree keys are ordered left-to-right; equality/range on leftmost prefixes use the index efficiently.

questions.prompt: A partial index WHERE status = 'open' is appropriate when:
questions.explanation: Partial indexes cover only predicate-matching rows — smaller/faster when hot queries match the predicate.

questions.prompt: An index on lower(email) helps:
questions.explanation: Expression indexes index a function's result; the query must use the same expression to benefit.

questions.prompt: An index-only scan avoids visiting the table when:
questions.explanation: Index-only scans return index data directly, but MVCC requires the visibility map to confirm rows are visible to all.

questions.prompt: Which workload symptom does NOT fit 'add an index'?
questions.explanation: Indexes cost write overhead; heavy-insert workloads suffer more indexes. The other symptoms are classic index wins.

questions.prompt: The default and most general-purpose PostgreSQL index type is:
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX defaults to B-tree, good for <, <=, =, >=, >, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL and ordered scans.

questions.prompt: GIN indexes are best suited for:
questions.explanation: GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes element→row postings, powering @>, ?, @@ searches.

questions.prompt: BRIN indexes work best when:
questions.explanation: BRIN stores per-block-range min/max — tiny and fast when correlation exists, useless on uncorrelated data.

questions.prompt: GiST versus SP-GiST:
questions.explanation: Both are extensible frameworks: GiST for overlapping-region types (ranges, geometry), SP-GiST for partitioned spaces.

questions.prompt: In EXPLAIN output, 'cost=0.00..183.34 rows=10000' the two numbers are:
questions.explanation: Costs are planner units (roughly page-fetches); the first is cost until first row output, second is total.

questions.prompt: EXPLAIN ANALYZE differs from plain EXPLAIN in that it:
questions.explanation: ANALYZE runs the statement (DML affects data! — wrap in transaction), showing actual vs estimated rows per node.

questions.prompt: A 'Seq Scan' plan node means:
questions.explanation: Sequential scan isn't inherently bad — when most rows match or the table is small, it beats index access.

questions.prompt: Bitmap Heap Scan + Bitmap Index Scan typically appears when:
questions.explanation: For moderate selectivity, PostgreSQL collects TIDs into a bitmap then reads heap in physical order — between seq and index scan.

questions.prompt: Estimated rows=10 vs actual rows=500000 in EXPLAIN ANALYZE suggests:
questions.explanation: Plan quality depends on selectivity estimates from ANALYZE statistics; big skew → bad join/scan choices.

questions.prompt: ANALYZE collects what for the planner?
questions.explanation: ANALYZE samples each table building pg_statistic entries; autovacuum also auto-analyzes changed tables.

questions.prompt: default_statistics_target / column statistics targets control:
questions.explanation: Raising the target improves plan quality on skewed data but slows ANALYZE and planner work.

questions.prompt: Correlated columns (e.g. city within state) fool the planner because:
questions.explanation: Extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS: ndistinct, dependencies, mcv) fix multi-column correlation misestimates.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, 'user' and 'group' are both:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL unifies users/groups as roles; LOGIN attribute permits connections, membership gives inherited rights.

questions.prompt: Role attributes like CREATEDB and CREATEROLE are:
questions.explanation: Attributes (LOGIN, SUPERUSER, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLS) are role flags granted at CREATE/ALTER ROLE.

questions.prompt: With INHERIT (default), a member role:
questions.explanation: INHERIT makes membership rights immediate; NOINHERIT requires explicit SET ROLE to assume the group role.

questions.prompt: GRANT SELECT ON t TO analyst permits:
questions.explanation: Object privileges are per-object-type action rights; WITH GRANT OPTION would additionally allow re-granting.

questions.prompt: GRANT ... WITH GRANT OPTION means the grantee:
questions.explanation: Grant option delegates administration of that privilege; REVOKE cascades through dependent grants.

questions.prompt: Column-level privileges (GRANT SELECT (a, b) ON t) allow:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports per-column SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/REFERENCES grants for fine-grained access.

questions.prompt: ALTER TABLE t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY without any policy means:
questions.explanation: With RLS enabled and no policy, a default-deny applies; the owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE is set.

questions.prompt: A policy's USING clause versus WITH CHECK clause:
questions.explanation: USING(expression) determines existing-row visibility; WITH CHECK(expression) constrains new/modified row values.

questions.prompt: Permissive versus restrictive policies combine:
questions.explanation: Rows must pass at least one permissive AND all restrictive policies — mixing gives AND-of-restrictive with OR-of-permissive.

questions.prompt: Who bypasses row security by default?
questions.explanation: Owner bypass needs ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY to close; superusers/BYPASSRLS always bypass.

questions.prompt: CREATE FUNCTION f(int) RETURNS int LANGUAGE sql AS 'SELECT $1 * 2' defines:
questions.explanation: SQL functions evaluate expressions/queries; $1 is the first argument.

questions.prompt: IMMUTABLE / STABLE / VOLATILE function categories describe:
questions.explanation: IMMUTABLE = same input→same output forever (index-safe); STABLE = constant within a statement; VOLATILE = anything.

questions.prompt: Why must an indexed expression like lower(email) only use IMMUTABLE functions?
questions.explanation: If the expression could change without a row update, index entries would lie — PostgreSQL enforces immutability.

questions.prompt: RETURNS SETOF int and RETURNS TABLE(id int, name text) both mean:
questions.explanation: Set-returning functions produce rows; TABLE(...) names the output columns.

questions.prompt: SECURITY DEFINER on a function means:
questions.explanation: SECURITY DEFINER functions run as owner — powerful for controlled access but dangerous if they take unvalidated input.

questions.prompt: A PL/pgSQL function body is structured as:
questions.explanation: PL/pgSQL is block-structured: optional label, DECLARE section, BEGIN/END body — blocks nest.

questions.prompt: Inside PL/pgSQL, assignment uses:
questions.explanation: := is the classic assignment; plain = is also accepted for assignment.

questions.prompt: FOUND in PL/pgSQL reports:
questions.explanation: The boolean FOUND is set after SELECT INTO, DML, FOR loops etc. — the idiom for 'did my statement do anything'.

questions.prompt: EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation THEN ... in a BEGIN block:
questions.explanation: EXCEPTION handlers trap matching SQLSTATE conditions; the failed substatement rolls back to the block start.

questions.prompt: %TYPE and %ROWTYPE in declarations:
questions.explanation: DECLARE v emp.name%TYPE pins v to that column's type; %ROWTYPE captures whole-row structure.

questions.prompt: CREATE PROCEDURE differs from CREATE FUNCTION mainly because procedures:
questions.explanation: Procedures (PG 11+) run via CALL and may perform transaction control — functions cannot.

questions.prompt: To run a procedure p(5):
questions.explanation: CALL invokes procedures; SELECT invokes functions.

questions.prompt: A BEFORE INSERT row trigger function returning NULL means:
questions.explanation: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger cancels the operation for that row; returning NEW proceeds.

questions.prompt: Inside a row-level trigger, NEW and OLD refer to:
questions.explanation: Trigger functions get NEW (proposed row) and/or OLD (existing row) depending on TG_OP.

questions.prompt: FOR EACH ROW versus FOR EACH STATEMENT triggers:
questions.explanation: Granularity choice: per-row logic (audit columns, validation) vs once-per-statement summary work.

questions.prompt: INSTEAD OF triggers exist primarily for:
questions.explanation: INSTEAD OF triggers intercept view DML; the function performs the real base-table operations.

questions.prompt: The classic audit-trail pattern (BEFORE UPDATE, set NEW.updated_at = now()) works because:
questions.explanation: BEFORE row triggers may rewrite fields of NEW — the canonical way to stamp audit columns.

questions.prompt: shared_buffers controls:
questions.explanation: shared_buffers is the main in-memory data cache; too small starves caching, too big wastes OS cache.

questions.prompt: work_mem is consumed:
questions.explanation: work_mem bounds each sort/hash node; complex plans multiply it — over-aggressive values cause memory pressure.

questions.prompt: ALTER SYSTEM SET x = y writes to:
questions.explanation: ALTER SYSTEM persists to postgresql.auto.conf (included by postgresql.conf); some params need restart or reload.

questions.prompt: The main reason PostgreSQL needs VACUUM is:
questions.explanation: MVCC retains dead tuples until VACUUM marks their space reusable — without it, tables bloat unboundedly.

questions.prompt: Standard VACUUM versus VACUUM FULL:
questions.explanation: Regular VACUUM is online (table stays usable); FULL compacts to minimum size but blocks all access.

questions.prompt: Autovacuum is triggered primarily by:
questions.explanation: The autovacuum daemon launches workers when dead-tuple estimates exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + scale_factor×rows.

questions.prompt: Transaction ID wraparound protection requires vacuuming because:
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL uses ~4B XIDs; VACUUM FREEZE marks old tuples permanently visible before wraparound would corrupt visibility.

questions.prompt: pg_dump produces:
questions.explanation: pg_dump emits SQL (or custom-format) for one DB; pg_dumpall covers the whole cluster including roles.

questions.prompt: To back up cluster-global objects like roles and tablespaces, use:
questions.explanation: pg_dump doesn't capture roles/tablespaces — pg_dumpall dumps them plus every database.

questions.prompt: Continuous archiving (WAL archiving + base backup) uniquely enables:
questions.explanation: Replaying archived WAL atop a base backup restores to an arbitrary timestamp — pg_dump cannot do this.

questions.prompt: The Write-Ahead Log exists primarily to:
questions.explanation: WAL records changes; after a crash, recovery replays WAL to reach a consistent state — the 'log first' rule.

questions.prompt: A checkpoint in PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: Checkpoints bound crash-recovery work: pages before the checkpoint are guaranteed on disk, enabling WAL recycling.

questions.prompt: Streaming (physical) replication ships:
questions.explanation: Physical replication streams WAL: the standby replays to stay byte-identical — whole-cluster, read-only replica.

questions.prompt: Logical replication differs in that it:
questions.explanation: Logical replication decodes WAL into row changes per publication — flexible subsets, cross-version possible.

questions.prompt: A replication slot guarantees:
questions.explanation: Slots pin WAL on the primary; an abandoned slot can fill disk — a classic operational hazard.

questions.prompt: pg_stat_activity shows:
questions.explanation: pg_stat_activity is the live 'who is doing what' view for diagnosing blocks and long queries.

questions.prompt: pg_stat_user_tables tracks per-table counters including:
questions.explanation: Cumulative stats views expose scan counts and dead tuples — the first stop for bloat/index-usage checks.

questions.prompt: USING (dept_id) versus ON a.dept_id = b.dept_id differ because:
questions.explanation: USING produces a single coalesced output column per join key; ON keeps both sides' columns.

questions.prompt: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE ...) tests:
questions.explanation: EXISTS is true if the subquery yields any row; correlated EXISTS links it to the outer row.

questions.prompt: SELECT t.* FROM t selects:
questions.explanation: alias.* scopes the star to one FROM item — useful in joins to grab one side's columns.

questions.prompt: VALUES (1,'a'),(2,'b') used in FROM produces:
questions.explanation: VALUES lists construct constant tables usable anywhere a table is — joins, inserts, CTEs.

questions.prompt: CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy') creates:
questions.explanation: Enum labels are fixed at type creation; ordering is the declaration order and storage is compact.

questions.prompt: Adding a value to an existing enum type uses:
questions.explanation: ALTER TYPE ADD VALUE appends (or positions) a new label; new values can't be used in the same transaction under older versions.

questions.prompt: The uuid type is preferred over text for identifiers because it:
questions.explanation: uuid is a dedicated 128-bit type with literal validation; generation needs functions like gen_random_uuid().

questions.prompt: inet / cidr types represent:
questions.explanation: Network types support >>, <<= containment and other operators for subnet logic.

questions.prompt: A sequence object (nextval('seq')):
questions.explanation: Sequences are standalone counter objects; nextval is not transactional — rolled-back values leave gaps.

questions.prompt: Why can identity/serial columns have gaps even without deletes?
questions.explanation: Sequence increments are outside MVCC rollback — aborted inserts consume values permanently, so gaps are normal.

questions.prompt: pg_hba.conf controls:
questions.explanation: Host-based authentication rules are matched top-down; first match wins — changes need a reload.

questions.prompt: The recommended password authentication method in modern PostgreSQL is:
questions.explanation: SCRAM-SHA-256 is the challenge-response standard; md5 is legacy, trust skips auth entirely.

questions.prompt: A 'serialization failure' error (SQLSTATE 40001) means:
questions.explanation: Serializable mode aborts transactions forming dangerous rw-antidependency cycles; clients must be ready to retry.

questions.prompt: Serializable isolation is stronger than Repeatable Read because it also prevents:
questions.explanation: Serializable adds anomaly detection atop the RR snapshot; the write-skew pattern is the classic anomaly it blocks.

questions.prompt: 'Table bloat' in PostgreSQL refers to:
questions.explanation: Every UPDATE/DELETE leaves dead tuples; if VACUUM can't keep pace they inflate scans — the bloat/vacuum relationship.

questions.prompt: Why does COUNT(*) stay relatively expensive in PostgreSQL on huge tables?
questions.explanation: Without a single row store, each tuple's visibility must be verified; index-only scans help when the visibility map is hot.

questions.prompt: max_connections sets:
questions.explanation: Beyond max_connections, new connections are refused; pooling (e.g. PgBouncer) manages excess clients.

questions.prompt: The visibility map supports:
questions.explanation: VACUUM marks all-visible pages in the VM; index-only scans consult it before skipping heap access.

questions.prompt: pg_dump custom format (-Fc) versus plain SQL:
questions.explanation: Custom/directory formats compress and allow selective restore/reorder; plain SQL needs psql replay in full.

questions.prompt: A limitation of filesystem-level backup is:
questions.explanation: Copying a live data dir without freeze/snapshot yields torn files; PITR or offline copies are the safe routes.

questions.prompt: A synchronous streaming replica differs from asynchronous because:
questions.explanation: sync replication confirms WAL reached the standby; async can lose recent commits on failover.

source_refs.title: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication
source_refs.section: 26 High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication

questions.prompt: pg_stat_statements (extension) provides:
questions.explanation: It fingerprints normalized queries and accumulates timing/count stats — the standard top-query tool.

questions.prompt: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT requires which to work deterministically?
questions.explanation: The conflict target must map to a unique index/constraint for the inference of which violation occurred.

questions.prompt: An EXCLUSION constraint (e.g. no overlapping booking ranges) enforces:
questions.explanation: EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, span WITH &&) forbids overlapping ranges — declarative no-double-booking.

questions.prompt: CUBE(a, b) produces grouping sets:
questions.explanation: CUBE enumerates the power set of its columns — cross-tab style multi-dimensional aggregation.

questions.prompt: ORDER BY can reference columns not in the select list:
questions.explanation: With DISTINCT/UNION the sort keys must appear in the output so the result is well-defined.

questions.prompt: EXCEPT NULL-handling: for row comparisons in set operations, NULLs are treated as:
questions.explanation: Set operations use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM semantics — NULLs count as equal for dedup/intersect/except.

questions.prompt: ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY x) divides rows into:
questions.explanation: ntile buckets the ordered rows into n near-equal groups — the ranking-family 'quantile' function.

questions.prompt: WITH regional AS (SELECT ...) SELECT * FROM regional — the CTE name scope is:
questions.explanation: CTE names live for the duration of one query — like an inline temporary view.

questions.prompt: BETWEEN SYMMETRIC 10 AND 5:
questions.explanation: SYMMETRIC removes the requirement that the lower bound be written first.

questions.prompt: coalesce(NULL, NULL, 3) and greatest(1, NULL, 5) return respectively:
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument; GREATEST and LEAST ignore NULL inputs in PostgreSQL, picking 5 here.

questions.prompt: x > ALL(SELECT ...) is true when:
questions.explanation: ALL requires the comparison hold against every result row — vacuously true on empty sets (a subtle trap).

questions.prompt: x IN (subquery) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: IN expands to = ANY — true when x equals any returned row; the empty-set case yields false.

questions.prompt: A self-join (emp e JOIN emp m ON e.mgr_id = m.id) is used for:
questions.explanation: Self-joins need aliases to distinguish the two roles of the same relation.

questions.prompt: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW versus RANGE over the same ORDER BY:
questions.explanation: RANGE's frame spans value-peers; ROWS's frame counts row positions — peers matter for ties.

questions.prompt: first_value(x) OVER w and last_value(x) OVER w on a full-partition frame give:
questions.explanation: With the default frame ending at CURRENT ROW, last_value returns the current row — the classic frame trap.

questions.prompt: WITH ... AS NOT MATERIALIZED requests:
questions.explanation: NOT MATERIALIZED hints the planner to fold the subquery in — overriding the multi-reference materialization default.

questions.prompt: SELECT 'a' UNION SELECT 'b' ORDER BY 1 sorts by:
questions.explanation: After a set op, ORDER BY refers to result columns (name or position), not source columns.

questions.prompt: An INNER JOIN ON true (or 1=1) behaves as:
questions.explanation: A tautological join condition degenerates to a Cartesian product.

questions.prompt: SELECT DISTINCT ON is:
questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL-specific syntax providing a concise per-group first-row idiom.

questions.prompt: OFFSET without LIMIT in PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: OFFSET alone is permitted; rows after the skipped prefix are returned in arbitrary order without ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: START TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE, READ ONLY:
questions.explanation: Transaction modes (isolation, read-write/read-only, deferrable) are set at BEGIN/START or per-statement.

questions.prompt: A READ ONLY DEFERRABLE serializable transaction is the documented pattern for:
questions.explanation: Deferrable read-only serializable transactions wait for a 'safe' snapshot — ideal for consistent exports.

questions.prompt: FOR UPDATE ... NOWAIT versus FOR UPDATE ... SKIP LOCKED:
questions.explanation: The two options serve different patterns: fail-fast vs work-queue-style 'grab free rows'.

questions.prompt: A covering index (INCLUDE (col)) lets index-only scans return:
questions.explanation: INCLUDE stores extra payload columns in index entries — covering queries without widening the key.

questions.prompt: Hash indexes in modern PostgreSQL:
questions.explanation: Hash indexes are crash-safe since v10 but narrow in utility (equality only); B-tree dominates practice.

questions.prompt: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) adds:
questions.explanation: BUFFERS instruments shared/local hits+reads, the key signal for I/O-bound plan nodes.

questions.prompt: SET search_path = '$user', public means unqualified names resolve:
questions.explanation: $user is the current user's namesake schema slot; pg_catalog is always searched implicitly first unless listed.

questions.prompt: REVOKE ... CASCADE versus RESTRICT:
questions.explanation: When a grantee re-granted via grant option, CASCADE removes the chain; RESTRICT protects against surprise revocation.

questions.prompt: Default privileges (ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES) exist to:
questions.explanation: Default privileges apply at object creation time — e.g. app tables auto-readable by a reporting role.

questions.prompt: PERFORM query in PL/pgSQL:
questions.explanation: PERFORM runs a query whose result is dropped — the PL/pgSQL way to call SELECT for effect.

questions.prompt: GET DIAGNOSTICS row_count = ROW_COUNT after DML in PL/pgSQL gives:
questions.explanation: GET DIAGNOSTICS retrieves statement metadata; FOUND is the simpler boolean version.

questions.prompt: A statement-level trigger cannot see NEW/OLD because:
questions.explanation: For statement triggers needing row access, REFERENCING NEW TABLE/OLD TABLE exposes transition relations.

questions.prompt: Function overloading in PostgreSQL permits:
questions.explanation: Functions are identified by name+arg types; return type alone cannot disambiguate.

questions.prompt: ANALYZE inside autovacuum's duties:
questions.explanation: The daemon schedules both vacuum (dead tuples) and analyze (stats) per change thresholds.

questions.prompt: WAL archiving (archive_mode) means:
questions.explanation: archive_command copies each finished segment — the foundation of continuous archiving.

questions.prompt: Logical replication publications select:
questions.explanation: CREATE PUBLICATION FOR TABLE lists what to replicate; subscriptions pull the decoded changes.

questions.prompt: CREATE TABLE t2 (LIKE t1 INCLUDING ALL) creates:
questions.explanation: LIKE clones structure; INCLUDING options choose which features (indexes, defaults, constraints) to carry.

questions.prompt: CREATE TABLE AS (CTAS) versus CREATE VIEW:
questions.explanation: CTAS materializes once — like a one-time materialized view; the base data changes are never reflected.

questions.prompt: NOT VALID on ADD CONSTRAINT means:
questions.explanation: NOT VALID + later VALIDATE minimizes locking during rollout of constraints on big populated tables.

questions.prompt: Attaching an existing table as a partition uses:
questions.explanation: ATTACH PARTITION moves a table under the partitioned parent — bulk-loading pattern: load, then attach.

questions.prompt: Concatenating text with NULL ('a' || NULL) yields:
questions.explanation: String concatenation propagates NULL — use concat() or COALESCE for null-safe concatenation.

questions.prompt: timestamp without time zone versus timestamptz semantics:
questions.explanation: timestamp is a calendar/clock reading with no instant meaning; timestamptz normalizes input to UTC.

questions.prompt: jsonb_each(doc) returns:
questions.explanation: jsonb_each explodes an object's top-level pairs — the extraction tool for unknown key sets.

questions.prompt: List each employee name with their department name (columns: name, dept) for employees that have a department. Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id ORDER BY e.name
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN pairs employees to departments; the departmentless employee is excluded.

questions.prompt: List every employee name and their department name (columns: name, dept), including employees with no department — dept must be NULL for them. Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id ORDER BY e.name
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps departmentless employees with a NULL dept; ordering must not depend on dept being non-null.

questions.prompt: List employees (columns: name, manager) with their manager's name; include employees without a manager (manager NULL). Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.mgr_id ORDER BY e.name
questions.explanation: A self-join with a LEFT JOIN handles the NULL mgr_id roots.

questions.prompt: Return each department id (dept_id) and the number of employees in it (cnt), including departments with zero employees. Order by dept_id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT d.id AS dept_id, count(e.id) AS cnt FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.id ORDER BY d.id
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN + count(e.id) counts only real employees; the empty department yields 0.

questions.prompt: Return departments (dept_id) whose employees' average salary exceeds 5000, with the average (avg_salary, rounded to 2 decimals). Order by dept_id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT dept_id, round(avg(salary), 2) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING avg(salary) > 5000 ORDER BY dept_id
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after aggregation; avg ignores NULL salaries — the edge case has no qualifying dept.

questions.prompt: Return each department id and the number of employees with a non-NULL salary (paid_count). Include departments where no employee has a salary. Order by dept_id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT d.id AS dept_id, count(e.salary) AS paid_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.id ORDER BY d.id
questions.explanation: count(expr) skips NULLs — exactly the count of paid employees; Grace's NULL salary is not counted.

questions.prompt: Return the names of employees who earn more than the average salary of all employees (ignore NULL salaries). Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT avg(salary) FROM employees) ORDER BY name
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery supplies the threshold; in the edge case no one exceeds their own average.

questions.prompt: Return the names of customers who have never placed an order. Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id) ORDER BY name
questions.explanation: Anti-join via NOT EXISTS; with zero orders every customer qualifies in the edge dataset.

questions.prompt: Return the name(s) of the highest paid employee(s) by non-NULL salary — there may be ties. Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary = (SELECT max(salary) FROM employees) ORDER BY name
questions.explanation: = with a scalar aggregate subquery; NULL salaries never satisfy the equality, so the all-NULL edge yields no rows.

questions.prompt: Return one sorted list of all distinct cities appearing in either employees or customers (column: city, no NULLs, no duplicates). Order by city.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT city FROM employees WHERE city IS NOT NULL UNION SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL ORDER BY city
questions.explanation: UNION deduplicates across both sources; the all-NULL edge yields an empty result.

questions.prompt: Return cities that appear in BOTH employees and customers (column: city). No duplicates, no NULLs. Order by city.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT city FROM employees WHERE city IS NOT NULL INTERSECT SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL ORDER BY city
questions.explanation: INTERSECT keeps only shared cities; disjoint edge data yields empty.

questions.prompt: Return cities of employees that have NO customer located there (column: city, distinct, non-NULL). Order by city.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT city FROM employees WHERE city IS NOT NULL EXCEPT SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL ORDER BY city
questions.explanation: EXCEPT returns left-set minus right-set; the overlapping edge yields empty.

questions.prompt: Classify each product (columns: name, tier) where tier is 'expensive' when price >= 100, 'moderate' when price >= 30, otherwise 'cheap'. Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name, CASE WHEN price >= 100 THEN 'expensive' WHEN price >= 30 THEN 'moderate' ELSE 'cheap' END AS tier FROM products ORDER BY name
questions.explanation: Searched CASE evaluates thresholds in order — put the highest first.

questions.prompt: Return order id and effective total (eff_total): the total if not NULL, else the sum of its order_items qty*price, else 0. Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT o.id, COALESCE(o.total, (SELECT sum(i.qty * i.price) FROM order_items i WHERE i.order_id = o.id), 0) AS eff_total FROM orders o ORDER BY o.id
questions.explanation: COALESCE chains the fallbacks; correlated subquery computes line totals when header total is missing.

questions.prompt: Return ids of orders whose total IS NULL (column: id). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE total IS NULL ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: IS NULL is the only correct test — = NULL would match nothing.

questions.prompt: Return each customer's id and display_city: their city if present, otherwise 'Unknown'. Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS display_city FROM customers ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: COALESCE substitutes a default for NULL — every row returns a non-null display_city.

questions.prompt: Return the distinct department ids that have employees (column: dept_id). Order by dept_id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY dept_id
questions.explanation: DISTINCT collapses duplicate dept_ids; WHERE removes the NULL-dept employees.

questions.prompt: Using DISTINCT ON, return each department's highest-paid employee (columns: dept_id, name, salary). If salaries tie, pick the alphabetically first name. Order by dept_id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT DISTINCT ON (dept_id) dept_id, name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC NULLS LAST, name
questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON (dept_id) keeps the first row per dept under the given ordering; NULLS LAST keeps NULL salaries from winning.

questions.prompt: Return the 3 highest non-NULL salaries (column: salary, may repeat). Order by salary descending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3
questions.explanation: ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT n is the top-N idiom; the edge dataset has fewer than 3 rows.

questions.prompt: Return the second page of employee names sorted by name: skip 2 rows, then take 2 (column: name).
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name FROM employees ORDER BY name OFFSET 2 LIMIT 2
questions.explanation: OFFSET/LIMIT implements pagination — deterministic only with ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: Return employees (columns: name, salary) ordered by salary ascending with NULL salaries last, then name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary ASC NULLS LAST, name
questions.explanation: NULLS LAST overrides PostgreSQL's default (NULLs sort largest, i.e. last for ASC anyway — but explicit is required for the DESC case this pattern generalizes to).

questions.prompt: Return each product's sku and a label (label) formed as 'NAME (CATEGORY)' e.g. 'Keyboard (accessories)'. Order by sku.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT sku, name || ' (' || category || ')' AS label FROM products ORDER BY sku
questions.explanation: || concatenates the pieces; all inputs are NOT NULL here so no NULL leak.

questions.prompt: Return products (name, price) whose name starts with 'M' (case-sensitive). Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'M%' ORDER BY name
questions.explanation: LIKE 'M%' anchors the first character; the lower-case edge row is correctly excluded.

questions.prompt: Return products (name) whose name contains a digit anywhere. Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name FROM products WHERE name ~ '[0-9]' ORDER BY name
