questions.explanation: POSIX ~ matches the regex anywhere in the string — 'Cable v2' qualifies.

questions.prompt: Using a WITH clause, return the names of employees whose salary is above their department's average salary (columns: name, dept_id, salary). Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: WITH dept_avg AS (SELECT dept_id, avg(salary) AS a FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id) SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary FROM employees e JOIN dept_avg d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id WHERE e.salary > d.a ORDER BY e.name
questions.explanation: The CTE computes per-dept averages once; the main query compares each row to its dept average.

questions.prompt: Using WITH, compute per-customer order counts (including customers with zero orders) then return only customers having at least 2 orders (columns: name, order_count). Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: WITH counts AS (SELECT c.id, c.name, count(o.id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name) SELECT name, order_count FROM counts WHERE order_count >= 2 ORDER BY name
questions.explanation: Two-stage logic reads cleanly as a CTE: first count, then filter.

questions.prompt: Using a CTE named totals that holds (order_id, grand_total = qty*price summed per order), return the grand total of all orders (column: total). Round to 2 decimals.
questions.reference_answer: WITH totals AS (SELECT order_id, sum(qty * price) AS grand_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT round(sum(grand_total), 2) AS total FROM totals
questions.explanation: The CTE expresses an intermediate aggregate; the outer query aggregates it further.

questions.prompt: The employees table forms a management tree via mgr_id. Using WITH RECURSIVE, return the ids of all employees reporting (directly or transitively) to employee id 1 — include id 1 itself (column: id). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (SELECT id, mgr_id FROM employees WHERE id = 1 UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.mgr_id FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.mgr_id = s.id) SELECT id FROM sub ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: The recursive term follows mgr_id links downward; employee 2's manager (id 5) is outside the tree so it stays out.

questions.prompt: Using WITH RECURSIVE, generate the integers 1 through 5 (column: n). Order by n.
questions.reference_answer: WITH RECURSIVE nums(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT n FROM nums ORDER BY n
questions.explanation: The classic counter recursion: base 1, recursive term stops when n reaches 5. A throwaway table keeps the dataset shape.

questions.prompt: employees.mgr_id chains upward to the CEO (mgr_id NULL). Using WITH RECURSIVE, return each employee id with their depth below the CEO: CEO depth 0, direct reports depth 1, etc (columns: id, depth). Order by depth, id.
questions.reference_answer: WITH RECURSIVE org AS (SELECT id, mgr_id, 0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE mgr_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.mgr_id, o.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.mgr_id = o.id) SELECT id, depth FROM org ORDER BY depth, id
questions.explanation: Multiple roots (Frank is dept-less AND mgr-less) — the base term picks every mgr_id NULL root; depth accumulates down the chain.

questions.prompt: Rank employees within each department by salary descending (columns: name, dept_id, salary, rnk). Ties share a rank (use rank()). Order by dept_id, rnk, name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name, dept_id, salary, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST) AS rnk FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY dept_id, rnk, name
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY scopes the ranking per dept; Bob and Carol tie at rank 1 in dept 1.

questions.prompt: Return each event's user_id, occurred_at and the number of seconds since that user's previous event (gap_seconds, NULL for the first). Order by user_id, occurred_at.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT user_id, occurred_at, EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM occurred_at - lag(occurred_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY occurred_at)) AS gap_seconds FROM events ORDER BY user_id, occurred_at
questions.explanation: lag() reaches the prior row per user partition — session-gap analysis without a self-join.

questions.prompt: Return each order's id, placed_at, total and a running total of non-NULL totals ordered by placed_at (running_total, rounded to 2 decimals). Order by placed_at, id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, placed_at, total, round(sum(COALESCE(total,0)) OVER (ORDER BY placed_at, id), 2) AS running_total FROM orders ORDER BY placed_at, id
questions.explanation: Default frame runs from partition start to current row — a running sum; COALESCE keeps NULLs out of the sum.

questions.prompt: Return the single highest-paid employee per department using a window function in a subquery (columns: name, dept_id, salary; include ties via rank()). Order by dept_id, name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name, dept_id, salary FROM (SELECT name, dept_id, salary, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST) AS r FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL) t WHERE r = 1 ORDER BY dept_id, name
questions.explanation: Filtering on a window result needs a subquery — windows can't appear in WHERE.

questions.prompt: Return each order id, total, and its share of the grand total as pct (round(100*total/sum(total) over (),2)). Skip NULL totals in both numerator and denominator by COALESCE-ing them to 0. Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, total, round(100 * COALESCE(total,0) / NULLIF(sum(COALESCE(total,0)) OVER (), 0), 2) AS pct FROM orders ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: OVER () aggregates the whole result set per row; NULLIF guards the all-NULL edge (division by zero).

questions.prompt: Return each status and how many orders have that status (cnt) — but count ONLY orders with non-NULL total using FILTER (columns: status, paid_cnt). Order by status.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT status, count(*) FILTER (WHERE total IS NOT NULL) AS paid_cnt FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status
questions.explanation: FILTER scopes the aggregate input per group without splitting queries; the edge shows 0.

questions.prompt: Return one row with per-status order counts side by side: shipped_cnt, pending_cnt, cancelled_cnt (use FILTER).
questions.reference_answer: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'shipped') AS shipped_cnt, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending_cnt, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled_cnt FROM orders
questions.explanation: Conditional aggregation via FILTER pivots statuses into columns — the empty edge returns one row of zeros.

questions.prompt: Return each department name and a comma-separated list of its employee names alphabetically (column: members; NULL for empty departments). Order by department name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT d.name, string_agg(e.name, ', ' ORDER BY e.name) AS members FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.name ORDER BY d.name
questions.explanation: string_agg folds the group into one string; the LEFT JOIN keeps empty departments with NULL members.

questions.prompt: Return each order's id, placed_at and the year it was placed (yr as integer via extract). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, placed_at, extract(year FROM placed_at)::int AS yr FROM orders ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: extract pulls date fields; the cast makes the numeric year an integer.

questions.prompt: Return each employee's id, hire_date, and the month truncated hire month (hire_month = first day of hire month via date_trunc). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, hire_date, date_trunc('month', hire_date)::date AS hire_month FROM employees WHERE hire_date IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: date_trunc('month', ...) normalizes dates to month starts — a standard bucketing idiom.

questions.prompt: Count orders per calendar month in 2024 (columns: mon as 'YYYY-MM' text, cnt). Order by mon.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', placed_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS mon, count(*) AS cnt FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND placed_at < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
questions.explanation: date_trunc buckets to month, to_char formats the label; the 2023 edge row is excluded by the range filter.

questions.prompt: Return product id and its attrs->>'color' as color for products that have a color attribute. Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, attrs ->> 'color' AS color FROM products WHERE attrs ? 'color' ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: ? tests top-level key existence on jsonb; ->> extracts the value as text.

questions.prompt: Return ids of products whose attrs contain the exact key-value pair "wireless": true (use containment @>). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id FROM products WHERE attrs @> '{"wireless": true}'::jsonb ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: @> requires structural containment — the string "yes" does not equal boolean true, so the edge row fails.

questions.prompt: Return ids of products whose tags array contains 'electronic' (use @>). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id FROM products WHERE tags @> ARRAY['electronic'] ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: Array @> checks left-contains-right membership — indexable with GIN.

questions.prompt: Return each product id with its first tag (first_tag = tags[1], may be NULL). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, tags[1] AS first_tag FROM products ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: Arrays are 1-based; tags[1] is NULL when tags is NULL or empty.

questions.prompt: Expand each product's tags into rows (columns: id, tag — one row per tag). Order by id, tag.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, tag FROM products CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(tags) AS tag ORDER BY id, tag
questions.explanation: LATERAL + unnest turns array elements into rows; NULL-tag products drop out (cross join with empty set).

questions.prompt: Using LATERAL, return each customer's name and their most recent order's total (last_total, NULL if none). Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT c.name, o.total AS last_total FROM customers c LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT total FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC LIMIT 1) o ON true ORDER BY c.name
questions.explanation: LATERAL evaluates the subquery per customer row — a per-group top-1 join.

questions.prompt: Return each department name and its top-2 salaries (columns: dept, salary) using LATERAL; departments with no employees must not appear. Order by dept, salary DESC.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT d.name AS dept, t.salary FROM departments d CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT salary FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id AND e.salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY e.salary DESC LIMIT 2) t ORDER BY dept, t.salary DESC
questions.explanation: LATERAL enables a per-department LIMIT — the 'top-N per group' pattern.

questions.prompt: Return total order count broken down by status AND a grand total row, using GROUPING SETS ((status), ()). Columns: status (NULL on the total row), cnt. Order by status NULLS LAST.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT status, count(*) AS cnt FROM orders GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((status), ()) ORDER BY status NULLS LAST
questions.explanation: The empty grouping () produces the grand-total row alongside per-status rows in one pass.

questions.prompt: Return ROLLUP revenue: per (status) sums of non-NULL total plus a grand total — columns: status, revenue. Use COALESCE(total,0) inside sum. Order by status NULLS LAST.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT status, round(sum(COALESCE(total,0)),2) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY ROLLUP(status) ORDER BY status NULLS LAST
questions.explanation: ROLLUP(status) = (status),() — subtotal plus grand total; the NULL-status grouping column distinguishes the total row.

questions.prompt: Return each product's name, price and price rounded to the nearest integer (rounded). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name, price, round(price) AS rounded FROM products ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: round on numeric halves away from zero — 0.50 → 1.

questions.prompt: Return each product's name and unit_price = price divided by stock — but NULL where stock is 0 instead of an error (use NULLIF). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name, price / NULLIF(stock, 0) AS unit_price FROM products ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: NULLIF(stock,0) turns the divisor into NULL for empty stock — the zero-stock product yields NULL not an error.

questions.prompt: Return each customer's id and initials: first letter of each word in name uppercased joined with '.' — single-word names give just the letter (column: initials). Hint: split on space.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, upper(left(split_part(name,' ',1),1)) || COALESCE('.' || upper(left(split_part(name,' ',2),1)), '') AS initials FROM customers ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: split_part indexes words; the third-word case keeps first-two-letter initials only — COALESCE avoids a stray NULL.

questions.prompt: Return each event's id and occurred_at plus occurred_at truncated to the day (day). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, occurred_at, occurred_at::date AS day FROM events ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: Casting timestamp::date drops the time component — simpler than date_trunc for a date result.

questions.prompt: Return names of customers who placed at least one 'shipped' order (column: name). Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT cust_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped') ORDER BY name
questions.explanation: IN with a filtered subquery returns matching customers once; no shipped orders → empty result.

questions.prompt: Return ids of employees whose mgr_id is NOT IN the set of department ids (orphaned managers chain). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id FROM employees WHERE mgr_id IS NOT NULL AND mgr_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM departments) ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: NOT IN is safe here only because departments.id is NOT NULL; employee 2's mgr_id 5 (edge: 99) points outside departments.

questions.prompt: Return order counts per customer (columns: cust_id, cnt) for customers with at least one order. Order by cnt DESC, cust_id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT cust_id, count(*) AS cnt FROM orders GROUP BY cust_id ORDER BY cnt DESC, cust_id
questions.explanation: GROUP BY cust_id aggregates orders per customer; empty orders → empty result.

questions.prompt: Return each employee's id and tenure in whole years at '2024-12-31' using age() extract (column: years). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, extract(year FROM age(DATE '2024-12-31', hire_date))::int AS years FROM employees WHERE hire_date IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: age(end,start) gives a y/m/d interval; extracting year yields whole years — the hire-on-boundary edge gives 0.

questions.prompt: Return customer names of customers whose every order total is NULL — they have at least one order and none has a non-NULL total. Order by name.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name HAVING count(o.total) = 0 ORDER BY c.name
questions.explanation: JOIN keeps only ordering customers; count(expr) skips NULLs so =0 means 'no non-null totals'.

questions.prompt: Return each product's id and a margin column: price - 30 if that is positive else 0 (use GREATEST). Order by id.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id, GREATEST(price - 30, 0) AS margin FROM products ORDER BY id
questions.explanation: GREATEST clamps the lower bound — a floor() idiom without CASE.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL never lets readers block writers under MVCC. Explain how multiversioning achieves this, what a 'snapshot' means concretely for a transaction, and what maintenance duty this design creates.
questions.reference_answer: Each UPDATE/DELETE writes a new tuple version while old versions persist for snapshots that may still see them. A transaction's snapshot fixes which commits are visible; readers traverse the version chain instead of locking. The cost is dead tuples that VACUUM must reclaim — bloat and the visibility-map/ID-wraparound machinery exist because of this trade.
questions.explanation: MVCC fundamentals — Ch. 13 and the vacuum chapter are the two sides of this design.

questions.prompt: A colleague says 'Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL prevents every anomaly, so we never need Serializable.' Evaluate this claim precisely: which anomalies each level blocks, what a serialization anomaly looks like (use write skew), and what error handling Serializable requires.
questions.reference_answer: Repeatable Read gives a transaction-long snapshot — no dirty/non-repeatable/phantom reads — but admits serialization anomalies: results impossible under any serial order. Write skew example: two on-call rules where each transaction reads a count > 0 then removes itself, leaving zero — both commit under RR. Serializable (SSI) detects such rw-antidependency structures and aborts one party; applications must catch SQLSTATE 40001 and retry.
questions.explanation: Isolation-level precision — Table 13.1 of the manual lists exactly which phenomena each level allows.

questions.prompt: You must index: (a) equality+range lookups on an order_date column, (b) jsonb containment queries, (c) a 500M-row append-only events table queried by event_ts, physically clustered by time, (d) an array 'tags' membership check. Choose index types and justify each choice including its tradeoffs.
questions.reference_answer: B-tree for (a) — ordered comparisons on sortable data. GIN for (b) and (d) — inverted posting lists for containment of elements/keys. BRIN for (c) — block-range summaries exploit physical ordering, tiny index on huge correlated data; it fails on uncorrelated data. Tradeoffs: GIN write cost, BRIN only for correlated data, B-tree size but general utility.
questions.explanation: Index-type selection is about data shape and query operators, not 'indexes make it faster'.

questions.prompt: A dashboard query is slow. Walk through how you would use EXPLAIN ANALYZE output (cost vs actual rows, scan types, buffers, loops) to diagnose it, and what stale statistics have to do with plan quality.
questions.reference_answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query showing per-node estimated vs actual rows, real time, and (BUFFERS) I/O. Big estimate/actual divergence indicates stale or inadequate statistics — ANALYZE (and statistics targets/extended stats) fixes planner input. Scan-type reasoning: seq scan on an unselective predicate is fine; nested loops with huge inner counts signal bad cardinality estimates; loops > 1 multiply child costs.
questions.explanation: Plan literacy is the core performance skill: estimates drive choices, ANALYZE feeds estimates.

questions.prompt: When should a PostgreSQL design use jsonb columns instead of normalized relational columns — and when must it not? Cover storage/indexing differences, query ergonomics, integrity guarantees and a concrete scenario for each choice.
questions.reference_answer: jsonb fits genuinely schemaless/sparse/evolving attributes and document-shaped payloads — GIN indexes support @>, ?, ?|. It forfeits column-level types, constraints, foreign keys and statistics; predicates need operators clients must know. Normalized columns fit structured, queried, constrained data — the default. Anti-pattern: burying relational keys inside jsonb blobs to avoid schema work.
questions.explanation: jsonb is a complement to the relational model, not a schema-free shortcut.

questions.prompt: Design a partitioning strategy for a multi-billion-row events table queried mostly by recent time windows, with cheap retention (drop old months). Cover partition method/key, pruning, the retention operation, unique-constraint implications and operational gotchas.
questions.reference_answer: PARTITION BY RANGE (event_ts) monthly; queries with event_ts predicates prune to few partitions. Retention = DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY or DROP on old monthly partitions — O(1) vs DELETE+VACUUM. Unique constraints must include the partition key — a global PK on id alone is impossible without event_ts. Gotchas: no pruning if the key isn't in WHERE, default partition traps, ATTACH for bulk loads, per-partition indexes.
questions.explanation: Partitioning is a data-lifecycle feature — pruning and cheap detach are the wins.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS stores all tenants' rows in shared tables. Compare three isolation designs: separate databases, schema-per-tenant, and shared tables + row-level security. Then specify the RLS policy needed (including FORCE and the migration risk) for tenant isolation.
questions.reference_answer: Separate DBs = strongest isolation, worst ops/schema proliferation. Schema-per-tenant = middle. Shared+RLS = simplest ops; CREATE POLICY tenant_iso ON t USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int) per table, ENABLE + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY so owners don't bypass. Risks: BYPASSRLS/superuser leaks, forgetting FORCE, leakproof-function ordering, policy expression cost on every query.
questions.explanation: RLS is the standard shared-schema tenancy tool — but it is opt-in and easily misconfigured.

questions.prompt: An autovacuum is falling behind on a high-churn table: dead tuples grow faster than workers reclaim them. Explain the symptoms (bloat, plan drift), the tuning knobs available, and why VACUUM FULL is not the routine answer.
questions.reference_answer: Symptoms: table/index bloat, slower scans, wasted space, wraparound risk if very old. Knobs: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor/cost_limit/vacuum_cost_delay per-table via storage parameters, more workers. FULL rewrites with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE — blocks all access; used for reclamation, not steady-state. The real fix is tuning frequency/aggressiveness and HOT-update-friendly fillfactor.
questions.explanation: Autovacuum tuning is workload-shaped — per-table storage parameters are the instrument.

questions.prompt: Design a backup strategy for a 500GB OLTP database requiring RPO ~ 0 and recovery to any minute in the last 30 days. Explain the components (base backup, WAL archive, testing) and why pg_dump alone cannot satisfy the requirements.
questions.reference_answer: Continuous archiving: scheduled base backups (pg_basebackup or tool) + WAL archive via archive_command to durable storage → PITR to any timestamp. pg_dump is a logical snapshot — consistent but point-in-time only as of dump start, no incremental replay; restores are full and slow. Recovery testing and monitoring the archive are mandatory; a backup that was never restored is a hope not a strategy.
questions.explanation: PITR = base backup + continuous WAL; dumps are for logical portability, not tight RPO.

questions.prompt: Choose between streaming (physical) and logical replication for these needs and justify: (a) a hot standby for failover, (b) replicating two tables to a reporting database on a different major version, (c) minimal-lag read scaling. Include the replication-slot disk-growth hazard.
questions.reference_answer: Physical streaming for (a) and (c) — byte-identical standby, WAL streaming, synchronous option for failover; read-only queries serve reporting/load. Logical for (b) — row changes per publication cross versions and subset tables. Slots pin WAL on the primary; a dead subscriber grows pg_wal until disk-full — monitor slot lag.
questions.explanation: Physical = whole-cluster byte copy; logical = selective row changes — different tools.

questions.prompt: Compare expressing a multi-step aggregation as nested subqueries versus WITH clauses. When does the CTE version perform differently (materialization) and when is it merely clearer? Give an example where materialization semantics matter.
questions.reference_answer: Pre-v12 CTEs were optimization fences always materialized; v12+ inlines singly-referenced non-recursive CTEs like views. MATERIALIZED forces one computation — valuable when an expensive result is referenced twice; NOT MATERIALIZED enables pushdown. Readability: named stages beat nested subqueries for pipelines; performance is now equivalent in the single-reference case.
questions.explanation: CTE performance changed in v12 — the 'always materialized' folklore is outdated.

questions.prompt: Explain why SELECT dept, name, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM emp cannot be filtered by WHERE r = 1 — and the two correct ways to get 'top earner per dept' (window subquery vs DISTINCT ON). Compare them.
questions.reference_answer: Window functions evaluate after WHERE over the FROM/WHERE result — the rank doesn't exist yet at filtering time. Solution A: wrap the ranked query in a subquery and filter outside (ties kept with rank()). Solution B: PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON (dept) with ORDER BY dept, salary DESC — shorter, single row per group (no tie support without care). DISTINCT ON is PG-specific; the subquery is portable.
questions.explanation: Logical evaluation order explains most 'why can't I' SQL errors — learn the pipeline.

questions.prompt: Two services update bank accounts and intermittently deadlock. Explain how the deadlock forms under MVCC (a row-lock ordering problem, not a read problem), what PostgreSQL does about it, and the design fixes (consistent ordering, NOWAIT/SKIP LOCKED, shorter transactions).
questions.reference_answer: Tx1 locks row A then requests B while Tx2 holds B requesting A — a cycle. Readers/writers don't block under MVCC, but row write locks do; deadlock_timeout detection aborts one cycle member. Fixes: lock rows in a canonical order (e.g. by id), keep critical sections short, FOR UPDATE NOWAIT to fail fast or SKIP LOCKED for queue semantics, retry the aborted transaction.
questions.explanation: Deadlocks are lock-ordering bugs; retries are part of the contract, not an accident.

questions.prompt: Compare serial, GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY and a stored generated column for an 'order_number' that must be sequential and for a 'line_total' computed from qty*price. Which mechanism fits each and what are the write-path rules?
questions.reference_answer: serial = sequence+default (overridable, gaps on rollback); IDENTITY ALWAYS = standard, system-controlled sequence, user values rejected unless OVERRIDING; GENERATED column = deterministic expression of same-row columns, no writes allowed at all. Sequential order_number → identity/serial; line_total → generated column since it derives from other columns.
questions.explanation: Sequences answer 'give me a number'; generated columns answer 'derive this value'.

questions.prompt: A finance dashboard aggregates yesterday's 50M rows in 8 seconds; management wants 5-minute freshness for an ops view and daily freshness for the finance view. Choose view vs materialized view per case and justify refresh strategy and staleness.
questions.reference_answer: Finance (daily): materialized view refreshed nightly/CONCURRENTLY — pays staleness for instant reads. Ops (5-min): a materialized view with 5-minute REFRESH CONCURRENTLY (needs unique index) or a plain view if the query is cheap — at 8s per refresh on 50M rows the matview is viable; a plain view re-runs 8s each read. Staleness contract drives the choice.
questions.explanation: Views trade compute for freshness; matviews trade freshness for compute.

questions.prompt: A booking table must forbid overlapping reservations for the same room. Compare CHECK, UNIQUE, trigger, and EXCLUSION constraint approaches; then show the declarative solution and its index requirement.
questions.reference_answer: CHECK sees one row only — cannot express pairwise non-overlap. UNIQUE prevents identical keys, not ranges. A trigger works but is hand-maintained and race-prone under concurrency. The declarative answer: EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, span WITH &&) — requires a GiST index on the range; every write checks operator-satisfaction against existing rows atomically.
questions.explanation: Exclusion constraints are PostgreSQL's declarative answer to pairwise row rules.

questions.prompt: Your team repeats CHECK (email ~ '.+@.+') on six tables. Design the domain-based refactor, explain what CREATE DOMAIN buys you over repeated CHECKs, and its limits (e.g., where domain constraints don't fire).
questions.reference_answer: CREATE DOMAIN email AS text CHECK (VALUE ~ '.+@.+') centralizes the rule — every column typed email inherits it; ALTER DOMAIN changes it in one place. Limits: domain checks fire on assignment, but casts/comparisons treat the value as the base type; planner ignores the constraint for estimates; constraints on domains can't reference other rows anyway.
questions.explanation: Domains are the DRY tool for per-type invariants — reuse, not duplication.

questions.prompt: Explain surrogate keys (identity/serial) vs natural keys for a 'users' table (email is a candidate key). Cover join cost, churn, uniqueness semantics and when exposing the surrogate publicly is a mistake.
questions.reference_answer: Surrogate bigint ids are compact join keys, stable, and opaque — but add no real-world meaning; the natural key still needs a UNIQUE constraint to prevent duplicate emails. Natural PKs save an index but leak business data and break on key churn (email change). Publicly sequential surrogates leak enumeration — pair with UUID for public exposure if needed.
questions.explanation: Surrogate for joins + unique constraint on the natural key is the usual settlement.

questions.prompt: Design the transaction boundaries for 'transfer funds between two accounts' (read balances, debit A, credit B, write audit log). Cover atomicity needs, savepoint use, isolation choice and what happens if the process dies mid-transaction.
questions.reference_answer: All four writes in one transaction — atomicity makes partial transfer impossible. Isolation: Read Committed suffices if balance checks happen under SELECT FOR UPDATE locks on the account rows; a race on the balance check is prevented by row locks not snapshot level. On crash, in-flight WAL/transaction state rolls back — no half-transfers. Savepoints could isolate optional steps (audit retry) without aborting the whole transfer.
questions.explanation: Atomicity is a property you design — group the writes that must live or die together.

questions.prompt: Explain ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ('upsert') semantics: how PostgreSQL picks the conflicting row, what EXCLUDED means, why concurrent inserts don't error, and when MERGE is the better fit.
questions.reference_answer: ON CONFLICT (col) proposes each row for insert; a violation on the inferred unique index switches to DO UPDATE on the existing row, with EXCLUDED referring to the would-be-inserted row. The speculative-insert path resolves races atomically — no lost updates under concurrency. MERGE suits multi-condition source-driven merges; ON CONFLICT is the simpler idempotent write.
questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT is the single-statement idempotent write — MERGE is the multi-action engine.

questions.prompt: Design least-privilege roles for: an app that reads/writes business tables, a reporting tool that reads them, and migrations that alter schema. Cover role hierarchy, default privileges and why the app shouldn't own its tables.
questions.reference_answer: app_rw: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on schema tables; reporting_ro: SELECT only; migrator: owns objects/DDL. App connects as app_rw — an SQL injection can damage data but not drop tables or grant rights. Default privileges on the migrator auto-grant app_rw/reporting_ro rights on future objects. Inheritance via GRANT role TO role; NOINHERIT where step-up should be explicit.
questions.explanation: Ownership is itself a privilege — keep DDL power out of the application's role.

questions.prompt: Explain why marking a function SECURITY DEFINER requires extra care: whose rights it runs with, the search_path injection attack, and the safe pattern (explicit SET search_path, input validation).
questions.reference_answer: SECURITY DEFINER runs as the function owner — a controlled privilege-elevation primitive. Attack: unqualified object names inside the body resolve along the caller's search_path; a malicious user could shadow objects in a schema they control appearing earlier in the path. Safe pattern: SET search_path = '' (or a pinned list) in the function, qualify names, validate inputs, keep the owner minimal-privileged.
questions.explanation: SECURITY DEFINER is delegation — pin search_path or the delegate can be impersonated.

questions.prompt: When is a trigger the right integrity tool and when is it the wrong one? Compare triggers with constraints and generated columns for: cross-row checks, audit columns, default computation, and cascade logic. Include statement vs row granularity and performance.
questions.reference_answer: Constraints are declarative, optimizer-visible, race-free — use them first (CHECK, FK, EXCLUDE). Generated columns replace simple per-row compute triggers. Triggers fit: cross-row rules beyond exclusion constraints, auditing NEW/OLD, complex cascades, INSTEAD OF view writes. Row triggers fire per row (n×cost on bulk); statement triggers + transition tables batch better. Triggers are procedural — easy to write bugs that fire under concurrency.
questions.explanation: Declarative first, generated columns second, triggers last — but indispensable when they fit.

questions.prompt: Explain the PL/pgSQL exception model: where errors can be caught, what a BEGIN..EXCEPTION block costs (subtransaction), what FOUND is after different statements, and one correct use for 'INSERT or handle conflict'.
questions.reference_answer: EXCEPTION WHEN condition THEN catches matching SQLSTATE-class errors in the enclosing block; the block rolls back to its start — internally a subtransaction (not free on hot paths). FOUND reflects the last statement (rows for DML/SELECT INTO/FOR, performed for PERFORM/EXECUTE). The pre-v15 idempotent insert: BEGIN INSERT ... EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation THEN NULL; END — today ON CONFLICT is cleaner.
questions.explanation: Exception blocks are subtransactions — expressive, but not free in tight loops.

questions.prompt: The planner chooses a catastrophic nested-loop join on a correlated (city, state) predicate pair. Explain why single-column statistics fail here, what extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS) fixes, and how you'd confirm the fix.
questions.reference_answer: The planner multiplies per-column selectivities assuming independence — correlated columns (city implies state) make the estimate orders of magnitude low → nested loop over millions. CREATE STATISTICS (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON city, state gives the planner the joint distribution; ANALYZE then records it. Confirm: EXPLAIN ANALYZE rows≈actual and the plan flips to hash/bitmap.
questions.explanation: Bad plans are often good planners fed bad statistics — fix the input, not the symptom.

questions.prompt: Defend or refute: 'A multicolumn index on (a, b) makes a redundant single-column index on (a) unnecessary.' Include leftmost-prefix reasoning, the caveat for queries on b alone, and write-cost considerations.
questions.reference_answer: Largely true: B-tree (a,b) orders by a first — equality/ranges on a alone use it efficiently, so a separate (a) index is redundant. Caveat: queries on b alone can't use (a,b) well (b is unordered within a-groups); and every index costs write/space — keeping both duplicates overhead. The reverse is not true: (a) does not serve (a,b) queries optimally.
questions.explanation: Index design is prefix algebra — order your keys to cover the query shapes you actually run.

questions.prompt: An ALTER COLUMN TYPE on a hot 200M-row table must ship without downtime. Explain what a naive ALTER does (rewrite + ACCESS EXCLUSIVE), and the staged-migration pattern that avoids it (add column, dual-write/backfill, validate, swap).
questions.reference_answer: A type change that alters storage forces a full table rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE — minutes of full outage. Pattern: ADD COLUMN new (metadata-only or cheap default), deploy dual-write or trigger, backfill in batches, validate, then swap names/redirect reads and drop old — possibly with NOT VALID constraint + VALIDATE to shorten locks. REINDEX/validations still need care on hot tables.
questions.explanation: Schema evolution on hot tables is a deployment pattern, not a single DDL statement.

questions.prompt: Explain search_path resolution: where unqualified names are sought, which schemas are implicitly searched, the security implications of a hostile schema on the path (especially for SECURITY DEFINER functions), and how to pin it.
questions.reference_answer: Unqualified names resolve left-to-right through search_path ($user then public by default); pg_catalog is searched implicitly unless listed. Creation lands in the first valid schema. Risk: if an attacker can create objects in a schema earlier on someone's path (or shadow built-ins), unqualified calls pick theirs — critical in SECURITY DEFINER context. Fix: SET search_path explicitly per role/function and qualify names.
questions.explanation: search_path is a name-resolution chain — every unqualified name is a security decision.

questions.prompt: timestamptz vs timestamp: design guidance for an events table in a multi-timezone product. Cover what each stores, how session TimeZone changes output, interval arithmetic pitfalls (DST), and a schema recommendation.
questions.reference_answer: timestamptz stores an absolute instant (UTC internally) — correct for 'when did it happen'; display follows session TimeZone. timestamp stores a wall-clock reading with no zone meaning — correct for '3pm local at the store' schedules. Pitfall: adding interval '1 day' across DST changes absolute vs calendar semantics differently per type. Recommendation: timestamptz + store reporting zones separately.
questions.explanation: timestamptz is for instants; timestamp is for unanchored wall-clocks — most 'times' are instants.

questions.prompt: A jsonb 'attrs' column supports arbitrary facet search (color, size...). Explain containment query + GIN indexing, jsonb_path_ops vs jsonb_ops tradeoff, and when an EAV relational design or generated columns + B-tree beats jsonb.
questions.reference_answer: attrs @> '{"color":"red"}' uses GIN: jsonb_ops indexes all keys/values supporting @>, ?, ?|, ?&; jsonb_path_ops is smaller/faster but only supports @> (and jsonpath). At scale with hot facets, generated columns extracting keys + B-tree or a real EAV/attribute table gives better selectivity and typed predicates; jsonb wins on schema flexibility.
questions.explanation: jsonb+GIN is real infrastructure — but typed columns still beat it on hot paths.

questions.prompt: An org-chart closure query must return all descendants of a node. Explain how WITH RECURSIVE evaluation works (working table, iteration, termination), why cyclic hierarchies break naive queries, and the two fixes (UNION vs CYCLE clause).
questions.reference_answer: The non-recursive term seeds the working table; each iteration joins new rows into the CTE until an empty iteration ends it. A cycle (a→b→a) without dedup loops forever. UNION (not ALL) deduplicates rows — cycles terminate but duplicates also die (correct for sets of nodes). The CYCLE clause marks repeated paths and stops re-expansion — better when path shape matters; SEARCH orders traversal depth/breadth.
questions.explanation: Recursive CTEs are graph traversal in SQL — termination is a property you must design for.

questions.prompt: Explain transaction ID wraparound: what XIDs are, why 32 bits forces recycling, what 'freezing' does, and what happens operationally if a database approaches wraparound (including why autovacuum can't be fully switched off).
questions.reference_answer: Every transaction consumes a 32-bit XID (~4B); visibility compares ages relative to current XID — after ~2B transactions the comparison wraps and old committed tuples would look 'future'. VACUUM freezes old tuples (marks them always-visible) before the horizon. Ignoring wraparound forces PostgreSQL into emergency aggressive vacuum, then shutdown-protection mode — hence autovacuum's mandatory role.
questions.explanation: Wraparound is why VACUUM is not optional — it is existential maintenance.

questions.prompt: Explain the write-ahead logging rule, what happens on a crash between 'data page written' and 'commit record flushed', and how checkpoints bound recovery work.
questions.reference_answer: WAL rule: a change's log record must reach stable storage before the data page it describes. On crash, recovery replays WAL from the last checkpoint — a commit whose record never flushed is simply absent (rolled back logically). Checkpoints flush dirty pages so replay only needs WAL after them; they trade burst I/O for bounded crash-recovery time.
questions.explanation: Durability comes from ordering: log first, data later — crash recovery is 'replay the log'.

questions.prompt: shared_buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem: explain what each bounds, why work_mem×nodes can exceed expectations, and a safe-first-tuning approach for a 16GB dedicated server.
questions.reference_answer: shared_buffers = the server's page cache (~25% RAM is a sane start). work_mem = per sort/hash node — a plan with 8 sorts can use 8×; OLTP keeps it modest, reporting can raise it per-session. maintenance_work_mem = vacuum/index-build workspace (separate budget). Approach: small conservative global values, measure, raise per-workload via SET LOCAL rather than globally.
questions.explanation: Memory tuning is about concurrency multipliers, not 'more is better'.

questions.prompt: Your app slows down every afternoon. Describe a monitoring workflow using pg_stat_activity (live state), pg_stat_statements (aggregate offenders), and pg_stat_user_tables (seq_scan vs idx_scan, dead tuples) to localize the cause.
questions.reference_answer: pg_stat_activity during the slowdown: find wait states, long queries, blocking chains. pg_stat_statements for the top cumulative time consumers (mean_exec_time×calls) — separates 'always slow' from 'afternoon storms'. pg_stat_user_tables reveals seq_scan-heavy hot tables needing indexes and n_dead_tup growth needing vacuum tuning. Correlate with cron/batch jobs overlapping the window.
questions.explanation: Diagnosis sequence: what runs now (activity) → what costs most overall (statements) → what tables suffer (stats).

questions.prompt: Design full-text search for a support-ticket system: tsvector column population (generated column vs trigger), the config/language choice, GIN indexing, query-side tsquery variants, and headline/ranking basics.
questions.reference_answer: Store a generated tsvector column from title+body (to_tsvector('english', ...)) or maintain via trigger; use a fixed dictionary config so lexemes are stable. GIN index on the vector. Query side: plainto_tsquery for free text, to_tsquery for boolean control, websearch_to_tsquery for user syntax; @@ matches, ts_rank orders; ts_headline renders snippets.
questions.explanation: FTS is a pipeline (document→vector→index→query→rank), not a WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: Your LEFT JOIN 'loses' unmatched rows after you add WHERE r.status='active'. Explain the bug precisely (evaluation order vs NULL padding), give the correct rewrite, and when the WHERE-form is actually intended.
questions.reference_answer: LEFT JOIN pads unmatched right columns with NULL; a WHERE on r.* filters those padded rows out — recreating an inner join. Fix: put the predicate in the ON clause (filter the right side before padding) or make it NULL-tolerant. The WHERE form is correct only when you genuinely want inner-join semantics — then write INNER JOIN for clarity.
questions.explanation: Predicate placement (ON vs WHERE) changes outer-join semantics — the classic bug.

questions.prompt: Compare CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF and GREATEST/LEAST for: defaulting a column, guarding division, mapping codes to labels, and clamping to a range. For each, give the idiomatic choice and one misuse to avoid.
questions.reference_answer: Default → COALESCE (first non-null chain). Division guard → NULLIF (x/NULLIF(y,0)). Code mapping → CASE (readable branches; simple CASE for equality). Clamp → GREATEST/LEAST (PG's NULL-ignoring semantics — beware assuming NULL propagation). Misuses: CASE re-evaluating volatile expressions per branch; COALESCE evaluating a subquery twice vs NULLIF clarity; GREATEST on all-NULL rows giving NULL.
questions.explanation: Each conditional has an idiom — pick the one that says what you mean.

questions.prompt: name LIKE 'Jo%' is fast but '%son' is not — explain left-anchored vs contains matching and B-tree index usage, what ILIKE changes for indexes, and the escape rules. Mention pg_trgm as the contains alternative.
questions.reference_answer: 'Jo%' is a left-anchored prefix — a B-tree on name can range-scan the prefix interval (collation caveat: needs C-locale-style ops or text_pattern_ops for LIKE). '%son' has no anchor — full scan. ILIKE doesn't change indexability (expression index on lower(name) helps). pg_trgm GIN indexes trigram similarity enabling contains/regex searches.
questions.explanation: Indexes need left edges — 'contains' searches need a different index structure.

questions.prompt: When is a text[] column better than a child table for multi-valued attributes (e.g. product tags)? Cover query/unnest ergonomics, GIN indexing, ordering/uniqueness semantics and the normalization tradeoff.
questions.reference_answer: Arrays fit small bounded lists queried as sets — unnest explodes for analysis, @>+GIN gives membership search, no join needed. Lost: per-element foreign keys, uniqueness constraints, ordering guarantees, per-element updates, standard tooling expectations. Child table = proper modeling when elements have identity/lifecycle or need FK/UNIQUE. tags[] for simple labels; line items never in arrays.
questions.explanation: Arrays are a denormalization convenience — choose them knowing exactly what integrity you gave up.

questions.prompt: When is a procedure better than a function in PostgreSQL? Cover CALL vs SELECT invocation, transaction control (COMMIT inside), return values vs OUT params, and one scenario each where each is wrong.
questions.reference_answer: Procedures run via CALL, return nothing directly (OUT params optional), and can commit/rollback mid-run — long batch jobs with periodic commits. Functions run in SELECT, return values/SETOF, cannot control transactions. Wrong uses: a procedure for a value needed in a query; a function for a job that must commit incrementally (would hold one giant transaction).
questions.explanation: Functions compute inside a transaction; procedures orchestrate work across commits.

questions.prompt: Explain UNLOGGED vs TEMPORARY vs regular tables: durability, visibility, WAL overhead, lifetime semantics — and pick the right kind for an ETL staging table, a session-scratchpad, and the canonical orders table.
questions.reference_answer: Regular: WAL-logged durable shared tables — orders. UNLOGGED: skips WAL (fast writes) but truncated on crash — ETL staging where reload is cheap. TEMPORARY: session-private, optionally ON COMMIT DROP, invisible to others — per-session scratchpad; also not WAL-logged but for isolation reasons.
questions.explanation: Table durability/visibility are independent axes — pick per data lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Enum type vs lookup table for an order status field: compare storage, adding values, renaming values, foreign-key semantics, cross-schema portability and reporting-tool expectations.
questions.reference_answer: Enum: compact 4-byte storage, declared order, type-safe — but adding values needs ALTER TYPE (transaction caveats), can't be dropped per-value, and tools see an opaque type. Lookup table: FK enforcement, ON UPDATE actions, values manageable via DML, self-documenting for BI joins — costs a join/int column. Enum suits stable closed sets; lookup table for evolving business vocabularies.
questions.explanation: Closed stable sets → enum; business-evolving vocabularies → table.

questions.prompt: Why does 'abc' + 1 fail but '10' + 5 return 15? Explain PostgreSQL's unknown-literal resolution, the difference between implicit/assignment/explicit casts, and the design risk of relying on implicit casts in application SQL.
questions.reference_answer: Unknown literals take the type context demands: + on '10' resolves it as integer; 'abc' fails integer input validation at parse/execution. Cast kinds: implicit (automatic, e.g. int→numeric), assignment (on column write), explicit (CAST/::). App risk: implicit behavior varies by context/version and hides conversions — explicit casts at boundaries make intent auditable and avoid 'it worked until the type changed'.
questions.explanation: Implicit casts are conveniences with rules — explicit intent survives schema evolution.

questions.prompt: An app serves 10k tenants via connection pooling — one DB role, many app users. Design the row-security integration: how the tenant id reaches the policy (SET LOCAL vs session GUC), transaction-scoping pitfalls in pooled transactions, and why per-request SET must be mandatory.
questions.reference_answer: Pattern: pool sets SET LOCAL app.tenant = '42' inside each transaction; policy USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int). SET LOCAL is transaction-scoped — resets at commit, safe for pooling. Pitfalls: a plain SET leaks across the pool boundary between checkouts; a transaction missing SET gets default-deny (fail closed — good). The pool middleware must guarantee the SET runs before any tenant query — a forgotten set must never return wrong-tenant data.
questions.explanation: RLS + pooling works — but only if the tenant context is transaction-scoped and mandatory.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table is read frequently by a filtered column and also receives frequent INSERT and UPDATE operations. Explain how adding a B-tree index affects both workloads, and when that index may not be worthwhile.
In an ER model, a dependent entity can exist only while its owning entity exists, and its identifying key includes the owner's primary key. Which relational mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: A weak entity is identified through its owner: the owner key is part of the weak entity's primary key and also a foreign key. The composite key prevents two owners from sharing partial-key values, and the foreign key plus deletion rules preserve existence dependence. A surrogate key alone does not encode the identifying relationship; a delimited list is non-atomic; and a nullable foreign key contradicts the stated existence dependency.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: An order must belong to exactly one customer, and a customer may place zero or more orders. Where should the foreign key be placed to represent this one-to-many relationship?
questions.explanation: On the many side, each order stores one customer key, so customer_id in orders can be NOT NULL and reference customer. Putting order_id in customer would allow at most one order per customer and creates a circular dependency. A junction table is needed for many-to-many, not one-to-many. Duplicating descriptive customer columns reintroduces update anomalies and does not enforce the relationship.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: A supplier and the parts it supplies are stored in part(part_id, part_name, supplier_id, supplier_name, supplier_city). Deleting the last part supplied by a supplier also erases the only record of that supplier's name and city. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: The row mixes two entities, part and supplier. Deleting the last part necessarily deletes the supplier information that has no separate home: that is a deletion anomaly. Insert anomalies and update anomalies are related redundancy problems, but the stated symptom is loss of facts on deletion. A phantom read is a transaction-isolation phenomenon and has nothing to do with schema design.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: An orders table repeats customer_phone on every order row. When a customer changes phone number, the application must update many rows, and a missed row leaves contradictory values. Which anomaly does this describe?
questions.explanation: The same customer fact is repeated across rows, so one logical change needs many physical updates; missing one creates inconsistency. That is the definition of an update anomaly. Deletion and insert anomalies concern losing facts or being unable to record facts; serialization anomalies belong to concurrency control, not to the schema's redundancy.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: An employee may have several skills. Which design both models the relationship correctly and keeps attribute values atomic?
questions.explanation: A multivalued attribute becomes its own relation whose key combines the owner key and the value key; each cell then holds one value. A delimited string and a JSONB array both store several values in one cell, which is not atomic in the relational model even though PostgreSQL permits those types. Fixed skill_1..skill_3 columns are a repeating group and impose an arbitrary limit.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of normalization?
questions.explanation: Normalization decomposes relations according to functional dependencies so that each fact is stored once, reducing insertion, update and deletion anomalies. It does not eliminate joins (good decompositions often require them), it is the opposite of adding redundant columns, and indexes are a physical performance concern unrelated to normal-form correctness.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Every loan must be associated with exactly one member, while a member may have no loans. Which relational constraint expresses the mandatory participation of loan in the relationship?
questions.explanation: Mandatory participation on the many side is enforced by making the foreign key NOT NULL: every loan row must name an existing member. UNIQUE would incorrectly restrict each member to one loan. Putting the foreign key in member reverses the relationship and cannot represent several loans per member. A numeric CHECK says nothing about existence of the referenced member.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: The table contact(customer_id, phone_1, phone_2, phone_3) stores up to three phone numbers per customer and leaves unused columns NULL. Which normal form is most directly violated, and why?
questions.explanation: 1NF requires each attribute position to hold one atomic value and forbids repeating groups. Numbered columns are a repeating group and also cap the number of phones. The table's key is the single attribute customer_id, so partial dependency (2NF) cannot arise here, and no transitive or non-superkey determinant is described; the defect is at the atomicity level.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Table customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT) stores one row per customer. Return one row per city with columns city (TEXT) and customers (BIGINT), counting the customers in that city. Include a group for NULL city. Order by city ascending with NULLs last.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT city, count(*) AS customers FROM customer GROUP BY city ORDER BY city NULLS LAST
questions.explanation: GROUP BY city forms one group per distinct non-NULL value and one group for all NULLs; count(*) counts rows in each group, not distinct customers, which is correct because customer_id is the primary key. NULLS LAST makes the NULL group deterministic. The empty dataset returns no rows, which is the correct result rather than an error.

questions.prompt: Table customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL) and table orders(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, amount NUMERIC(10,2)). Return order_id (INT), name (TEXT) and amount for every order. If an order's customer_id has no matching customer, return the order with a NULL name. Order by order_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customer c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_id
questions.explanation: The relationship is optional from the order side in this dataset, so a LEFT JOIN keeps every order and produces NULL when no customer matches, including an orphan key and a NULL key. Duplicate customer names are not a problem because the join uses the key. With no orders the result is empty, and the column set is still determined by the SELECT list.

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C,D) has functional dependencies AB -> CD and D -> A. A BCNF decomposition produces R1(A,D) and R2(B,C,D). Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: The candidate keys are AB and BD: AB+ is all attributes, and BD+ reaches A through D -> A and then C through AB -> C. D -> A violates BCNF. The split has common attribute D, and D -> A makes D a key of R1, so the join is lossless. R2 has no nontrivial projected dependency, but AB -> CD cannot be checked inside either relation because it needs A from R1 and B,C,D from R2. BCNF decompositions therefore need not preserve dependencies.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C,D,E) satisfies AB -> C, C -> D, D -> E and E -> B. Which set is exactly the set of candidate keys?
questions.explanation: AB+ = {A,B,C,D,E}. AC+ reaches D through C -> D, E through D -> E, and B through E -> B, so AC is a key. AD+ reaches E through D -> E, B through E -> B, and C through AB -> C, so AD is a key. AE+ reaches B through E -> B, C through AB -> C, and D through C -> D, so AE is a key. No pair without A determines all attributes: BC+ lacks A and every other pair is smaller. Hence exactly AB, AC, AD and AE are minimal keys.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C,D,E) has functional dependencies AB -> C, C -> D and D -> E. The only candidate key is AB. Which set of relations is a correct 3NF synthesis of R?
questions.explanation: The given FDs form a minimal cover, so synthesis creates one relation per dependency: (A,B,C), (C,D), (D,E). The candidate key AB is contained in R1, so no extra key relation is needed. Each relation's determinant is a key of that relation, so the result is in BCNF, lossless and dependency-preserving. Option B loses AB -> C; the unchanged relation is not in 3NF because C -> D and D -> E are transitive; option A does not preserve any of the original dependencies.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C) satisfies B -> C and is decomposed into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). Which functional dependency is the reason the decomposition is lossless?
questions.explanation: The common attribute is B. Losslessness requires the common attributes to be a superkey of at least one projection. B -> C means B determines every attribute of R2(B,C), so B is a key of R2 and the join cannot invent tuples. Attribute preservation alone does not guarantee losslessness, and no dependency on A or C is given.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table stores tags TEXT[] with several tag values in one row. Relationally, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: 1NF is a relational-model property: each attribute position holds a single value. PostgreSQL's array type is a deliberate extension that permits non-1NF storage, not evidence of atomicity. A child relation with one tag per row restores 1NF and supports constraints, joins and dependency reasoning. There is no composite key described here, and array use neither implies nor prevents 3NF.

questions.prompt: Person is specialized into Employee and Contractor. A person may be both, and every person must be at least one of the two. Which mapping enforces the model most faithfully in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Shared attributes belong in the supertype, and each subtype table references it with the same primary key, so a person can appear in both subtype tables (overlapping specialization). A foreign key from subtype to supertype enforces that subtype rows have a person, but SQL cannot enforce the reverse 'every person has a subtype' constraint; that requires a trigger, assertion-like check, or a role table. Duplicated subtype tables lose identity; nullable role columns cannot represent both roles independently; the UNIQUE constraint in option D forbids overlap.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: Relation R(student_id, course_id, student_name, course_title, grade) has primary key (student_id, course_id), with student_id -> student_name and course_id -> course_title. Which decomposition reaches 2NF and preserves both dependencies and the join?
questions.explanation: Both non-prime attributes depend on a proper subset of the composite key, so 2NF requires removing each partial dependency into its own relation. The enrollment relation keeps the full-key dependency grade. Joining back on student_id and course_id is lossless because each common attribute is a key of its reference relation, and all three original dependencies are enforceable inside one relation each. Option C repeats the attributes and does not normalize; option A is the original 1NF relation.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Relation R(Student, Course, Teacher) has functional dependencies (Student, Course) -> Teacher and Teacher -> Course. Its candidate keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Teacher). Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Teacher -> Course has a non-superkey determinant, so BCNF fails. Course is prime (it appears in the candidate key (Student, Course)), so 3NF's prime-attribute exception applies and R is in 3NF. Splitting on Teacher is lossless because Teacher is a key of (Teacher, Course). The dependency (Student, Course) -> Teacher requires both Student and Course, which no single decomposed relation contains, so it is not preserved. 2NF is about partial dependencies by non-prime attributes; Course is prime.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Payment numbers are unique only within a loan, and a payment cannot exist without its loan. Which primary-key definition correctly maps this weak entity?
questions.explanation: The identifying owner key loan_id plus the partial key payment_no forms the weak entity's composite primary key. The foreign key enforces existence dependence, and ON DELETE CASCADE removes payments when their loan disappears. A nullable owner key permits orphans; adding amount to the key changes identity; and uniqueness on payment_no alone contradicts the statement that numbers repeat across loans.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C,D) satisfies AB -> C, C -> D and D -> B. Its candidate keys are AB, AC and AD. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Every attribute is prime (A, B, C and D each occur in at least one candidate key), but BCNF cares about determinants, not whether attributes are prime. C and D are not superkeys, so C -> D and D -> B violate BCNF. Because D and B are prime, 3NF's exception applies and the relation is in 3NF. 2NF is satisfied because the key is composite and no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset; 1NF concerns atomic values.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Table category(category_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, parent_id INT) represents a self-referencing one-to-many relationship; NULL parent_id marks a root. Assuming no cycles, return category_id, name, depth (INT, 0 for roots) and root_name (TEXT, the name of the top-level ancestor) for every category reachable from a root. Rows whose parent chain never reaches a root are not returned. Order by depth ascending, then category_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (SELECT category_id, name, 0 AS depth, name AS root_name FROM category WHERE parent_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT c.category_id, c.name, t.depth + 1, t.root_name FROM category c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.category_id) SELECT category_id, name, depth, root_name FROM tree ORDER BY depth, category_id
questions.explanation: The recursive term starts from roots and adds one level per iteration while carrying the root name, which implements the parent-child relationship without assuming a fixed depth. In the edge dataset the two roots are returned with the same name, which is legal because names are not keys, and the orphan whose parent does not exist is unreachable and therefore excluded. ORDER BY makes the result deterministic across executions.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: Table employee(employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept_id INT, dept_name TEXT) may contain transitive-dependency violations. Return dept_id, name_variants (BIGINT: distinct non-NULL dept_name values) and employees (BIGINT: rows in the department) for every non-NULL dept_id that has more than one distinct non-NULL dept_name. Order by name_variants descending, then dept_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT dept_id, count(DISTINCT dept_name) AS name_variants, count(*) AS employees FROM employee WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id HAVING count(DISTINCT dept_name) > 1 ORDER BY name_variants DESC, dept_id
questions.explanation: If dept_id -> dept_name held, each department would have one distinct non-NULL name. The HAVING clause surfaces only departments where that is false. NULL department names are not counted as a variant, so a department with several NULLs and one real name is consistent; rows with NULL dept_id belong to no department and are excluded. The edge dataset contains no violation and returns no rows.

questions.prompt: A supply chain records supply(supplier_id, supplier_name, supplier_city, part_id, part_name, project_id, project_name, quantity). The functional dependencies are: supplier_id -> supplier_name, supplier_city; part_id -> part_name; project_id -> project_name; and (supplier_id, part_id, project_id) -> quantity. (a) Identify the candidate key and prove it is minimal. (b) State the highest normal form and name every dependency that prevents the next form. (c) Decompose the relation into 3NF, listing primary and foreign keys. (d) Show that the decomposition is lossless-join and dependency-preserving.
questions.reference_answer: (a) The candidate key is {supplier_id, part_id, project_id}. It determines quantity directly and all descriptive attributes through the three single-attribute determinants. Removing any attribute loses the ability to distinguish supply facts for different suppliers, parts or projects, so it is minimal. (b) The highest normal form is 1NF. 2NF fails because supplier_name and supplier_city depend on supplier_id alone, part_name depends on part_id alone, and project_name depends on project_id alone; each is a proper subset of the composite key. Since 2NF fails, 3NF and BCNF are not reached. (c) supplier(supplier_id PK, supplier_name, supplier_city); part(part_id PK, part_name); project(project_id PK, project_name); supply(supplier_id PK/FK REFERENCES supplier, part_id PK/FK REFERENCES part, project_id PK/FK REFERENCES project, quantity). (d) Each partial dependency is removed by joining on a common attribute that is a key of the reference relation (supplier_id, part_id, project_id), so every split is lossless by the common-attribute test. Every functional dependency is enforced inside exactly one relation: the three descriptive dependencies in supplier, part and project, and the quantity dependency in supply. The result is also in BCNF.
questions.explanation: The triple is the key because quantity is meaningful only for a supplier-part-project combination. Partial dependencies on each single key attribute keep the original relation in 1NF. Splitting into supplier, part, project and supply removes them, preserves each dependency in one relation and joins back through keys, so the decomposition is both lossless and dependency-preserving.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data
Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C,D) satisfies the functional dependencies A -> B and B -> C. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Compute the attribute closure: start with {A}; A -> B adds B; B -> C adds C; no dependency has a left side contained in {A,B,C} that produces D. Therefore A+ = {A,B,C}, A is not a superkey, and no dependency implies D -> A. A candidate key must determine every attribute, which A does not.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C,D) has functional dependencies AB -> C, C -> D and D -> A. Which set is exactly the set of candidate keys?
questions.explanation: AB+ = {A,B,C,D}, so AB is a key and neither A nor B alone is. BC+ = {B,C,D,A}, so BC is a key. BD+ = {B,D,A,C}: D -> A adds A, then AB -> C adds C, so BD is also a key. AC+ = {A,C,D} and does not contain B, so AC is not a key. The three keys are minimal because no single attribute of any of them determines all four attributes.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: The relation enrollment(student_id, course_id, course_title, grade) has primary key (student_id, course_id) and the functional dependency course_id -> course_title. Which statement identifies the 2NF violation and its correct repair?
questions.explanation: 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute from depending on part of a candidate key. course_title is non-prime and depends on course_id alone, a proper subset of {student_id, course_id}. Removing that partial dependency yields course(course_id, course_title) and enrollment(student_id, course_id, grade). Depending on the full key is exactly what is allowed; grade is not the problem.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C) has functional dependencies AB -> C and C -> B. The candidate keys are AB and AC. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: 3NF permits a functional dependency X -> Y when X is a superkey or every attribute of Y is prime. C is not a superkey, but B is part of candidate key AB, so the dependency is allowed by 3NF. BCNF has no prime-attribute exception, so C -> B violates BCNF. 2NF concerns dependencies on part of a composite key by non-prime attributes; B is prime, and 1NF is about atomic values, not repeated symbols.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: The relation order_item(order_id, items) stores a value such as 'pen,notebook,stapler' in items. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: A value that packs several items into one cell is not atomic, so the relation is not in 1NF regardless of the string type. The repair is a child relation with one row per order-product pair, keyed by both identifiers. 2NF and 3NF presuppose 1NF and concern dependencies among attributes, not multiple values hidden inside one attribute.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Every laptop must be assigned to exactly one employee, and an employee has at most one laptop. Laptop participation is total. Which mapping avoids a nullable unique foreign key?
questions.explanation: The foreign key belongs on the side with total participation: laptop.employee_id NOT NULL guarantees every laptop has an owner, and UNIQUE guarantees an employee owns at most one laptop. Placing the key on employee makes it nullable for employees without a laptop. Merging imposes wide nullable columns and mixes entities; a junction table models many-to-many and would allow several owners per laptop.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: Relation R(A,B,C) satisfies B -> A and is decomposed into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). Is the decomposition lossless, and why?
questions.explanation: For a binary decomposition, the join is lossless if the common attributes form a superkey of at least one side. The common attribute is B, and B -> A means B determines every attribute of R1(A,B), so B is a key of R1. Therefore projecting onto {A,B} and {B,C} and joining back cannot create spurious tuples. Attribute preservation is not the same property as losslessness, and B -> C is irrelevant.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: A supplier supplies parts to projects. Quantity is recorded for a specific supplier, part and project, and one supplier-part pair can supply several projects. Which schema represents this relationship correctly?
questions.explanation: The fact 'this supplier supplied this quantity of this part to this project' depends on all three entities, so the associative relation's key is the triple. Binary tables cannot record a quantity that is meaningful only for the triple. Repeating parts per project duplicates part facts, and an array hides a multivalued relationship in a non-atomic value.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: Given only the functional dependency A -> B, which dependency follows by the augmentation axiom?
questions.explanation: Augmentation says that if X -> Y holds, then XZ -> YZ holds for any attribute set Z. Adding C to both sides of A -> B yields AC -> BC. B -> A would require a different dependency; A -> C cannot be inferred because C appears nowhere in the premise; C -> B is not implied either.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Which statement about 3NF synthesis and BCNF decomposition is correct?
questions.explanation: The 3NF synthesis algorithm produces a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition. BCNF is stricter and a lossless BCNF decomposition may split a dependency across relations, so dependency preservation is not guaranteed. 3NF also forbids transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on a non-superkey; BCNF has no prime-attribute exception at all.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Table customer_email(row_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT NOT NULL, email TEXT) records contact rows, and the same customer may appear more than once. Return email (TEXT), copies (BIGINT: rows with that email) and ids (BIGINT: distinct customer IDs with that email) for every non-NULL email used by more than one distinct customer. Order by copies descending, then email ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT email, count(*) AS copies, count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS ids FROM customer_email WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY email HAVING count(DISTINCT customer_id) > 1 ORDER BY copies DESC, email
questions.explanation: The audit looks for one email attached to several customers, which is evidence that email is not a key and that the relation stores redundant contact facts. count(*) counts rows, while count(DISTINCT customer_id) counts customers; the edge dataset has three rows but two customers, so both numbers are needed. NULL emails are excluded because a NULL is not a shared value.

questions.prompt: Table customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL) and table orders(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, amount NUMERIC(10,2)). Return customer_id, name, order_count (BIGINT) and total (NUMERIC, 0 when there are no orders or all amounts are NULL) for every customer, including customers with no orders. Order by customer_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, count(o.order_id) AS order_count, coalesce(sum(o.amount), 0) AS total FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name ORDER BY c.customer_id
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps customers without orders. count(o.order_id) ignores the NULL produced by the join, so the count is 0, while count(*) would incorrectly return 1. sum ignores NULL amounts, and coalesce turns the all-NULL or no-row sum into 0. Grouping by both customer_id and name keeps the query valid even though names are not unique.

questions.prompt: A library stores loans in loan(member_id, member_name, member_city, book_id, book_title, book_author, loan_date, due_date). The functional dependencies are: member_id -> member_name, member_city; book_id -> book_title, book_author; and (member_id, book_id, loan_date) -> due_date. A member may borrow the same book again on a different date. (a) Identify the candidate key. (b) Determine the highest normal form and name each dependency that prevents the next form. (c) Decompose the relation into 3NF, listing keys and foreign keys. (d) Explain why the decomposition is lossless-join and dependency-preserving.
questions.reference_answer: (a) The candidate key is {member_id, book_id, loan_date}. It determines due_date directly and determines the member and book attributes through member_id and book_id; each proper subset loses at least one attribute, so it is minimal. (b) The highest normal form is 1NF. 2NF fails because the non-prime attributes member_name and member_city depend on member_id alone, and book_title and book_author depend on book_id alone; both are proper subsets of the composite key. Because 2NF fails, 3NF is not reached. (c) member(member_id PK, member_name, member_city); book(book_id PK, book_title, book_author); loan(member_id PK/FK REFERENCES member, book_id PK/FK REFERENCES book, loan_date PK, due_date). (d) Each split removes a partial dependency and joins back on a common attribute that is a key of one side (member_id in member, book_id in book), so each step is lossless by the common-attribute test. Dependency preservation holds because member_id -> name, city is enforced in member; book_id -> title, author is enforced in book; and the key dependency on all three attributes is enforced in loan.
questions.explanation: The composite key includes the loan date because the same member can borrow the same book again. Partial dependencies on member_id and book_id keep the original relation in 1NF only. Separating member, book and loan removes them; the common attributes are keys of the reference relations, so the decomposition is lossless, and each dependency is enforceable inside one relation.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model
