questions.prompt: A customer may have been referred by another customer, but many customers have no referrer. Which schema models this optional self-referencing relationship correctly?
questions.explanation: Optional participation permits NULL, so the self-referencing foreign key must be nullable; roots simply store NULL. A NOT NULL self-reference makes the first customer impossible to insert. Storing a name instead of a key loses identity and reintroduces update anomalies. A mandatory referrer table contradicts the statement that many customers have no referrer.

source_refs.title: The Entity-Relationship Model - Toward a Unified View of Data

questions.prompt: A relation is in 2NF but not in 3NF because a non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute. Which operational problem remains?
questions.explanation: The transitive dependency is redundancy: the dependent fact is stored once per determinant occurrence, creating update, insert and delete anomalies. Non-atomic values are a 1NF problem; dependence on part of a composite key is the 2NF problem already removed; and 2NF does not imply 3NF for any key shape.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: The setup creates order_line(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, unit_price NUMERIC(8,2) NOT NULL, qty INT NOT NULL, discount NUMERIC(8,2), net NUMERIC(10,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (unit_price * qty - discount) STORED). Return order_id and net for every row, ordered by order_id ascending. A NULL discount must produce a NULL net.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT order_id, net FROM order_line ORDER BY order_id
questions.explanation: A stored generated column is computed by the database from the generation expression on every insert and update, so the SELECT reads a stored value rather than recomputing it. Because the expression uses ordinary arithmetic, a NULL discount makes the whole subtraction NULL: orders 2 and the edge rows report NULL, while order 1 reports 20.00 and order 3 reports 9.00. The column cannot be written directly.

questions.prompt: The setup creates account(account_id INT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING', opened_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT '2024-01-01') and inserts rows that sometimes name code and opened_on. Return account_id, code and opened_on for every row, ordered by account_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT account_id, code, opened_on FROM account ORDER BY account_id
questions.explanation: The identity column fills account_id from its sequence, so the INSERT statements never supply it and the generated values are 1, 2 and 3. Omitting code applies 'PENDING' and omitting opened_on applies 2024-01-01, while explicitly supplied values replace the defaults. The edge dataset exercises each default separately: one row supplies only code and receives the default date, and one row supplies only opened_on and receives the default code.

questions.prompt: A table is declared PARTITION BY RANGE (created_on) with one partition per month. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: With declarative partitioning the parent is a logical table with no storage of its own; inserted rows are routed to the partition whose bounds contain the partition key, and an insert with no matching partition fails unless a default partition exists. The planner can prune partitions when the query constrains the partition key. A primary key or unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key, but may include additional columns; partitions are not created automatically.

questions.prompt: Explain what a materialized view is in PostgreSQL, how it differs from an ordinary view, and how REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW keeps it current. State what the REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY variant requires and why a materialized view can return stale data.
questions.reference_answer: An ordinary view stores only a query and is evaluated each time it is referenced, so it always reflects current base-table data. A materialized view executes its query once and stores the resulting rows on disk, so reads are fast but reflect the data as of the last refresh. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW re-executes the defining query and replaces the stored contents; until the next refresh the materialized view can return stale rows after base tables change. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY is intended to keep the view readable while it refreshes, and it requires the materialized view to have a unique index that covers all rows, so that the old and new contents can be compared. It cannot be used on a materialized view created WITH NO DATA that has never been populated, and it is slower than a plain refresh.
questions.explanation: The answer must distinguish stored results from a stored query, describe REFRESH as re-running the query, and explain staleness. It must state that CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and permits reads during refresh.

questions.prompt: Table enrolment is created with PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id). Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: A primary key is a composite unique constraint plus NOT NULL on every participating column. Uniqueness applies to the combination, not to each column separately, so one student may enrol in many courses. NULLs are rejected in primary-key columns, and a constraint is part of the table definition from creation onward.

questions.prompt: Which statement about automatically updatable views is correct?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL makes a view automatically updatable when it selects from exactly one table or updatable view and contains no DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING, LIMIT, OFFSET, set operation, aggregate, window or set-returning function. WITH CHECK OPTION adds a guard: an insert or update through the view is rejected if the resulting row would not satisfy the view's own WHERE clause. Views with GROUP BY require an INSTEAD OF trigger to be modified.

questions.prompt: What does REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY require, and how does it differ from a plain refresh?
questions.explanation: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY compares the old and new contents, so it needs a unique index that covers every row of the materialized view, and it allows concurrent reads while it runs. The plain form takes an exclusive lock that blocks readers. Neither form performs incremental updates: the defining query is re-executed in full. The view must already be populated, so a view created WITH NO DATA cannot be refreshed concurrently before its first normal refresh.

questions.prompt: When a child table is created with INHERITS (parent), which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Table inheritance copies column definitions and check/not-null constraints into the child, but indexes, primary keys, unique constraints and foreign keys are not inherited. By default a SELECT on the parent includes rows from descendant tables; ONLY parent restricts it to the parent. Each table stores its own rows; there is no shared storage.

questions.prompt: The setup creates sale(sale_id INT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL, unit_price NUMERIC(8,2) NOT NULL, qty INT NOT NULL, net NUMERIC(10,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (unit_price * qty) STORED). Return region and sum(net) aliased revenue for every region, ordered by region ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT region, sum(net) AS revenue FROM sale GROUP BY region ORDER BY region
questions.explanation: Each row stores its generated net value: 20, 15, 32 and 5. Grouping by region sums those stored values to 35 for north and 37 for south, in region order. The empty dataset produces no groups, so the aggregate query correctly returns no rows rather than a single NULL row.

questions.prompt: The setup creates payment(payment_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT NOT NULL, paid_on DATE NOT NULL, amount NUMERIC(8,2) NOT NULL). The pair (customer_id, paid_on) is being considered as a candidate key. Return customer_id, paid_on and count(*) aliased payments for every pair that occurs more than once, ordered by customer_id then paid_on ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT customer_id, paid_on, count(*) AS payments FROM payment GROUP BY customer_id, paid_on HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY customer_id, paid_on
questions.explanation: A candidate key must be unique, so the audit groups by the proposed key columns and keeps only groups with more than one row. Customer 1 has three payments on 2024-01-05 and therefore cannot be identified by (customer_id, paid_on) alone; the result reports that pair with a count of 3. In the edge dataset every pair is unique, so HAVING removes all groups and the result is empty.

questions.prompt: The setup creates invoice(invoice_id INT PRIMARY KEY, unit_price NUMERIC(8,2) NOT NULL, qty INT NOT NULL, discount NUMERIC(8,2), subtotal NUMERIC(10,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (unit_price * qty - discount) STORED). Return invoice_id and subtotal for every invoice whose stored subtotal is at least 10, ordered by invoice_id ascending. Rows whose subtotal is NULL must not appear.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT invoice_id, subtotal FROM invoice WHERE subtotal >= 10 ORDER BY invoice_id
questions.explanation: subtotal is a stored generated column, so the predicate can reference it directly; the database computed it from the base columns. Invoice 1 stores 15.00 and invoice 4 stores 16.00, so both qualify; invoice 3 stores 8.00 and is filtered out. Invoice 2 and every edge row have a NULL discount, which makes the subtraction NULL, and NULL >= 10 is unknown, so those rows are excluded rather than returned.

questions.prompt: The setup creates orders, order_line and the view order_total, whose stored query groups order_line by order and sums qty * unit_price as total. Return order_id and total for every order whose total is at least 20, ordered by order_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT order_id, total FROM order_total WHERE total >= 20 ORDER BY order_id
questions.explanation: The view stores an aggregate query, so querying it returns one row per order with the computed total. Order 1 totals 20.00 and order 3 totals 24.00, while order 2 totals 15.00 and is removed by the WHERE clause on total. In the edge dataset order_line is empty, so the inner join produces no groups and the view returns no rows. Filtering on total is valid because total is an output column of the view.

questions.prompt: Table session_log(session_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, started_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'unknown', note TEXT) is empty. The statement INSERT INTO session_log DEFAULT VALUES; is executed. What is stored?
questions.explanation: DEFAULT VALUES inserts a row in which every column receives its default. The identity column generates a value, started_at takes its declared default, and note has no default and is nullable, so it becomes NULL. The statement is valid whenever every NOT NULL column can be satisfied by a default or identity.

questions.prompt: The statement INSERT INTO archive (sale_id, amount) SELECT sale_id, amount FROM sale WHERE status = 'closed'; is executed. Which rows are added to archive?
questions.explanation: INSERT ... SELECT inserts one row for every row the SELECT returns, so the WHERE clause decides which sales are archived. The source can be non-empty and the target can already hold rows; nothing prevents appending.

questions.prompt: Table account has a nullable verified BOOLEAN column. The statement UPDATE account SET verified = FALSE WHERE verified IS NULL; is executed twice in a row. What is the effect?
questions.explanation: The WHERE clause selects only rows whose value is NULL, so the first run sets them to FALSE. After that no row satisfies the predicate, so the second run updates zero rows. UPDATE never rewrites rows that fail the WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: Table task(task_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT) is used with INSERT INTO task (title) VALUES ('write report') RETURNING task_id; What does the statement return?
questions.explanation: RETURNING is available on INSERT as well as UPDATE and DELETE and reports values from the rows the statement affected. Here it surfaces the identity value generated for the new row, so the client learns the key without a second query.

questions.prompt: What is MERGE used for?
questions.explanation: MERGE compares source rows with target rows using an ON condition and runs the action of the first matching WHEN clause, so one statement can update matched rows, insert unmatched source rows and, in PostgreSQL 17, delete target rows with no source match. It is not a storage or set-operation command.

questions.prompt: INSERT INTO tag (tag_id, label) VALUES (1, 'a'), (1, 'b'); is run on tag(tag_id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT), and no row with tag_id = 1 exists yet. What is the outcome?
questions.explanation: A single INSERT statement is atomic: the primary key is checked for each proposed row, and a violation aborts the statement, so the first row is not kept either. MySQL-style per-row continuation and silent replacement both require different syntax and are not PostgreSQL behaviour.

questions.prompt: The setup creates shipment(shipment_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, carrier TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending', note TEXT) and then runs the INSERT statements shown in the dataset. Return shipment_id, carrier, status and note for every stored row, ordered by shipment_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT shipment_id, carrier, status, note FROM shipment ORDER BY shipment_id
questions.explanation: Each INSERT stores exactly the columns it names; an identity column fills its own value and any column omitted from the column list receives its default or NULL. In the first dataset one insert names status explicitly as 'delivered' while the others fall back to 'pending', and every note is NULL; the second dataset has status 'pending' everywhere because no insert names it. Because the id is GENERATED ALWAYS, the statements cannot supply shipment_id themselves.

questions.prompt: The setup creates sale(sale_id INT PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT, amount INT) and archive(sale_id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount INT), inserts rows into sale and leaves archive empty. The next step is INSERT INTO archive (sale_id, amount) SELECT sale_id, amount FROM sale WHERE status = 'closed'; Writing the INSERT itself is not possible in the sandbox, so return exactly the sale_id and amount rows that this statement would add to archive, ordered by sale_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT sale_id, amount FROM sale WHERE status = 'closed' ORDER BY sale_id
questions.explanation: INSERT ... SELECT copies one row per row returned by its SELECT, so the archived rows are exactly the 'closed' sales: 1, 3 and 4, including sale 3 whose NULL amount is copied unchanged. The second dataset has no closed sales, so the INSERT would add nothing and the correct result is empty.

questions.prompt: Explain RETURNING in PostgreSQL INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. State what values it exposes, give one example of INSERT ... RETURNING and one of DELETE ... RETURNING, and explain why returning the affected rows inside the same statement is preferable to issuing a follow-up SELECT.
questions.reference_answer: RETURNING computes an output row for every row the statement inserted, updated or deleted, and may reference that row's columns. For INSERT INTO task (title) VALUES ('x') RETURNING task_id, the generated identity value is returned. For DELETE FROM task WHERE task_id = 7 RETURNING *, the deleted row's contents are returned, which is useful for archiving. UPDATE ... RETURNING reports the values after the update. Because the rows are returned by the same statement, the client avoids a second query that could see different data if another session changed the rows in between, and it avoids guessing which row was affected. The values correspond exactly to the rows this statement modified, inside the same transactional snapshot.
questions.explanation: The answer must define RETURNING across the three statements, give a valid example, and justify atomicity: the returned rows are exactly the affected rows in the same statement, so a follow-up SELECT can race.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL 17 executes MERGE INTO stock s USING feed f ON s.item = f.item WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET qty = f.qty WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (item, qty) VALUES (f.item, f.qty) RETURNING merge_action(), s.item; What does RETURNING produce?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL 17 adds RETURNING to MERGE. The output covers every row inserted, updated or deleted by the command, and merge_action() reports which action ran for that row. Rows skipped because no WHEN clause applied are not reported.

questions.prompt: MERGE INTO product p USING feed f ON f.product_id = p.product_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET price = f.price WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE; is executed. Which rows does the NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause act on?
questions.explanation: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is a PostgreSQL extension that addresses rows of the target which the source never matched, so it is the natural place to delete products no longer present in the feed. Source rows with no target match are the ordinary NOT MATCHED [BY TARGET] case, which inserts.

questions.prompt: A MERGE source table contains two rows with the same join key, and both match one target row through an unconditional WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE. What happens?
questions.explanation: MERGE requires at most one candidate change row per target row. When several source rows match, only one is used to modify the target and any later attempt to modify the same row errors, so the whole statement fails. Deduplicating or aggregating the source before the MERGE is the standard fix.

questions.prompt: WITH pulled AS (DELETE FROM inbox WHERE processed RETURNING *) INSERT INTO archive (id, body) SELECT id, body FROM pulled ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING; is executed. What is the result?
questions.explanation: The DELETE in the CTE runs once and its RETURNING rows feed the INSERT. Because ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING is evaluated on the target, ids already archived are skipped, while the source rows are deleted regardless. The combination does not fail, and no duplicate id can be created because archive enforces uniqueness.

questions.prompt: UPDATE account a SET (tier, score) = (SELECT m.tier, m.score FROM metrics m WHERE m.account_id = a.account_id); is executed, and one account has no metrics row. What happens to that account?
questions.explanation: A multi-column assignment with a subquery sets every listed column from the subquery's single row. When the subquery yields no row, the row value is NULL, so every assigned column becomes NULL. All target rows are updated, which is why a WHERE EXISTS guard is usually added when unmatched rows should keep their values.

questions.prompt: WITH changed AS (UPDATE task SET done = TRUE RETURNING task_id) SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM changed) AS updated, (SELECT count(*) FROM changed) AS total; is executed. What do the two subqueries report?
questions.explanation: A WITH query is evaluated once per statement even when referenced several times; both subqueries therefore see the same set of rows returned by the UPDATE's RETURNING clause. There is no double execution and no restriction on referencing the CTE more than once.

questions.prompt: Table invoice(invoice_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, total INT) already contains ids 1 to 5, and the statement INSERT INTO invoice (invoice_id, total) OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (100, 50); is executed. What is the consequence?
questions.explanation: OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is exactly the escape hatch that lets an explicit value into a GENERATED ALWAYS identity column, so the statement succeeds. The sequence itself is not synchronized by the insert, which leaves a future collision unless the sequence is advanced or restarted manually. Option D describes behaviour that PostgreSQL does not perform automatically.

questions.prompt: DELETE FROM price p USING price older WHERE p.product_id = older.product_id AND older.valid_from < p.valid_from; is executed. What does it do?
questions.explanation: The target and the USING table are the same table under different aliases, which PostgreSQL allows. A row is deleted when a row with the same product_id and a smaller valid_from exists, so only rows that are not the earliest are removed; equal valid_from values do not delete each other because the comparison is strict.

questions.prompt: The setup creates account(account_id INT PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT) and staging(account_id INT PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT). The next step is UPDATE account a SET email = s.email FROM staging s WHERE s.account_id = a.account_id AND s.email IS DISTINCT FROM a.email; Writing the UPDATE is not possible in the sandbox, so return the rows the statement would change with columns account_id, old_email and new_email, ordered by account_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT a.account_id, a.email AS old_email, s.email AS new_email FROM account a JOIN staging s ON s.account_id = a.account_id WHERE s.email IS DISTINCT FROM a.email ORDER BY a.account_id
questions.explanation: UPDATE ... FROM changes each target row whose join partner supplies a value that is distinct from the stored one, and IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a comparable value. Account 1 is equal and skipped; account 2 changes from NULL to 'b@x.edu'; account 3 changes from 'c@x.edu' to NULL; account 4 has no staging row and is untouched; staging id 5 has no target row and changes nothing. The already-in-sync dataset yields no changes.

questions.prompt: The setup creates product(product_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL) and feed(product_id INT PRIMARY KEY, price INT). The next step is MERGE INTO product p USING feed f ON f.product_id = p.product_id WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE; Writing the MERGE is not possible in the sandbox, so return the target rows it would delete with columns product_id and name, ordered by product_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT p.product_id, p.name FROM product p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM feed f WHERE f.product_id = p.product_id) ORDER BY p.product_id
questions.explanation: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE addresses target rows for which the ON condition matched no source row, so the delete set is the anti-join of product against feed. In the first dataset only product 2 is absent from the feed; feed row 4 is a source-only row, which this clause does not address. The second dataset is fully matched, so the correct result is empty.

questions.prompt: Compare INSERT ... ON CONFLICT with MERGE in PostgreSQL 17 for a data-loading job. Address which statements can express which actions, how each treats a source that yields several rows per target key, what RETURNING offers in each, transaction and locking behaviour, and when you would choose one over the other.
questions.reference_answer: ON CONFLICT is an INSERT extension: it can skip or update a conflicting row, using a unique index as arbiter, but it cannot delete and it cannot update rows that the incoming set does not mention. MERGE can express INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, including PostgreSQL 17's WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE for target rows absent from the source, and PostgreSQL 17 adds RETURNING with merge_action(). Both require at most one incoming row per target row; duplicates make ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE raise an error about affecting a row twice, and make MERGE raise an error when it would modify the same target row again, so the source must be deduplicated. Both run as a single statement inside the caller's transaction and take row locks on the rows they change; ON CONFLICT relies on the unique index for arbitration, while MERGE performs a join between source and target, so its plan and locking depend on that join. Choose ON CONFLICT for simple keyed upserts where only conflicting keys matter; choose MERGE when the job must also delete target rows missing from the source or apply different actions to different classes of rows in one statement.
questions.explanation: The answer must distinguish action coverage (upsert versus insert/update/delete), name the unique index as arbiter for ON CONFLICT, describe the single-source-row-per-target rule for both, mention PostgreSQL 17 MERGE RETURNING/NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, and give a defensible selection rule.

questions.prompt: The statement INSERT INTO stock (item, qty) VALUES ('bolt', 5) ON CONFLICT (item) DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty WHERE stock.qty < EXCLUDED.qty is executed, and the stored qty for 'bolt' is 9. What happens?
questions.explanation: A WHERE clause attached to DO UPDATE is a condition on the update itself. When it is false, the conflicting row is left unchanged and the proposed row is not inserted either, so the statement simply skips that row. It never turns a conflict into an insert.

questions.prompt: A MERGE statement has two WHEN MATCHED clauses, the first guarded by AND s.priority = 'high' and the second unconditional. A target row matches a source row whose priority is 'low'. Which clause runs?
questions.explanation: MERGE evaluates WHEN clauses in the order written and runs the first one whose condition holds; later clauses are not applied to the same row. Several WHEN MATCHED clauses are legal, which is how priority-dependent actions are expressed.

questions.prompt: The statement WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM inbox WHERE archived RETURNING *) INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM moved; is executed. What is the effect?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL allows data-modifying statements inside WITH. The DELETE runs once, and its RETURNING output is the row set the INSERT consumes, so the move is atomic within the statement. A CTE is executed once even if referenced more than once, and both operations see the same snapshot.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 17, for UPDATE, what values does a RETURNING clause report?
questions.explanation: In PostgreSQL 17, RETURNING reports the row as it stands after the statement, so it shows the new values; there is no OLD relation in RETURNING. PostgreSQL 18 added OLD/NEW support, so version matters. Capturing previous values in 17 requires reading them beforehand or using a trigger. Rows matched by WHERE are reported even when the new value equals the old one.

questions.prompt: A unique expression index is defined on lower(email). Which conflict target lets INSERT ... ON CONFLICT resolve it explicitly?
questions.explanation: The unique index is an expression index on lower(email), and an expression index is not a table constraint, so ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT cannot name it. Column-list inference matches a unique index whose expressions equal the listed expressions, so the target must be (lower(email)); a bare email does not match an index on lower(email). DO ANYTHING is not PostgreSQL syntax, and a function name without its argument is not an expression.

questions.prompt: Which MERGE statement correctly uses an inline VALUES list as its source?
questions.explanation: A VALUES list used as a MERGE source must be a parenthesized subquery with a table alias and explicit column names, so that ON and the actions can refer to src.item. Without the alias and column list the source columns have no deterministic names. The other options are syntax that PostgreSQL does not accept.

questions.prompt: DELETE FROM stale s USING current c WHERE s.sale_id = c.sale_id RETURNING s.sale_id, s.amount; is executed. What does RETURNING contain?
questions.explanation: RETURNING reports the rows the DELETE removed, so it contains stale columns only. The USING table participates in the join but no row of current is deleted, and RETURNING with USING is valid.

questions.prompt: The setup creates account(account_id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance INT) and inserts rows, some with a NULL balance. The next step is UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE balance IS NOT NULL; Writing the UPDATE is not possible in the sandbox, so return the rows the statement would leave with columns account_id and balance (the new value), ordered by account_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT account_id, balance + 100 AS balance FROM account WHERE balance IS NOT NULL ORDER BY account_id
questions.explanation: The UPDATE applies to rows whose balance is non-NULL, so the resulting rows are 1 -> 100, 3 -> 350 and 4 -> 60; account 2 is excluded because NULL IS NOT NULL is false, and its NULL balance is not treated as zero. The second dataset has no matching row, so the statement would update nothing and the correct result is empty.

questions.prompt: The setup creates customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL) and staging(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL). The next step is INSERT INTO customer (customer_id, name) SELECT customer_id, name FROM staging ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO NOTHING; Writing the INSERT is not possible in the sandbox, so return the staging rows that the statement would skip because their customer_id already exists in customer, with columns customer_id and name, ordered by customer_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT s.customer_id, s.name FROM staging s JOIN customer c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id ORDER BY s.customer_id
questions.explanation: The conflict target is customer_id, so DO NOTHING skips exactly the staging rows whose key is already present. In the first dataset staging keys 2 and 3 have no customer match, so nothing is skipped; in the second dataset customer_id 2 conflicts and is skipped while 3 and 4 would be inserted. The join expresses that key overlap directly, so the second dataset returns one skipped row.

questions.prompt: The setup creates shipment(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, payload JSONB NOT NULL) and inserts JSON objects. Return order_id and the carrier value extracted from payload as text, aliased carrier, ordered by order_id ascending. Rows whose object has no carrier key, or whose carrier value is JSON null, must show NULL.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT order_id, payload ->> 'carrier' AS carrier FROM shipment ORDER BY order_id
questions.explanation: The ->> operator extracts an object field as text, so the JSON string "dhl" becomes the SQL text dhl. A missing key and a JSON null both yield SQL NULL, which is why order 3 and the JSON-null row report NULL instead of an error or an empty string. Using -> instead would return a JSON value rather than text.

questions.prompt: The setup creates booking(room_id INT PRIMARY KEY, period INT4RANGE NOT NULL) with half-open integer ranges. Return room_id for every booking whose period overlaps int4range(4, 6), ordered by room_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT room_id FROM booking WHERE period && int4range(4, 6) ORDER BY room_id
questions.explanation: The && operator tests whether two ranges have any common point. Because ranges are half-open, [1,5) and [5,9) both contain points that fall inside [4,6), while [10,12) does not. In the edge dataset [1,4) and [6,9) are merely adjacent to the test range and share no point with it, so the result is empty.

questions.prompt: Explain what a PostgreSQL domain is and what a collation controls. For the domain, describe how a constraint attached to the domain is enforced across every column that uses it. For collation, explain how the choice between the C collation and a locale-aware collation can change ORDER BY results and comparisons.
questions.reference_answer: A domain is a user-defined data type built on an existing base type, optionally with a DEFAULT, a NOT NULL constraint and CHECK constraints. For example CREATE DOMAIN positive_price AS numeric CHECK (VALUE > 0) creates a reusable type; every column declared with positive_price rejects values that violate the check, so the rule is defined once and enforced everywhere the domain is used. ALTER DOMAIN can add or drop constraints, and by default adding a CHECK validates existing column values. Casting a domain value to its base type produces an ordinary base-type value without the domain's constraints. A collation is the set of rules for comparing and sorting text. COLLATE selects it per expression or column, while the database and column defaults apply otherwise. The C collation compares byte values, so uppercase letters sort before lowercase letters and accents are not normalized, whereas a locale-aware collation such as en_US orders letters alphabetically, ignoring case and treating accented letters near their unaccented forms. The same text can therefore sort differently, and a unique index built with one collation can consider two strings equal that another collation considers distinct.
questions.explanation: The answer must define a domain as a named type with optional constraints, explain that its CHECK/NOT NULL rules apply to every column of that domain, and define a collation as the comparison and sort rules for text. It must give at least one concrete consequence, such as a rejected out-of-range value or a different ORDER BY result under C versus a locale-aware collation.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what do round(2.5::numeric) and round(2.5::float8) return?
questions.explanation: numeric is exact decimal arithmetic and rounds a tie away from zero, so 2.5 becomes 3. float8 follows binary floating-point rules that round ties to the nearest even integer, so 2.5 becomes 2. This is a genuine semantic difference between the two families of numeric types, not a display artifact.

questions.prompt: What does the expression DATE '2024-03-01' - DATE '2024-02-01' return?
questions.explanation: The date - date operator returns an integer count of days, and 2024 is a leap year so February has 29 days. Subtracting two timestamps, by contrast, returns an interval. Neither subtraction produces a timestamp.

questions.prompt: The table flag(v BOOLEAN) contains the three rows TRUE, NULL and TRUE. What do SELECT bool_and(v) and SELECT bool_or(v) return?
questions.explanation: Like other ordinary aggregates, bool_and and bool_or ignore NULL inputs rather than propagating them. The remaining values are all TRUE, so bool_and is TRUE and bool_or is TRUE. With only NULL inputs both aggregates return NULL, but that is not this dataset.

questions.prompt: For the expression 'ab'::char(4) || 'cd', what does PostgreSQL return?
questions.explanation: A character(4) value is blank-padded in storage, but trailing spaces are removed when the value is converted to text for the concatenation operator, so 'ab' becomes 'ab' and the result is 'abcd'. Padding is a storage and comparison property of character(n), not content that the operator carries into the result.

questions.prompt: A domain is defined as CREATE DOMAIN positive_int AS integer CHECK (VALUE > 0). Which statement about using it is correct?
questions.explanation: A domain packages a base type with constraints, and those constraints are enforced whenever a value is stored in any column of that domain, so zero and negatives are rejected everywhere the domain is used. Casting a domain value to its base type yields an unconstrained base value, whereas casting a base value to the domain applies the domain's constraints.

The inet type stores an address optionally with a netmask. The << operator asks whether the left address or network is strictly contained by the right one, so a host address (/32) inside 192.168.1.0/24 qualifies; >> asks the symmetric question and is also true here. Identical netmasks make << false, since containment is strict. Both operators return boolean.

questions.prompt: A text value is cast to boolean. Which of these input strings is NOT accepted by PostgreSQL as a boolean value?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL accepts TRUE/FALSE, the spellings t/f, true/false, y/n, yes/no, on/off and 1/0, plus unique prefixes of true and false. 'enable' is none of these and no prefix rule makes it valid, so the cast fails. The other three options are documented synonyms for true.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how character(n) and character varying(n) store and compare values?
questions.explanation: Values of type character(n) are physically padded with spaces to the declared width; trailing spaces are removed when the value is converted to another string type, and comparisons ignore them, so different declared widths can compare equal. character varying(n) stores the value without padding and only enforces the maximum length. Comparisons never raise an error merely because the declared lengths differ.

questions.prompt: Which PostgreSQL type stores a document that has been parsed into searchable lexemes for full-text search?
questions.explanation: to_tsvector parses a document into normalized lexemes and stores them, with positions, in a tsvector. A tsquery is the query side of the same search, built from search terms and operators. Plain text holds the original document, and jsonb is a structured document type, not a search representation.

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of tsvector and tsquery and the @@ operator in PostgreSQL full-text search. Show how a document is prepared and queried, describe what normalization does to words such as 'running', and explain why a LIKE '%term%' predicate is a poor substitute for full-text search.
questions.reference_answer: to_tsvector('english', body) parses body into lexemes, lowercases them, removes stop words and stems them, so 'running' becomes the lexeme 'run'. to_tsquery('english', 'run') builds a tsquery from search terms, and body_vector @@ query returns TRUE when the document matches. Because both sides pass through the same dictionary, a search for 'running' matches a document containing 'runs'. A LIKE '%term%' predicate compares raw characters: it does not stem, so 'running' does not match 'run'; it cannot express phrase, AND/OR or negated term logic; and a leading wildcard prevents ordinary index use, whereas GIN/GiST indexes on tsvector support the @@ operator.
questions.explanation: The answer must define tsvector as the normalized document, tsquery as the normalized query, @@ as matching, and show stemming so that inflected forms match. It must state at least two concrete reasons why LIKE with a leading wildcard is worse.

questions.prompt: What do round(-1.7) and trunc(-1.7) return for a numeric argument?
questions.explanation: round moves to the nearest integer, so -1.7 becomes -2. trunc discards the fractional part toward zero, so -1.7 becomes -1. On negative values the two functions therefore diverge; trunc is not a synonym for rounding.

questions.prompt: Columns a and b are both declared INT. The expression a / b is evaluated with a = 7 and b = 2. What is the result, and how do you obtain 3.5?
questions.explanation: Division between two integers performs integer division, which truncates the fractional part, so 7 / 2 is 3. Promoting one operand to numeric or double precision changes the operator to a fractional division and yields 3.5. No rounding and no error occurs.

questions.prompt: What does mod(-7, 3) return in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: mod returns the remainder of the division and takes the sign of the dividend, so -7 = (-3) * 3 + 2 does not describe the result; the truncating quotient is -2, leaving remainder -1. The positive counterpart mod(7, 3) is 1, which is why the sign must be checked explicitly when a non-negative remainder is required.

questions.prompt: Given that the column middle_name is NULL, how do 'An' || middle_name || 'Le' and concat('An', middle_name, 'Le') differ?
questions.explanation: The || operator is NULL-propagating: a NULL operand makes the whole concatenation NULL. concat is a function that treats NULL arguments as empty strings, so it returns 'AnLe'. This difference matters when building labels from optional columns.

questions.prompt: For a UTF-8 database and the value name = 'é' (one character, two bytes), what do char_length(name) and octet_length(name) return?
questions.explanation: char_length counts characters, so the accented character counts once. octet_length counts bytes in the server encoding, and in UTF-8 'é' occupies two bytes. Neither function pads or trims the value.

questions.prompt: Column code contains the value 'A_B'. Which LIKE pattern matches that literal underscore rather than treating it as the single-character wildcard?
questions.explanation: In LIKE, _ matches any single character, so 'A_B' also matches 'AXB'. Escaping the underscore with an ESCAPE character makes it literal. 'A__B' requires two extra characters, and SIMILAR TO keeps _ as a wildcard as well.

questions.prompt: Which statement about pattern matching is correct?
questions.explanation: LIKE treats the pattern as a whole-string match unless % wildcards extend it, so 'Post' does not match 'PostgreSQL'. The ~ operator matches a substring anywhere unless the pattern is anchored with ^ and $. ILIKE is the case-insensitive counterpart of LIKE.

questions.prompt: Given today = DATE '2024-02-28', what is today + 1?
questions.explanation: Adding an integer to a date advances the date by that number of days, and calendar rules apply, so 2024-02-28 plus one day is 2024-02-29 because 2024 is a leap year. Adding an interval would also work, but an integer is not interpreted as seconds.

questions.prompt: For the text 'database systems', which statement correctly contrasts plainto_tsquery and phraseto_tsquery?
questions.explanation: plainto_tsquery turns the input into terms combined with AND (&), so each term may appear anywhere. phraseto_tsquery combines the terms with the phrase operator <->, which requires them to be adjacent and in the given order. Both run the words through the text search dictionary, so stemming is applied in both.

questions.prompt: In a tsquery, what does the expression 'alpha <-> beta' require?
questions.explanation: The <-> operator is the phrase operator: it requires its operands to be adjacent and in the specified order. The & operator means both anywhere, | means either, and ! negates. Sentence proximity, not strict adjacency, would be expressed with a distance operator such as <N>.

questions.prompt: What does websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'database or network -nosql') produce?
questions.explanation: websearch_to_tsquery parses the input as 'databas' | 'network' & !'nosql' (terms are stemmed). The minus negates only the following term, and & binds more tightly than |, so the query means database OR (network AND NOT nosql). A document that contains database and nosql but not network still matches. The function never raises an error for such input, which is why it suits raw user text.

questions.prompt: A child table has a foreign key column customer_id referencing customers(customer_id). Does the foreign key automatically provide an index for queries that filter or join on the child's customer_id?
questions.explanation: A foreign key constraint enforces referential integrity; it does not create an index on the referencing side. When a parent row is deleted or its key changes, PostgreSQL must find child rows that reference it, and joins on the child column also need an index. Without one, those operations can scan the whole child table. Primary key and UNIQUE constraints are the constraints that create indexes automatically.

questions.prompt: Which constraint automatically creates an index on the constrained column in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints are enforced with a unique B-tree index, which is why lookups by the constrained columns are fast. CHECK and NOT NULL are validated per row without an index. A FOREIGN KEY is also validated without creating an index on the referencing column.

questions.prompt: A B-tree index exists on orders(created_at). A query runs SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20. What is the main benefit of the index?
questions.explanation: An ordered index scan can produce rows in created_at order and stop after the requested limit, avoiding a sort of the whole table. It does not guarantee that only 20 rows are read when filters are applied or the plan combines it with other operations. A plain index stores keys and row references, not full rows, and the query still needs ORDER BY to define the required order.

questions.prompt: A table has 2 million rows. Query A filters an indexed column matching about 0.1% of rows; Query B filters a different indexed column matching about 45% of rows. Explain why the planner may use an index for A but a sequential scan for B. Include selectivity, random I/O and the small-table case.
questions.reference_answer: A filter matching 0.1% of 2 million rows selects about 2000 rows. An index can locate those rows with relatively few page reads, so the random I/O is justified. A filter matching 45% selects about 900000 rows; visiting that many heap pages in index order causes many random reads and repeated page visits, while a sequential scan reads each page once in physical order. The planner compares estimated costs using statistics, so it may choose the sequential scan. For a small table, even a selective filter may use a sequential scan because the whole table fits in a few pages and the index lookup overhead is not repaid.
questions.explanation: Index usefulness depends on selectivity and access cost, not on the existence of an index alone. The planner estimates how many rows match from column statistics, estimates heap page visits, and compares the result with the cost of reading the table sequentially.

questions.prompt: A team proposes adding an index for every column that appears in a WHERE clause. Explain the costs of this strategy: storage, write amplification, maintenance and planner overhead. Then describe a procedure for deciding whether a proposed index is worth keeping.
questions.reference_answer: Each index is a separate structure that stores keys and row references, consumes disk and memory, and must be updated on every insert, update and delete that changes its columns. More indexes mean more WAL, more maintenance work, and potentially more planner time to consider access paths. Low-selectivity or rarely used indexes cost writes without helping reads. A practical procedure is to start from measured, frequent queries, propose the smallest set of indexes that support them, verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan, monitor write overhead, and drop indexes that are unused or redundant after a representative period.
questions.explanation: Index design is a workload trade-off. The goal is not to index every predicate but to buy the most read improvement for the least write and storage cost, using evidence rather than guesses.

questions.prompt: Why might a DBA use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY instead of CREATE INDEX on a busy production table?
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY allows ordinary writes to continue while the index is built. It performs more work and takes longer, can leave an invalid index if it fails, and cannot run inside a transaction block. It is still a normal index, not a clustered one, and the index build is WAL-logged.

questions.prompt: Queries run WHERE status = 'open' AND created_at >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY created_at. Which B-tree index best supports both the filter and the ordering?
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree is ordered by its leading column first. With status leading, an equality condition fixes the status prefix and the trailing created_at values are then ordered, so the index supports both the filter and the requested order. With created_at leading, a range scan cannot efficiently apply the status filter by index. A bitmap scan combines indexes but does not preserve order, and sorting on status alone is not a good reason to prefer the wrong column order.

questions.prompt: A parent table is deleted from frequently. The child table has a foreign key to it but no index on the child's foreign key column. What is the likely performance impact?
questions.explanation: Referential integrity checks must locate child rows that reference the parent key being deleted or changed. Without an index on the child's foreign key column, that lookup can scan the child table, so parent deletes and key updates can be slow. The constraint does not create a reverse index, and it does not impose an exclusive table-level lock for the transaction.

questions.prompt: An indexed varchar column code is compared as WHERE code = 42 while the application sends an integer parameter. What happens, and what is the clean fix?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL resolves operators by argument types. There is no character varying = integer operator, so WHERE code = 42 raises 'operator does not exist: character varying = integer'. Passing the value as text keeps the existing varchar = varchar operator and the plain index usable. If a cast on the column is intended, such as code::integer = 42, the plain varchar index no longer matches and an expression index on the cast is required. Nullability and work_mem are unrelated.

questions.prompt: An orders table with 50 million rows serves three workloads: (a) WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; (b) WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < now() - interval '1 day'; (c) a nightly report that groups by status. Propose indexes for (a) and (b), explain the column order, and explain why a new index for (c) may be a poor trade-off. Describe how you would verify the effect with EXPLAIN and usage statistics.
questions.reference_answer: For (a), an index on (customer_id, created_at DESC) supports the equality on customer_id, returns rows in the requested order and lets the scan stop after 20 rows; the DESC direction matches the index ordering and avoids a sort. For (b), a partial index on (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending' is small because only pending rows are stored and matches the predicate; alternatively a composite (status, created_at) index works but is larger. For (c), status has low cardinality and the report reads a large fraction of the table, so a sequential scan is usually efficient and an index would add write and storage cost for little read benefit; a materialized view or summary table refreshed nightly may be a better fit. Verification means comparing EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after, checking actual rows and buffers, and monitoring pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan and write latency.
questions.explanation: The proposal must connect each index to a specific query shape, explain why the column order or partial predicate matches, and justify rejecting the low-cardinality reporting index. Verification must use measured plans and usage counters.

questions.prompt: In pg_stat_activity, what does a session with state = 'idle in transaction' indicate?
questions.explanation: The state shows that BEGIN has been issued and the transaction has not ended, but no statement is running at that moment. Such sessions can hold locks, block vacuum from cleaning up rows, and keep an old snapshot alive. Very long ones are usually an application bug; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout can terminate them. Active work is shown as 'active', and a plain idle session has no open transaction.

questions.prompt: In pg_stat_database, what does xact_rollback count?
questions.explanation: The counter records transactions that rolled back, whether the application issued ROLLBACK or a statement error aborted the transaction. Lock waits are visible in pg_stat_activity, checkpoints in the checkpoint statistics, and removed rows in the vacuum and table statistics.

questions.prompt: Which utility creates a physical base backup of a running PostgreSQL cluster?
questions.explanation: pg_basebackup copies the cluster's data files while the server runs, producing a physical base backup that can be combined with archived WAL for point-in-time recovery or used to initialize a standby. pg_dump and pg_dumpall produce logical dumps that do not include the WAL needed for recovery to an arbitrary point. ANALYZE only refreshes planner statistics.

questions.prompt: Explain why simply increasing max_connections can make a PostgreSQL server slower, and how a connection pooler changes the picture. Cover per-connection memory, context switching, and the difference between idle sessions and active work.
questions.reference_answer: Each client connection has a dedicated server process with its own memory, including catalog caches and potentially large per-operation buffers such as work_mem while a query runs. Raising max_connections allows more concurrent sessions, but many active backends compete for CPU, memory and I/O and increase context switching, which can reduce throughput. Idle sessions still consume process memory and connection slots even though they do no work. A pooler keeps a small, controlled set of server connections and multiplexes many application connections onto them, so the database sees fewer backends; it must manage transaction or session state carefully and is not a substitute for fixing long-running transactions.
questions.explanation: Answer should distinguish concurrency from throughput: more connections add memory and scheduling overhead, while a pooler separates client concurrency from server concurrency.

questions.prompt: Autovacuum does more than reclaim space. Explain its two main jobs, VACUUM and ANALYZE, and what can go wrong when each falls behind on a high-churn table.
questions.reference_answer: VACUUM removes or marks reusable the dead row versions left by updates and deletes, updates the visibility map, and helps prevent transaction ID wraparound; if it falls behind, the table and its indexes bloat, scans read more pages, and eventually the database approaches a wraparound emergency. ANALYZE samples the table and refreshes statistics such as value distributions and distinct counts; if it falls behind, the planner underestimates or overestimates row counts and may choose bad joins or scans. Autovacuum schedules both, but thresholds and cost limits determine whether they keep up.
questions.explanation: The answer must separate space reclamation and wraparound protection from statistics refresh. They are related background jobs with different failure symptoms.

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between WAL, COMMIT durability and checkpoints. Why does PostgreSQL not need to write every data page at commit, and how do checkpoints affect crash recovery time and I/O spikes?
questions.reference_answer: At commit, PostgreSQL flushes the transaction's WAL records and reports success, so the change is durable even though the corresponding data pages may still be dirty in shared buffers. Data pages are written later. A checkpoint flushes dirty data pages, marks a redo position in the WAL, and allows older WAL to be recycled. After a crash, recovery starts from the last checkpoint and replays WAL from that point, so frequent checkpoints mean a shorter recovery but more frequent I/O; infrequent checkpoints reduce background I/O but make crash recovery longer. checkpoint_completion_target spreads the write work over the interval to avoid spikes.
questions.explanation: The answer must connect the write-ahead rule to durability at commit, deferred data-page writes, and the checkpoint's role as a recovery starting point with an I/O trade-off.

questions.prompt: What does a successful COMMIT guarantee?
questions.explanation: Commit makes the transaction's changes permanent from the application's point of view. With synchronous commit PostgreSQL waits for the WAL records to be flushed before reporting success, but data pages may still be written later by the background writer or a checkpoint. Indexes are updated as part of the changes, not rebuilt at commit, and transaction locks are released when the transaction ends.

questions.prompt: What is a dirty read?
questions.explanation: A dirty read observes uncommitted data from another transaction, which could still roll back. PostgreSQL does not allow dirty reads at any supported isolation level; READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement and only sees committed data. Re-reading a row and getting the same values describes repeatable behaviour, while seeing newly committed rows is a non-repeatable or phantom phenomenon, not a dirty read.

questions.prompt: Two transactions update different rows of the same table at the same time. What normally happens?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL uses row-level locks for ordinary UPDATE and DELETE; different rows do not conflict, so the two transactions can proceed concurrently. An UPDATE does take a table-level lock, but it is a mode that does not block ordinary row updates. Deadlocks require conflicting lock waits, and uncommitted changes are not visible to other transactions.

questions.prompt: A client disconnects while its transaction is still open. What happens to the transaction?
questions.explanation: If a connection is lost before COMMIT, the server cannot know whether the client intended to commit, so the transaction is rolled back. Its uncommitted changes are discarded and its locks and snapshot are released, allowing vacuum to proceed. PostgreSQL does not auto-commit an interrupted transaction.

questions.prompt: Explain how SAVEPOINT works, including ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT and RELEASE, and give a realistic case where partial rollback is better than aborting the whole transaction.
questions.reference_answer: SAVEPOINT name marks a point inside the current transaction. After a later statement fails, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes all changes made after the savepoint while keeping the transaction and the work before the savepoint alive. RELEASE discards the savepoint marker without undoing its work. A typical case is a batch that inserts many rows: each item is wrapped in a savepoint so a duplicate or invalid row can be rolled back individually and the batch can continue, instead of aborting and reprocessing everything. Savepoints create subtransactions, so using one per row has overhead and should be measured.
questions.explanation: The answer must distinguish rolling back to a savepoint from rolling back the whole transaction and explain the practical cost of subtransactions.

questions.prompt: Compare optimistic and pessimistic concurrency control in an application using PostgreSQL. Where does SELECT FOR UPDATE fit, and where do version checks plus retry or SERIALIZABLE transactions fit? Give one trade-off of each.
questions.reference_answer: Pessimistic control prevents conflicts before they happen: SELECT FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows so another transaction must wait, which is simple but can serialize work and create lock waits or deadlocks. Optimistic control lets transactions proceed and checks at write time, for example with a version column incremented in an UPDATE whose WHERE clause includes the old version; if no row is updated, the application retries. SERIALIZABLE with retry on serialization failures takes this further by detecting dangerous interleavings. Optimistic control has less blocking but requires correct retry logic and can waste work under high contention; pessimistic control is easier to reason about for short, hot updates but reduces concurrency.
questions.explanation: The answer must match each technique to a scenario and name a real cost, not claim one approach is always better.

questions.prompt: A statement fails inside an open transaction. Explain why subsequent statements fail until the transaction is rolled back, and how a savepoint changes the recovery path.
questions.reference_answer: In PostgreSQL an error aborts the whole transaction, not just the failed statement. The session is left in a failed transaction state, and further commands are rejected with a message such as 'current transaction is aborted' until the application issues ROLLBACK or COMMIT; COMMIT in this state effectively rolls back. The reason is that the database cannot guarantee a consistent state after a failed operation without undoing the transaction's earlier effects. If a SAVEPOINT was established before the failing statement, ROLLBACK TO that savepoint clears the error, undoes only the work after the savepoint, and allows the transaction to continue.
questions.explanation: The answer must explain the failed-transaction state, why only a full rollback normally clears it, and the savepoint exception.

questions.prompt: Design application retry handling for PostgreSQL serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001) and deadlocks (40P01). Explain where the retry boundary goes, which errors are retryable, how to avoid duplicate side effects, and what to log and alert on.
questions.reference_answer: Both errors abort the current transaction, so the retry boundary must be the whole transaction, not a single statement. The application should detect the SQLSTATE, roll back, and replay the transaction from the beginning with a bounded number of attempts, exponential backoff and jitter to avoid synchronized retries. Retrying should not duplicate external side effects: keep the transaction free of irreversible external calls, or use an outbox and idempotency keys. Only transient concurrency errors should be retried; constraint violations, syntax errors and authorization failures are permanent and must surface to the caller. Log the SQLSTATE, attempt count, transaction identity and latency, and alert on a rising retry rate because it signals contention or an inefficient access pattern, not a healthy success.
questions.explanation: The answer must place the retry at transaction scope, distinguish transient from permanent errors, and protect side effects and observability.

questions.prompt: How does PostgreSQL implement SERIALIZABLE isolation?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE builds on snapshot isolation and adds Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which monitors read-write antidependencies and aborts a transaction when the pattern could produce a serialization anomaly. It does not use two-phase locking for ordinary reads, so readers do not block writers, and it does not serialize transactions with a global mutex. A serialization failure means the application must roll back and retry the whole transaction; the server does not retry statements inside it.

questions.prompt: Transaction A runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and finds no row matching id = 10. Transaction B then inserts id = 10 and commits. What does PostgreSQL's row locking prevent?
questions.explanation: SELECT FOR UPDATE locks rows that exist; if the predicate matches no row, there is no row to lock. PostgreSQL does not take gap locks like some other databases, so a concurrent insert into the missing key range can proceed. To coordinate this, use a unique constraint, an advisory lock, or SERIALIZABLE isolation, which detects a dangerous dependency and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure.

questions.prompt: Under what condition can an UPDATE avoid creating new index entries for the updated row (a HOT update)?
questions.explanation: A HOT update keeps the new row version on the same page and avoids new index entries when no indexed column is changed and there is enough free space, often reserved with a lower fillfactor. The old version is chained to the new one, and index entries point to the chain. A primary key, the isolation level, or having no indexes at all are not the conditions; tables with no indexes can of course avoid index work, but HOT still matters for indexed tables.

questions.prompt: In EXPLAIN output, what does an Index Scan node mean?
questions.explanation: An Index Scan traverses the index to find entries that match the predicate, then fetches the corresponding heap tuples to check visibility and return columns. An Index Only Scan can avoid heap fetches when all needed columns are in the index and the visibility map permits it. A plan with no index access shows a Seq Scan, not an Index Scan.

questions.prompt: In an EXPLAIN plan node, what does the rows= value estimate?
questions.explanation: Each plan node has an estimated row count per execution based on statistics and selectivity estimates. It is not exact; EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds actual rows and loops so estimates can be compared with reality. Bytes are not shown as rows, and worker counts appear only for parallel plans.

questions.prompt: When is a sequential scan usually a reasonable choice?
questions.explanation: A sequential scan reads the table's pages in physical order, which is efficient when the table is small or most rows are needed. For a broad predicate, an index would visit many heap pages in less predictable order and can be slower than reading the table once. A table with indexes can still use a sequential scan, and single-row lookups usually favor an index instead.

questions.prompt: Which predicate most likely prevents a plain B-tree index on the email column from being used?
questions.explanation: A B-tree index is ordered by the leading characters of the value. A pattern with a leading wildcard, such as LIKE '%@example.com', has no fixed prefix, so the index cannot narrow the search and a scan is likely. Equality, range and IN predicates on the indexed column can use the index. Solutions for suffix searches include trigram indexes or full-text search, not a plain B-tree.

questions.prompt: Explain the main components of PostgreSQL's plan cost estimates, such as seq_page_cost, random_page_cost, cpu_tuple_cost and estimated row counts. Why is cost not a number of milliseconds, and how can actual timings differ from estimates?
questions.reference_answer: The planner assigns costs per operation using configuration constants and statistics. Reading a page sequentially has seq_page_cost, a randomly accessed page has random_page_cost, and processing a row or evaluating an operator has CPU costs. It multiplies these by estimated page and row counts derived from table statistics and selectivity estimates. The units are relative cost units, not milliseconds; their purpose is to compare alternative plans consistently. Actual time can differ because of caching, concurrency, I/O variability, inaccurate statistics, or because cost constants do not model every hardware effect. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports actual time and rows for comparison.
questions.explanation: The answer must separate relative cost units from wall-clock time and connect estimates to statistics and workload conditions.

questions.prompt: Explain what ANALYZE collects for the planner, including distinct value estimates, histograms and correlation. Why do stale statistics lead to bad plans, and what changes after a large data load?
questions.reference_answer: ANALYZE samples a table and records statistics that describe its columns: the estimated number of distinct values, a histogram of value distribution used for range selectivity, null fraction, average width and the correlation between physical row order and column order. The planner uses these to estimate how many rows a predicate returns and therefore which scan or join is cheapest. After a large insert, delete or update, the stored statistics can describe an old distribution, so selectivity estimates may be far too low or high and the planner can choose a bad nested loop, a sequential scan or a poor join order. Running ANALYZE after a bulk load, or relying on autovacuum, refreshes the estimates. Skewed or correlated columns may need a higher statistics target or extended statistics.
questions.explanation: The answer must name concrete statistics, link them to selectivity and plan choice, and explain the post-load stale-statistics failure.

questions.prompt: Explain what EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) reports for buffer usage. What is the difference between shared hits and reads, why are hits usually cheaper, and how can caching change the actual timing of a plan?
questions.reference_answer: BUFFERS adds counts of shared buffer blocks hit and read, plus local and temporary blocks, for each plan node. A shared hit means the required block was already in PostgreSQL's shared buffers; a read means it had to be fetched from the operating system or disk. Hits are usually much cheaper because they avoid I/O, although they still cost CPU and memory bandwidth. Caching can make a plan look fast on a warm cache and slow on a cold one, and it can change the planner's cost assumptions because random_page_cost may overstate or understate real SSD behavior. Measuring both warm and cold runs, and comparing estimated rows with actual rows, separates I/O effects from estimation errors.
questions.explanation: The answer must define hits and reads, explain the cost difference, and connect cache state to plan timing and planning assumptions.

questions.prompt: A query runs SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 and an index exists on created_at. What is the main benefit, and what is the main caveat?
questions.explanation: An ordered index scan can walk the index in created_at order and stop after the LIMIT is satisfied, avoiding a sort. If the query also filters on a column not in the index, the scan may inspect many index entries and heap rows before finding 10 matches, so a composite or partial index may be better. A bitmap scan does not preserve index order, and the planner still estimates selectivity.

questions.prompt: A boolean column is true for about half the rows. Queries sometimes filter is_active = true. Why is a plain B-tree index on is_active often a poor choice, and what is a better option?
questions.explanation: With two evenly distributed values, an equality predicate selects about half the table, so an index does not narrow the search enough to justify random heap access and write maintenance. If the workload actually targets a rarer subset, a partial index on that predicate stores only the interesting rows and is much smaller; if the query combines is_active with another filter, a composite index may be the better fit. B-tree does support boolean keys, and an index on this column does not disable indexes on other columns.

questions.prompt: An API paginates events with ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 OFFSET 10000. Explain why later pages become slower even with an index on created_at, and how keyset pagination changes the plan and the index requirements. Give one limitation of keyset pagination.
questions.reference_answer: With OFFSET, PostgreSQL must still produce and discard the first 10000 ordered rows before returning 50, so the work grows with the offset even when an index supplies the order. Keyset pagination remembers the last seen sort key, for example (created_at, id), and requests rows with created_at < last_created_at or a tuple comparison, so an index on (created_at DESC, id DESC) can seek directly to the next page and return only the requested rows. The limitation is that the client must carry the cursor, and the ordering key must be unique or made unique with a tiebreaker; arbitrary page jumps and changes to the sort order are harder.
questions.explanation: The answer must explain offset work, show how a keyset predicate uses an index, and name a real usability limitation.

questions.prompt: A prepared statement uses a generic plan that performs poorly for skewed parameter values. What does PostgreSQL do, and what is a reasonable response?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL normally tries custom plans for the first executions and compares their estimated cost with a generic plan; it may keep using the generic plan if that looks cheaper. With skewed data, the average generic plan can be much worse than a custom plan for specific values. Responses include forcing a custom plan for that statement, restructuring the query, improving statistics, or using dynamic SQL where appropriate. It does not permanently freeze the first plan or create indexes per parameter.

questions.prompt: What does GRANT SELECT ON orders TO PUBLIC mean?
questions.explanation: PUBLIC is a pseudo-role that represents all roles. Granting a privilege to PUBLIC makes it available to every current and future role, so it is usually too broad for application tables. It is not a normal group, and it is not limited to the current session. Auditing and revoking PUBLIC grants is a core least-privilege step.

questions.prompt: Which setup best follows least privilege for a normal application role?
questions.explanation: An application role should be able to reach the schema and perform the specific data operations it needs, without owning objects or holding administrative attributes. Superuser, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE and broad ownership turn an application compromise into a database-wide compromise. Schema USAGE is required to reference objects, while CREATE on the schema is only needed for creating objects.

questions.prompt: On a schema, what is the difference between the USAGE and CREATE privileges?
questions.explanation: Schema USAGE allows a role to look up and access objects in the schema, subject to privileges on those objects. Schema CREATE allows creating new objects in it. Having USAGE does not grant table privileges, and CREATE does not imply SELECT on existing tables. Both are separate from ownership.

questions.prompt: Who can normally ALTER or DROP a table?
questions.explanation: Ownership carries the right to alter and drop an object, and superusers can act as owners. Ordinary privileges such as SELECT or schema USAGE do not include DDL rights. For least privilege, application roles should not own the tables they use.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity, for example with a password, certificate or peer credentials. Authorization then checks the role's privileges for each action, such as SELECT on a table or CREATE on a schema. GRANT manages authorization, not authentication, and both concepts apply to ordinary roles and superusers.

questions.prompt: What does SET ROLE analyst do in a session?
questions.explanation: SET ROLE changes current_user for subsequent commands, so privilege checks use the selected role, provided the session user is a member or has been granted the role. The session user and the connection remain the same, and no role is created or granted to PUBLIC. RESET ROLE returns to the session user's default role.

questions.prompt: Explain PostgreSQL's authorization model: roles, role membership, object privileges, schema USAGE and ownership. How is a privilege check performed for a SELECT on a table?
questions.reference_answer: Every login and group is a role. A session authenticates as a role, and that role's privileges, plus privileges inherited through role membership, determine what it may do. To SELECT from a table, the role needs SELECT on the table and, if the table is in a named schema, USAGE on that schema so the name can be resolved. Ownership confers implicit rights on the object, and a superuser bypasses ordinary checks. Privileges can be granted and revoked at database, schema, table, column and sequence level, and PUBLIC represents all roles. Least privilege means granting the smallest set of these rights that the workload needs.
questions.explanation: The answer must show that authorization combines role membership, object privileges, schema access and ownership rather than a single grant.

questions.prompt: Why are PUBLIC grants and default privileges a security risk? Describe how to audit them and how ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES can make future objects safer.
questions.reference_answer: PUBLIC means every role, including roles created later, so a grant to PUBLIC on a table or function exposes it to the whole database. Defaults matter as well: PostgreSQL grants EXECUTE on functions and USAGE on types and domains to PUBLIC by default, which can expose SECURITY DEFINER routines. Auditing means checking relacl and proacl (for example through pg_class and pg_proc), information_schema.role_table_grants, role memberships and ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES settings. Revoke unnecessary PUBLIC grants and set default privileges for the role that creates objects so new tables, sequences and functions start with only the intended grants. Remember that default privileges apply per creating role and can be set FOR ROLE.
questions.explanation: The answer must explain why PUBLIC is broad, give concrete audit sources, and show that defaults govern future objects.

questions.prompt: Explain row-level security at an introductory level: enabling it, defining policies, USING versus WITH CHECK, and who bypasses it by default. Why does enabling RLS without a policy deny access?
questions.reference_answer: After ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, a table with no policies has a default-deny behaviour for ordinary users: no rows are visible and no rows may be written. A policy attaches an expression to a command. For SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE, USING controls which existing rows the role may see or target. For INSERT and UPDATE, WITH CHECK controls which new row versions may be written. Permissive policies are combined with OR, while restrictive policies are combined with AND. The table owner normally bypasses RLS, and superusers or roles with BYPASSRLS always do; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes owner queries subject to policies too. RLS filters rows, so it complements rather than replaces table privileges.
questions.explanation: The answer must distinguish USING from WITH CHECK, explain default deny and name the normal bypass cases.

questions.prompt: A login role is a member of reporting but was granted membership with INHERIT FALSE. What must it do to use reporting's privileges?
questions.explanation: INHERIT FALSE, or a member role with NOINHERIT, means the member does not automatically use the granted role's privileges. It must switch with SET ROLE, provided it has membership, and RESET ROLE afterwards. Membership does not become a PUBLIC grant, and no restart is needed.

questions.prompt: A table has a serial column whose default calls nextval on a separate sequence. An application role has INSERT on the table but no privilege on the sequence. What happens on INSERT?
questions.explanation: A serial column is a separate sequence object, and evaluating its default requires sequence access. The application role needs USAGE or UPDATE on the sequence in addition to INSERT on the table. Table INSERT does not imply sequence privileges, and the failure happens immediately rather than at sequence exhaustion.

questions.prompt: A role must see only the name and department columns of employees and only rows for its own department. Which design fits best?
questions.explanation: Column privileges restrict which columns can be read but do not filter rows, so they are insufficient for the row requirement by themselves. A view can project the allowed columns and apply a row filter, and the role is granted access to the view rather than the base table; a security barrier or SECURITY DEFINER view must be designed carefully. Alternatively, column grants plus an RLS policy handle columns and rows separately. UI hiding is not a database control, and an index does not restrict access.

questions.prompt: An application builds SQL by concatenating user input. Explain how parameterized queries prevent injection, and how least privilege and RLS limit the blast radius if a defect still allows injected SQL. Mention one danger of SECURITY DEFINER and one of dynamic SQL.
questions.reference_answer: Parameterized queries send SQL text and values separately, so input is treated as data and cannot change the statement's structure.
