String concatenation lets an attacker terminate a literal and add clauses, UNIONs or stacked statements, so prevention is the first control. If a defect remains, least privilege limits what the application role can read or change; RLS can restrict rows even when the role can run a query. A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the owner's privileges and can bypass the caller's restrictions if it is carelessly written, especially with an unsafe search_path. Dynamic SQL inside functions or procedures must use parameters (for example EXECUTE ... USING) and quote identifiers with format/quote_ident, or it reintroduces injection.
questions.explanation: The answer must separate prevention (parameters) from containment (privileges, RLS) and give one concrete definer or dynamic-SQL risk.

questions.prompt: Design a privilege audit for an existing PostgreSQL database. What would you inspect for roles, memberships, table and schema grants, sequences, default ACLs, row security and unused accounts? What would you report and remediate?
questions.reference_answer: Start with roles and attributes: superuser, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLS, LOGIN and password validity, plus role memberships that may cascade privileges. Inspect schema USAGE and CREATE grants, table ACLs (relacl), column grants, sequence grants, function EXECUTE grants and default ACLs for future objects, including PUBLIC entries. Check which tables have RLS enabled, which have FORCE, and which policies exist; a table with RLS enabled and no policy is default-deny. Review ownership so application roles do not own production objects. Identify unused or shared accounts and stale grants, then remediate by revoking unnecessary PUBLIC and group grants, separating migration and runtime roles, setting default privileges, and re-testing the application. Report findings by object, grantee, privilege source and risk, with an owner and a deadline.
questions.explanation: The answer must cover more than table grants: roles, memberships, sequences, defaults, RLS, ownership and unused accounts, plus a remediation plan.

questions.prompt: A table owner enables row-level security and defines policies, but queries run by the owner still see all rows. What explains this, and what changes it?
questions.explanation: By default the owner of a table is not subject to its row security policies, and superusers or roles with BYPASSRLS always bypass them. ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes owner queries subject to policies, but it still does not restrict superusers or BYPASSRLS. RLS applies to SELECT as well as writes, and reconnecting is not the mechanism. For a genuine test, query as a non-owner role without BYPASSRLS.

questions.prompt: A row security policy calls a user-defined function. Which risk matters most?
questions.explanation: A policy expression is evaluated as part of the query and can call functions. A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with its owner's rights, so it can bypass the caller's restrictions if it reads protected tables or returns too much data; keep policy functions simple, owned by a trusted role, and with a safe search_path. PostgreSQL does evaluate user-defined functions in policies, LEAKPROOF is a planner property and not an RLS switch, and policies do not automatically run as the table owner.

questions.prompt: An RLS policy on orders contains a subquery against accounts. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Policy expressions are part of the query, and a subquery against another table is subject to that table's row security and the caller's privileges. The result can be fewer rows than expected or extra planning and execution cost. Policies may reference other tables, and they do not gain owner rights just by being policies. Design policies to be simple and indexed, and test with the actual application roles.

questions.prompt: A non-superuser restores a pg_dump into a new database and finds ownership errors and missing grants. What is the safest explanation and response?
questions.explanation: A plain or custom pg_dump can include ALTER ... OWNER and GRANT/REVOKE commands. A non-superuser may not be able to set ownership to the original roles or grant privileges it does not hold, producing errors or a partially restored security model. --no-owner and --no-privileges skip those commands so the restoring role owns the objects and can apply a reviewed privilege plan. Default privileges do not retroactively fix restored tables, and ignoring the errors can leave a database with the wrong exposure.

questions.prompt: What does SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS add over SCRAM-SHA-256 for PostgreSQL password authentication?
questions.explanation: SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS uses channel binding so the client and server can verify that they are talking over the same TLS connection, which raises the bar for a man-in-the-middle that proxies TLS. It still uses a salted password verifier, does not encrypt the whole session by itself, and does not remove authentication. It requires TLS and client support; password_encryption controls the stored verifier format, not authorization.

questions.prompt: A table uses RLS to hide rows from a tenant. A unique constraint or foreign key check needs to inspect rows the tenant cannot see. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Referential integrity and uniqueness checks are performed against the whole table and bypass RLS, because otherwise integrity could depend on who is writing. That means a duplicate-key or foreign-key error can reveal that a hidden value exists. Use opaque keys, avoid exposing constraint details in errors, and treat RLS as row visibility for queries rather than a mechanism for hiding the existence of keys.

questions.prompt: An attacker obtains the credentials of the application's database role. Threat-model the damage and design defense in depth. Cover role privileges, RLS, schema ownership, SECURITY DEFINER code, network and authentication controls, auditing and response.
questions.reference_answer: With the application role's credentials, the attacker can do whatever that role can do, from whatever network location the authentication rules allow. Least privilege limits the blast radius: the role should have only required DML on required tables, no superuser, BYPASSRLS, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE or DDL, should not own tables, and should not be able to read unrelated schemas. RLS should be enabled with FORCE where appropriate, and the role must not bypass it; SECURITY DEFINER functions must be minimal, owned by a dedicated role, and set a safe search_path, because a compromised caller may reach them. Network controls should restrict where the role can connect, require TLS, and use strong SCRAM authentication or certificates; secrets should be rotated and never embedded in client code. Auditing should record connections and privileged operations, monitor unusual query volume, and alert on errors. Response includes revoking or rotating the credential, terminating sessions, reviewing what was accessed, restoring from a known-good backup if integrity was affected, and closing the exposure that leaked the secret.
questions.explanation: The answer must connect the stolen role's exact privileges to the damage, then layer least privilege, RLS, definer safety, network and auth controls, audit and incident response.

questions.prompt: A SQL function is declared RETURNS void. What does that mean for the caller?
questions.explanation: RETURNS void means the function has no result value. It is still executed for its side effects, for example when called as SELECT perform_maintenance();. Inside PL/pgSQL, PERFORM is the usual way to discard a result. It is not restricted to triggers, and it does not return a table.

questions.prompt: What return type must a trigger function declare?
questions.explanation: A function used by CREATE TRIGGER must return type trigger. For a row-level BEFORE trigger, returning NEW lets the operation proceed with the possibly modified row, while returning NULL skips the operation for that row. AFTER trigger return values are ignored. void, integer and the table row type are not valid trigger function return types.

questions.prompt: What does CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION do when a function with the same name and argument types exists?
questions.explanation: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION updates an existing function in place when the name and argument types match, preserving grants and dependencies. It does not create a duplicate signature, and it cannot change the function's return type; that requires DROP and CREATE. It also does not drop dependent objects automatically.

questions.prompt: What does RAISE NOTICE do inside a PL/pgSQL function?
questions.explanation: RAISE NOTICE reports a diagnostic message; depending on client and log settings it is shown to the client and written to the server log. It does not abort execution. RAISE EXCEPTION aborts the current transaction, and RAISE does not change isolation levels or write audit rows by itself.

questions.prompt: An AFTER UPDATE row trigger runs. What can it do with NEW?
questions.explanation: An AFTER trigger runs after the row change has been applied, so NEW and OLD are available for reading, but returning a modified NEW does not alter the stored row. To validate or modify the row before it is written, use a BEFORE trigger and return NEW. AFTER triggers are appropriate for auditing and cascading actions.

questions.prompt: In a PL/pgSQL set-returning function, what does RETURN NEXT do?
questions.explanation: RETURN NEXT adds the current values to the result set and lets the function continue, which is how a set-returning function can build multiple rows. A plain RETURN without an expression ends the function. RETURN NEXT does not commit transactions and is not limited to one scalar result.

questions.prompt: Design a trigger that maintains an updated_at column on UPDATE. State whether it should be BEFORE or AFTER, what it returns, how it accesses the row, and one risk for bulk loads or security.
questions.reference_answer: Use a BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW trigger. In the trigger function, assign NEW.updated_at = now() and RETURN NEW so the modified row is written. BEFORE is required because the change must happen before the row is stored; an AFTER trigger could only write a second UPDATE. NEW refers to the new row version and OLD to the previous one. Risks: the trigger fires for every row, so a bulk load can be much slower than a set-based update, and the function should have a safe search_path and not run as a careless SECURITY DEFINER routine. Consider whether the application can set the column itself before adding per-row overhead.
questions.explanation: The answer must choose BEFORE, return NEW and assign NEW.updated_at, then name a real operational risk.

questions.prompt: Compare SQL-language functions, PL/pgSQL functions and an external language for implementing a business rule. Consider set-based work, control flow, performance and maintainability, and recommend a default.
questions.reference_answer: A SQL-language function is best when the logic can be expressed as a single query or a few statements; PostgreSQL may inline it into the calling query, which can improve performance, and it keeps the logic declarative. PL/pgSQL is appropriate for procedural control flow, loops, exception handling and multiple statements, but row-by-row loops are usually slower than set-based SQL and should be reserved for cases that need them. An external language can reuse libraries but adds deployment, trust and performance overhead and may require superuser installation. The practical default is set-based SQL, then PL/pgSQL for procedural needs, and an external language only with a clear justification.
questions.explanation: The answer must connect each option to a concrete strength and cost, and give a defensible default.

questions.prompt: Explain how to validate input inside a PL/pgSQL function: using constraints, explicit checks and RAISE, and when to catch an exception. What should the caller receive on invalid input?
questions.reference_answer: Prefer declarative constraints when the rule belongs to the data: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE and foreign keys are enforced consistently for every writer. For procedural rules, test the values and use RAISE EXCEPTION with a clear message and, where appropriate, an ERRCODE so callers can distinguish error classes. Catch exceptions only when the function can recover or add context; catching and swallowing an error hides failures. On invalid input the caller should receive a failure, not a fabricated success value, and the transaction should not be left in a misleading state. Exception blocks create subtransactions, which have a cost, so do not wrap every statement.
questions.explanation: The answer must prefer constraints for data rules, show RAISE for procedural rules, and explain why errors must not be swallowed.

questions.prompt: A trigger on table A updates table B, and a trigger on B updates A. What is the main control for preventing runaway recursion?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL does not automatically stop a trigger from causing another trigger that eventually re-fires the first one. Use a WHEN condition, inspect pg_trigger_depth(), or restructure the logic so only one layer owns the relationship. A read-only transaction prevents writes but is not a general fix, and BEFORE versus AFTER does not by itself prevent recursion. Infinite recursion can consume resources or hit limits.

questions.prompt: What do transition tables provide for statement-level triggers?
questions.explanation: Transition tables are declared with REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS ... and NEW TABLE AS ... on an AFTER statement-level trigger, and give the trigger a relation-like view of all rows affected by the statement. That supports set-based auditing or cascading work without a per-row trigger. They do not expose other transactions' rows, do not change a row trigger's timing, and do not persist results automatically.

questions.prompt: Design an audit trail for changes to a business table. Cover trigger timing and granularity, old and new row capture, transaction identity, bulk operations, recursion, failure semantics and permissions. What would you sacrifice to keep the audit reliable?
questions.reference_answer: A row-level AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE trigger can write one audit row per change with operation, table, key, OLD and NEW as JSONB, current_user, transaction ID and timestamp. AFTER is appropriate because the change has succeeded and the trigger return value is ignored. For bulk operations, a per-row trigger can be expensive; a statement-level AFTER trigger with transition tables can process the whole set, or the loader can write an audit summary. Prevent recursion by ensuring the audit table has no trigger that writes back to the business table and by guarding with WHEN or pg_trigger_depth(). Decide failure semantics: if the audit insert fails, should the business change fail too? For high-assurance auditing, let it fail the transaction rather than silently lose the record. The audit writer needs INSERT on the audit table but the application should not be able to update or delete audit rows; use a dedicated role, revoke UPDATE and DELETE, and consider partitioning and retention. The cost is extra write amplification and latency, which is the price of a trustworthy trail.
questions.explanation: The answer must choose a concrete trigger design, handle bulk and recursion, and make an explicit reliability trade-off.

questions.prompt: A nightly load inserts millions of rows into a table that has row-level triggers. Explain why this is slow, how statement-level triggers with transition tables or a staging table can help, and what risks come with disabling triggers.
questions.reference_answer: Row-level triggers execute the trigger function once per inserted row, so millions of rows mean millions of function calls and possibly many extra statements or index writes. A statement-level trigger with transition tables runs once and can process the affected rows set-based, which is usually much faster. A staging table can accept the raw load and then apply one set-based INSERT or MERGE, with validation and auditing performed in bulk. Disabling triggers with ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER can speed the load, but it requires ownership or superuser, skips integrity and audit logic, and risks inconsistent data; it should be a controlled, short operation with a re-enable and verification step. Always measure before and after, because the trigger body itself may be doing per-row queries that can be rewritten set-based.
questions.explanation: The answer must explain per-row cost, offer a set-based alternative, and state the integrity and privilege risks of disabling triggers.

questions.prompt: A B-tree index is added on a frequently filtered column. Which statement best describes the effect?
questions.explanation: An index is a trade-off: it can make selective reads cheaper but consumes space and must be maintained on writes, so bulk changes can slow down. The planner compares costs and may ignore the index, for example when most rows match or the table is small. Only a UNIQUE index or constraint enforces uniqueness.

questions.prompt: A composite B-tree index is created on (customer_id, created_on). Which predicate can use it efficiently?
questions.explanation: A B-tree on (customer_id, created_on) is ordered by customer_id first, then created_on within each customer. It can be used when customer_id is constrained, optionally with a range on created_on. A predicate on created_on alone cannot use the index efficiently because the leading column is unconstrained. Equality on both columns works, but a range on the trailing column is also supported.

questions.prompt: Why does adding several indexes to a table slow down INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements?
questions.explanation: Each index is a separate data structure keyed on its columns. An insert or a change to an indexed column requires an entry in every affected index, which adds I/O and CPU work. Writers are not serialized by a table-wide lock, indexes are updated incrementally rather than rebuilt, and an index stores keys and row references, not a copy of the table.

questions.prompt: Queries run WHERE lower(email) = 'a@example.com' on a large table that has a plain B-tree index on email. Why is the index not used, and what helps?
questions.explanation: A plain index on email stores email values, while the predicate compares lower(email). The planner would need an index whose key is the same expression, created as CREATE INDEX ... ON t (lower(email)). PostgreSQL supports expression indexes, and the function used must be immutable. Nullability and the B-tree text support are not the reason.

questions.prompt: A status column is 'pending' for about 1% of rows, and almost all queries filter status = 'pending'. Which index is the best fit?
questions.explanation: A partial index is defined with a WHERE predicate; it contains only the rows satisfying that predicate, so it is much smaller than a full index and is only maintained for matching rows. Queries must include a predicate that implies the index predicate to use it. Low cardinality alone does not prevent indexing, and a highly selective filter is exactly where an index can help.

questions.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL write changes to the write-ahead log (WAL)?
questions.explanation: WAL is the crash-recovery mechanism: change records are written and flushed before the modified data pages reach disk, so after a crash the server can replay committed changes. It exists independently of replication, although replication reuses the same stream. It is not a plan cache and not a row cache.

questions.prompt: In streaming replication, what does a hot standby server receive from the primary and what can it do?
questions.explanation: Streaming replication ships WAL records from the primary to the standby, which continuously applies them. A hot standby accepts read-only queries, and because applying can trail the primary, replica reads can be slightly stale. There is no shared-memory row transfer and no per-checkpoint logical dump.

questions.prompt: What does ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '16MB'; do?
questions.explanation: ALTER SYSTEM stores the override in postgresql.auto.conf, which is read in addition to postgresql.conf. Whether the running server picks the value up after a reload or needs a restart depends on the parameter's context; work_mem is a user-context parameter, so a reload is enough (sessions adopt the new value before their next command), while postmaster-context parameters require a restart. A session-level change would be SET, not ALTER SYSTEM, and the cluster is never recreated.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the pg_stat_activity view is correct?
questions.explanation: pg_stat_activity is a live, one-row-per-backend view: it reports the state, wait event and current query of each server process. It is not historical; statement history requires an extension such as pg_stat_statements. For privacy, non-superusers see limited information about other users' sessions unless they have pg_read_all_stats. Client backends and autovacuum workers both appear in the same view.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts the default PostgreSQL index type with the hash type?
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX without a type creates a B-tree, which serves equality, range and ORDER BY-style comparisons. A hash index supports only equality. GIN is specialized for composite values such as arrays, jsonb and full-text lexemes, not the default for scalar columns. The operator support differs, not just the size.

questions.prompt: What are the table statistics collected by ANALYZE used for?
questions.explanation: ANALYZE samples table contents and stores distributions such as most common values and histograms. The planner uses them to estimate how many rows a condition will match and to compare plan costs. If statistics are stale, estimates can be badly wrong and a poor plan may be chosen, which is why autovacuum and manual ANALYZE matter. Constraints and query results are unrelated.

questions.prompt: A table has row-level security enabled with no policies defined. What happens when an ordinary user selects from it?
questions.explanation: Row-level security is deny-by-default: once ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set and no policy grants access, ordinary users see no rows. Access is granted by CREATE POLICY expressions. The table owner bypasses row security unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, but an ordinary user is filtered. There is no syntax error and no implicit sampling.

questions.prompt: How is a PostgreSQL procedure created with CREATE PROCEDURE invoked, and how does it differ from an ordinary function?
questions.explanation: Procedures are called with the CALL statement and are designed for procedural work that may include transaction control. Functions return a value, can be used inside SQL expressions, and may not commit or roll back. Procedures accept parameters, and the planner never invokes them implicitly.

questions.prompt: A procedure contains a COMMIT statement. Under which condition can it execute that COMMIT?
questions.explanation: The CALL documentation states that if CALL is executed in a transaction block, the called procedure cannot execute transaction control statements; they are allowed only when CALL runs in its own transaction. Procedures do support COMMIT and ROLLBACK, which is a key difference from functions, but an enclosing explicit transaction block removes that ability.

questions.prompt: The relation enrollment(student_id, course_id, instructor_id, instructor_email) has candidate key {student_id, course_id} and functional dependencies {student_id, course_id} -> instructor_id and instructor_id -> instructor_email. Assuming every determinant is minimal unless stated otherwise, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: The candidate key is {student_id, course_id}. instructor_id depends on the whole key, so there is no partial dependency and 2NF holds. But instructor_email depends on instructor_id, which is not a superkey; instructor_email is therefore transitively dependent on the key and both 3NF and BCNF fail. Decompose into enrollment(student_id, course_id, instructor_id) and instructor(instructor_id, instructor_email).

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Table enrollment(student_id INT, course_id INT, instructor_id INT, instructor_email TEXT) records course enrollments. To audit whether instructor_id -> instructor_email holds, return one row per instructor with columns instructor_id (INT) and email_variants (BIGINT): the number of distinct non-NULL emails recorded for that instructor. Include instructors that have only NULL emails (their count is 0). Order by instructor_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT instructor_id, count(DISTINCT instructor_email) AS email_variants FROM enrollment GROUP BY instructor_id ORDER BY instructor_id
questions.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT instructor_email) ignores NULL, so an instructor whose only email is NULL yields 0. An instructor with two distinct emails yields 2, which proves that instructor_id -> instructor_email does not hold in that dataset; the audit surfaces the violation instead of hiding it.

questions.prompt: A hospital stores appointments in appointment(appointment_id, patient_id, clinician_id, clinician_email, room_code, room_building, appointment_date) with functional dependencies: (1) appointment_id -> patient_id, clinician_id, room_code, appointment_date; (2) clinician_id -> clinician_email; (3) room_code -> room_building. Assume each appointment has exactly one clinician and one room, and room_code identifies a room uniquely. (a) Identify the only candidate key and explain why it is minimal. (b) Determine the highest normal form of appointment and name the dependency that violates the next form. (c) Decompose into 3NF relations, listing keys and foreign keys. (d) Is your decomposition lossless-join and dependency-preserving? Justify briefly.
questions.reference_answer: (a) The only candidate key is {appointment_id}. By (1) it determines every attribute; a single attribute has no proper nonempty subset, so it is minimal. (b) The highest normal form is 2NF. The key is single-attribute, so no partial dependency exists. 3NF fails because clinician_id and room_code are non-superkey determinants: clinician_email is transitively dependent on appointment_id via clinician_id, and room_building is transitively dependent on appointment_id via room_code. BCNF fails for the same reason. (c) appointment(appointment_id PK, patient_id, clinician_id REFERENCES clinician, room_code REFERENCES room, appointment_date), clinician(clinician_id PK, clinician_email), room(room_code PK, room_building). (d) Each step is a lossless decomposition by the common-attribute test: the common attribute (clinician_id, then room_code) is a key of one resulting relation. The decomposition is dependency-preserving because each functional dependency is enforced inside a single relation: (1) in appointment, (2) in clinician, (3) in room. The result is also in BCNF.
questions.explanation: The key is appointment_id; single-attribute keys make 2NF automatic, but non-superkey determinants clinician_id and room_code create transitive dependencies, so 3NF fails. Splitting on those determinants yields three relations whose only determinants are keys, making the result BCNF, lossless and dependency-preserving.

source_refs.title: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model

questions.prompt: Explain the structure of a WITH RECURSIVE query in PostgreSQL. Identify the base term and the recursive term, state what the recursive term must reference, and explain why a termination condition is required. Describe the difference between UNION and UNION ALL in this context.
questions.reference_answer: A WITH RECURSIVE query defines a common table expression that can refer to itself. It has the form WITH RECURSIVE name AS (base term UNION [ALL] recursive term) SELECT ... FROM name. The base term runs once and produces the starting rows. The recursive term references the CTE name and is evaluated repeatedly, each time consuming the rows produced by the previous iteration, until an iteration returns no rows. Without a termination condition, such as a level counter or a join that stops at the root, the recursion never becomes empty and the query runs until it is cancelled or runs out of resources. UNION removes duplicate rows between iterations, which can stop a cycle in a cyclic graph; UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster but can loop forever on a cycle. A typical use is walking an employee table from a manager down through subordinates by joining the table to the CTE on the parent key.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify the base term as the non-recursive starting rows, the recursive term as the part that references the CTE, and the repeated evaluation until no rows are produced. It must explain a termination condition and distinguish UNION (duplicate removal) from UNION ALL (duplicates kept, faster, cycle risk).

questions.prompt: The expression CASE WHEN rating >= 4 THEN 'high' WHEN rating >= 2 THEN 'mid' END is evaluated with rating = 1. What is the result?
questions.explanation: A searched CASE evaluates its WHEN conditions in order and returns the result of the first one that is true; later branches are not evaluated. If none is true and there is no ELSE, the result is NULL. No implicit lowest category and no error occurs.

questions.prompt: The table customer(city, state) contains the rows ('Hue', NULL), ('Hue', NULL) and ('Hue', 'Thua Thien Hue'). How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT city, state FROM customer return?
questions.explanation: DISTINCT operates on the complete selected row, not on one column. For the purpose of duplicate elimination, NULL values are considered equal, so the two ('Hue', NULL) rows collapse into one and the result has two rows. This differs from the = comparison, for which NULL = NULL is unknown.

questions.prompt: What does the PostgreSQL expression 2 ^ 3 return?
questions.explanation: In PostgreSQL, ^ is the exponentiation operator: 2 ^ 3 raises 2 to the third power and yields 8 (as a floating-point value). It is not exclusive-or and not multiplication. Unary minus binds more tightly than ^, so -2 ^ 2 means (-2) ^ 2 and yields 4; write -(2 ^ 2) to square first and then negate.

questions.prompt: A client pages through results with ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET n, and many rows share the same score. What is the correctness risk?
questions.explanation: LIMIT/OFFSET are applied to an ordered result, but an ORDER BY on a non-unique column leaves the order of tied rows unspecified and it may differ between executions. Separate executions can therefore place a tied row on two pages or on none. Adding a unique column, such as a primary key, as a final ORDER BY key makes paging deterministic. Keyset pagination is the scalable alternative.

questions.prompt: With a default sort, where do NULL values appear in ORDER BY score ASC and ORDER BY score DESC?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL sorts NULLs as if they were larger than any non-NULL value, so ascending order places them last and descending order places them first. ORDER BY ... NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST overrides the default explicitly; NULL rows are not removed.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 2 INTERSECT SELECT 2 return?
questions.explanation: INTERSECT has higher precedence than UNION and EXCEPT, so the intersection of the second and third SELECT is computed first and yields 2; the union with 1 then produces {1, 2}. Mixing set operations is legal, and parentheses can make a different grouping explicit. When in doubt, parenthesize.

questions.prompt: Why does SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customer ORDER BY lower(city) fail in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: With DISTINCT, the output is a set of rows, and PostgreSQL requires each ORDER BY expression to match an output column. lower(city) is not in the select list, so the query is rejected with 'for SELECT DISTINCT, ORDER BY expressions must appear in select list'. Selecting lower(city) AS city_key or ordering by the selected city column avoids the error. DISTINCT and ORDER BY can otherwise be combined normally.

questions.prompt: What happens when SELECT price * qty AS total FROM item WHERE total > 100 ORDER BY total is executed?
questions.explanation: WHERE is evaluated before the select list, so an output alias does not exist at that point; the query raises 'column total does not exist'. ORDER BY, by contrast, may reference output column names and accepts total. Repeating price * qty in WHERE, or wrapping the query in a subquery that exposes total, resolves the problem.

questions.prompt: Consider SELECT dept, count(*) AS n FROM employee WHERE active GROUP BY dept HAVING count(*) > 2 ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 3. Which statement about how the clauses interact is correct?
questions.explanation: The logical processing order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, then ORDER BY and LIMIT. WHERE therefore sees individual rows and cannot filter on an aggregate; HAVING is the aggregate filter. ORDER BY sorts the result of the select list, and LIMIT is applied last to that ordered result. An output alias such as n may be used in ORDER BY, but not in WHERE.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: A table already holds production rows and must gain a new nullable column without losing data. Which statement does this?
questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN extends an existing table in place; the new column is nullable by default and existing rows receive NULL. CREATE TABLE would try to create a second table, UPDATE cannot introduce a column, and INSERT adds rows rather than columns.

questions.prompt: Which statement deletes selected rows from a table while keeping the table definition and all other rows?
questions.explanation: DELETE removes the rows that satisfy its WHERE clause and leaves the table structure and the remaining rows intact. DROP TABLE removes the table itself, ALTER ... DROP COLUMN removes a column from every row, and TRUNCATE empties the whole table because it does not accept a WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: The statement UPDATE product SET price = price * 2; is executed on a table where every row is non-NULL. What is the effect?
questions.explanation: Without a WHERE clause the UPDATE applies to every row, and the right-hand expression is evaluated from the row's current value, so the new price is twice the old one. An UPDATE never adds columns, and referring to the column being assigned is valid.

questions.prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY constraint on a column guarantee?
questions.explanation: A primary key combines NOT NULL with uniqueness and is backed by a unique index. Allowing repeated NULLs is the behaviour of a plain UNIQUE constraint in PostgreSQL, not of a primary key. Physical row order is never guaranteed by any constraint.

questions.prompt: Table note(note_id INT PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT, pinned BOOLEAN) has no defaults. The statement INSERT INTO note (note_id, body) VALUES (1, 'hello'); is executed. What is stored in pinned?
questions.explanation: Columns omitted from the INSERT column list receive their declared default; without a default the value is NULL. PostgreSQL has no implicit FALSE default for booleans, listing every column is not required, and no implicit text conversion occurs.

questions.prompt: The statement ALTER TABLE customer DROP COLUMN nickname; is executed. What is the result?
questions.explanation: DROP COLUMN removes the column definition and its stored values from every row; the table and its other columns survive. Emptying a column without removing it is UPDATE ... SET col = NULL, not DROP COLUMN, and dropping a table is DROP TABLE.

questions.prompt: Table order_line(quantity INT) is created with the constraint CHECK (quantity > 0). What happens when an INSERT supplies quantity = 0?
questions.explanation: A CHECK constraint must evaluate to TRUE or NULL for every inserted or updated row; a row for which it evaluates to FALSE is rejected and the statement fails. PostgreSQL never silently repairs the value or downgrades the violation to a warning.

questions.prompt: Which statement inserts two rows into tag(tag_id, label) in a single command?
questions.explanation: A multi-row VALUES list is the standard way to insert several rows in one statement. Repeating the VALUES keyword is a syntax error, SELECT 1, 'sql' AND 2, 'db' is not valid row construction, and the last option uses two statements rather than one command.

questions.prompt: The setup creates product(product_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price INT) and then the view cheap_product, whose stored query selects product_id, name and price from product where price < 100. Rows were inserted after the view was created. Return product_id, name and price for the rows the view exposes, ordered by product_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT product_id, name, price FROM cheap_product ORDER BY product_id
questions.explanation: A view stores a query, not a copy of the data, and rows inserted after CREATE VIEW are visible when the view is queried: the view's WHERE price < 100 keeps products 1 and 3 and drops 2 and 4. The empty dataset correctly returns no rows.

questions.prompt: The setup creates ticket(ticket_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, subject TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open') and inserts rows, sometimes naming status and sometimes omitting it. Return ticket_id, subject and status for every row, ordered by ticket_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT ticket_id, subject, status FROM ticket ORDER BY ticket_id
questions.explanation: The identity column fills ticket_id automatically, so the INSERT statements never supply it and the generated values start at 1. Omitting status applies the declared 'open' default, while an explicit value such as 'closed' is stored as given. The second dataset therefore contrasts defaulted and explicit status values.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL 17 executes MERGE INTO stock s USING delivery d ON s.item = d.item WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET qty = s.qty + d.qty WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (item, qty) VALUES (d.item, d.qty). What does the statement guarantee?
questions.explanation: MERGE evaluates the source against the target and applies the first matching WHEN clause per target row, so a target row is modified at most once; if several source rows match the same target row, PostgreSQL 17 raises a cardinality error instead of updating twice. WHEN NOT MATCHED refers to source rows with no target match and inserts them; the clause order does not create a second pass. MERGE was introduced in PostgreSQL 15 and extended in 17, so the statement is valid.

questions.prompt: Table account has UNIQUE (lower(email)) as its only unique index on email. The statement INSERT INTO account (email) VALUES ('a@x.edu') ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING; is executed. What happens?
questions.explanation: Inference for ON CONFLICT (column list) looks for a unique index whose expressions match the listed expressions exactly. An index on lower(email) does not match the bare expression email, so arbiter inference fails and the statement errors. Naming the expression makes the arbiter explicit; an expression index is not a constraint, so ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT cannot name it.

questions.prompt: INSERT INTO account (account_id, email) SELECT account_id, email FROM staging ON CONFLICT (account_id) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email; is executed, and staging contains the same account_id twice. What happens?
questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE requires that each target row be touched at most once per statement; a duplicate key inside the incoming result set would touch the same row twice, so PostgreSQL raises an error. The fix is to deduplicate the source before the insert. There is no defined first/last winner and no automatic merging.

questions.prompt: Table line references header with a constraint declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED. Inside one transaction, a line row is inserted before its header row. What happens?
questions.explanation: A constraint declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED is checked at the end of the transaction rather than after each statement, so the temporarily missing header is acceptable while the header is inserted before COMMIT. It is still enforced at commit, so option C is wrong. NOT DEFERRABLE constraints, the default, are checked immediately.

questions.prompt: Table invoice(id INT, qty INT, unit_price INT, total INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * unit_price) STORED) is created. What happens when an INSERT supplies a value for total?
questions.explanation: A stored generated column is maintained by the database: its value is computed on insert and on every update of the referenced columns, and only DEFAULT may be written for it. Supplying a literal is an error, because the database will not accept a value it cannot verify against the expression.

questions.prompt: A column amount is declared TEXT and holds numeric text. The statement ALTER TABLE sale ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE INT; fails. Which change makes the conversion explicit and correct?
questions.explanation: Without a USING clause PostgreSQL only applies an assignment cast, and TEXT to INT is not one, so the statement fails. USING defines the per-row expression that produces the new value, here an explicit cast. A DEFAULT clause does not convert existing values, CASCADE is unrelated to type conversion, and CTAS creates a new table rather than altering this one.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts CREATE TABLE copy (LIKE sale INCLUDING ALL) with CREATE TABLE copy AS SELECT * FROM sale?
questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE ... LIKE produces an empty table that inherits column definitions, and INCLUDING ALL adds defaults, constraints, indexes and identity properties. CREATE TABLE AS materializes the query result, so it copies rows and column types, but it does not carry primary keys, unique constraints or foreign keys.

questions.prompt: Table ticket has an identity column, and table comment references ticket(ticket_id). The statement TRUNCATE TABLE ticket RESTART IDENTITY; is executed with no other options. What happens?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE refuses to run when another table has a foreign key to the target unless that table is included with CASCADE. RESTART IDENTITY resets owned sequences, so the option is meaningful; it is not ignored. Referencing tables are never silently modified without CASCADE.

questions.prompt: Which view can PostgreSQL update automatically, without an INSTEAD OF trigger or rule?
questions.explanation: A view is automatically updatable when it has exactly one base relation, no DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING, set operation, aggregate or window function, and every output column maps to a base column. Aggregates, set operations and DISTINCT break the mapping, so those views need an INSTEAD OF trigger or rule to accept writes.

questions.prompt: Table line(order_id INT, product_id INT, FOREIGN KEY (order_id, product_id) REFERENCES order_item(order_id, product_id)) uses the default MATCH SIMPLE. The row (NULL, 99) is inserted. What happens?
questions.explanation: MATCH SIMPLE, the default, requires the foreign key condition to hold only when all key columns are non-NULL; a single NULL disables the check for that row. MATCH FULL would reject a partially NULL key, and no automatic lookup of product_id occurs in either mode.

questions.prompt: The setup creates customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL) and orders(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, status TEXT, qty INT, unit_price INT), then the view open_order_value whose stored query joins orders to customer, keeps rows with status 'open', and computes line_value = qty * unit_price. Return order_id, name and line_value for every view row, ordered by order_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT order_id, name, line_value FROM open_order_value ORDER BY order_id
questions.explanation: The view's stored query is evaluated when the view is read, so the join, the status filter and the multiplication all apply at query time. Orders 10 and 12 survive with computed values 100 and 60; the closed order 11 is filtered out, and order 13 disappears because its NULL customer_id matches no customer through the inner join. The dataset without open orders returns no rows.

questions.prompt: The setup creates article(article_id INT PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT UNIQUE) using the default NULL treatment and inserts rows, including more than one row with a NULL code. Return code and copies (BIGINT) giving the number of rows stored per code, ordered by code ascending with NULL values last.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT code, count(*) AS copies FROM article GROUP BY code ORDER BY code NULLS LAST
questions.explanation: UNIQUE compares with equality, and NULL is never equal to NULL, so all three NULL-coded rows are accepted and GROUP BY collects them into one group of three. Every non-NULL code is unique, so each has copies = 1. A UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT constraint would have rejected the second NULL insert instead.

questions.prompt: Compare DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP TABLE in PostgreSQL. Address (a) which rows or objects each removes, (b) filtering and WHERE, (c) transactional behaviour and rollback, (d) foreign-key dependencies and required options, (e) identity sequences and RESTART IDENTITY, and (f) the locking consequences you would weigh before running each in production.
questions.reference_answer: DELETE is DML: it removes rows that satisfy an optional WHERE clause, leaves the table, its constraints and its sequences in place, and is fully transactional, so it can be rolled back and each deleted row is logged. TRUNCATE removes every row, accepts no WHERE clause, keeps the table definition, and in PostgreSQL is transactional, though it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table and is much cheaper than row-by-row deletion. It refuses to run when a foreign key references the table unless the referencing tables are included with CASCADE, and RESTART IDENTITY resets owned sequences. DROP TABLE removes the definition and all rows and is DDL; it is transactional but requires ownership and is blocked by dependent objects unless CASCADE, which can cascade far beyond the intended target. In production, DELETE is chosen for selective removal and lets concurrent readers continue, at the cost of bloat and vacuum work; TRUNCATE is chosen for emptying a whole table but blocks other access while it runs; DROP is chosen only when the object itself is no longer needed.
questions.explanation: The answer must separate the three commands by scope (rows versus all rows versus object), by filtering, by transactionality, by foreign-key behaviour, by identity handling and by locking, and must connect each to an appropriate production use.

questions.prompt: Table account(account_id INT PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE) already holds account_id = 7. The statement INSERT INTO account (account_id, email) VALUES (7, 'new@example.edu') ON CONFLICT (account_id) DO NOTHING; is executed. What is the result?
questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT (account_id) DO NOTHING names account_id as the arbiter; when a conflict with the existing key occurs, the proposed row is discarded and the command still succeeds. Replacing the email requires DO UPDATE, and a duplicate key is an error only when no conflict action is supplied.

questions.prompt: In INSERT INTO t (id, qty) VALUES (1, 5) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, what does EXCLUDED refer to?
questions.explanation: EXCLUDED is the special relation holding the row that the INSERT attempted to add. Referring to it lets the update copy the proposed values; the stored row is referenced through the target table name, not through EXCLUDED.

questions.prompt: The statement UPDATE sale s SET amount = p.amount FROM price p WHERE p.sale_id = s.sale_id; is executed and a sale matches more than one price row. What does PostgreSQL guarantee?
questions.explanation: UPDATE ... FROM joins the target to the source, and a target row that matches several source rows is still updated only once; which match supplies the value is not defined. A deterministic result therefore requires the source side to be unique per key. No cardinality error is raised, and UPDATE never inserts rows.

questions.prompt: The statement DELETE FROM sale s USING customer c WHERE c.customer_id = s.customer_id AND c.status = 'closed'; is executed. Which rows are deleted?
questions.explanation: DELETE ... USING names extra tables that the WHERE clause may reference; only rows of the deletion target (sale) that satisfy the join and filter are removed. Customer rows are never deleted by a DELETE targeting sale, and sales with no match fail the join condition and survive.

questions.prompt: Which statement about identity columns compared with serial is correct in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Identity columns are the standard replacement for serial. Both use a sequence, but GENERATED ALWAYS rejects an explicit insert value unless the statement says OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE; GENERATED BY DEFAULT accepts explicit values. Serial is the older, non-standard shorthand.

questions.prompt: Table order_line references order with ON DELETE RESTRICT, while table audit_note references order with ON DELETE CASCADE. An order that has rows in both tables is deleted. What happens?
questions.explanation: Referential actions are enforced per constraint. RESTRICT prevents the deletion while a referencing row exists, and the whole statement fails atomically, so the order is not deleted and the CASCADE effect never happens. SET NULL applies only when the constraint declares ON DELETE SET NULL.

questions.prompt: Table customer(email TEXT UNIQUE) uses the default NULL treatment. Two rows are inserted with email = NULL. What happens?
questions.explanation: A UNIQUE constraint compares values with equality, and NULL is never equal to NULL, so any number of NULLs may coexist. A constraint declared UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT would reject the second NULL. No value is rewritten.

questions.prompt: CREATE TABLE sale_backup AS SELECT * FROM sale; is executed. What does the new table contain?
questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE AS materializes the query result once; later changes to sale do not appear. Column names and types are derived from the query, but constraints such as primary keys, unique constraints and foreign keys are not copied. A view or a materialized view is a different object.

questions.prompt: ALTER TABLE sale ADD CONSTRAINT sale_amount_ck CHECK (amount >= 0) NOT VALID; is executed on a table that already contains a negative amount. What is the effect?
questions.explanation: NOT VALID skips the initial scan of existing rows, which is why the statement succeeds despite the stored negative amount. The constraint is enforced for every new or changed row. Existing rows can be checked later with ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. Nothing is deleted or rewritten automatically.

questions.prompt: Which statement about TRUNCATE TABLE sale is correct in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE empties the table; it has no WHERE clause, so it cannot remove selected rows. In PostgreSQL TRUNCATE is transactional and rolls back with the transaction. It does not drop the table; DROP TABLE removes the definition.

questions.prompt: The setup creates dept(dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT NOT NULL) and emp(emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept_id INT, name TEXT), then the view dept_headcount whose stored query left-joins emp to dept and groups by department, producing dept_id, dept_name and headcount = count(emp.emp_id). Return dept_id, dept_name and headcount for every row of the view, ordered by dept_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT dept_id, dept_name, headcount FROM dept_headcount ORDER BY dept_id
questions.explanation: A view stores the query, so the aggregate is recomputed on every read. Because the view left-joins from dept, Sales has headcount 0 rather than disappearing, and the employee with a NULL dept_id matches no department and is not counted. The empty dataset returns no rows.

questions.prompt: The setup creates note(note_id INT, body TEXT) with no primary key or unique constraint and inserts some note_id values more than once. Return note_id and copies (BIGINT) for the note_id values that are stored more than once, ordered by note_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT note_id, count(*) AS copies FROM note GROUP BY note_id HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY note_id
questions.explanation: Without a primary key or unique constraint INSERT performs no duplicate checking, so the same note_id can be stored repeatedly. GROUP BY with HAVING count(*) > 1 surfaces those keys; note_id 1 appears twice and note_id 3 three times in the first dataset, and the clean dataset correctly returns no rows. Declaring note_id as a primary key would have rejected the repeated values instead.

questions.prompt: Explain how INSERT ... ON CONFLICT works in PostgreSQL. Cover which object acts as the arbiter, the difference between DO NOTHING and DO UPDATE, the role of EXCLUDED, what happens when no unique index matches the conflict target, and why this is safer than a SELECT-then-INSERT sequence under concurrent writers.
questions.reference_answer: ON CONFLICT requires an arbiter: a unique index or unique/Primary key constraint on the conflict target, either named with ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT or inferred from a column list. DO NOTHING discards the proposed row silently; DO UPDATE applies an update whose SET expression may read EXCLUDED, the proposed row, and the existing row through the table name. If no matching unique index exists, PostgreSQL raises an error because it cannot detect the conflict. A SELECT followed by INSERT is a race: two sessions can both find no row and then both insert. ON CONFLICT resolves the conflict atomically inside the INSERT, so one statement succeeds and the intended action (skip or update) is applied without a window for a duplicate-key failure.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify the unique index as the arbiter, contrast DO NOTHING with DO UPDATE, explain EXCLUDED, note the error when no matching index exists, and justify the concurrency advantage over check-then-insert.

questions.prompt: Table customer(customer_id, name, city) has one row per customer. Which statement returns one row per customer with columns name and city_label, where city_label contains the city value?
questions.explanation: AS renames the output column without changing the value, so city AS city_label produces the requested label. Option B asks for a column named city_label that does not exist; option A assigns the label to name instead of city; option D is a comparison expression that references an undefined identifier.

questions.prompt: Which join returns every row of the left table and fills columns from the right table with NULL when no matching row exists?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves the left input and NULL-extends unmatched rows. INNER JOIN discards unmatched rows on both sides. RIGHT JOIN preserves the right input, not the left. CROSS JOIN forms every pair with no matching condition.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Which clause filters individual rows before grouping and therefore cannot contain an aggregate such as count(*)?
questions.explanation: WHERE runs on individual rows before groups exist, so aggregates are not available. HAVING runs after grouping and is the place for aggregate conditions. ORDER BY sorts the final result, and SELECT evaluates output expressions after grouping.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: The query SELECT region_id, count(*) FROM sales GROUP BY region_id returns one row per region. What does count(*) count inside each group?
questions.explanation: count(*) counts rows in the current group and ignores no column values. NULL region_id rows form their own group when GROUP BY is used. count(region_id) would instead skip NULLs. The table-wide count would require removing GROUP BY; distinct counting requires count(DISTINCT ...).

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Table customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT). Return customer_id, name, and name_length (INT, the number of characters in name) for customers whose city is not NULL. Order by name ascending, then customer_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT customer_id, name, length(name) AS name_length FROM customer WHERE city IS NOT NULL ORDER BY name, customer_id
questions.explanation: length returns the character count and is labelled name_length. WHERE ... IS NOT NULL keeps only rows with a city; writing city <> 'x' would also drop NULL cities. The secondary sort key customer_id makes the order deterministic when names repeat, and the edge dataset correctly returns no rows.

questions.prompt: Explain the logical order in which the clauses FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT and ORDER BY are processed. Then explain why an output alias defined in SELECT cannot be referenced in WHERE but can be used in ORDER BY.
questions.reference_answer: Logical processing starts with FROM (including joins), then WHERE filters individual rows, then GROUP BY forms groups, then HAVING filters groups, then SELECT computes the output expressions and aliases, and finally ORDER BY sorts the result (LIMIT/OFFSET apply after sorting). WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so a SELECT alias does not exist yet and referencing it there is an error. ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT, so PostgreSQL accepts output names there. The physical plan may reorder operations, but the logical order determines which names and aggregates are visible.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is visibility: WHERE sees input columns but no output aliases or aggregates; HAVING sees grouped aggregates; ORDER BY sees the SELECT list. Naming the stages in the correct order and connecting them to alias visibility is the learning objective.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Compare INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. Explain what NULL extension means for unmatched left rows, and explain what happens to the row count when a row on the left matches several rows on the right.
questions.reference_answer: INNER JOIN returns only pairs that satisfy the join condition: left rows without a match disappear, and right rows without a match also disappear. LEFT JOIN returns every left row; when no right row matches, the right-side columns are filled with NULL (NULL extension). The result is a bag, not a set: if one left row matches three right rows, it appears three times with the three right-side values, so joins can multiply rows. Aggregating after such a join can overcount unless the query pre-aggregates the many side or counts distinct keys.
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN is a match filter; LEFT JOIN preserves the left side and NULL-extends. Neither removes duplicates by itself, so a one-to-many join produces repeated left rows and can inflate counts and sums.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group of rows that share the DISTINCT ON expressions, where 'first' is defined by the query's ORDER BY, which must begin with those expressions. DISTINCT, by contrast, compares entire output rows, so (region_id, sale_id) pairs are deduplicated, not regions. DISTINCT ON does not require the expression to appear twice, and it is not equivalent to DISTINCT.

questions.prompt: Table t(x INT) holds the rows 1, 2 and NULL. The statement SELECT x FROM t WHERE NOT (x > 5) is executed. Which result set does PostgreSQL return?
questions.explanation: Comparing NULL with 5 yields UNKNOWN. NOT UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so WHERE discards the NULL row. Rows 1 and 2 both satisfy NOT (x > 5) because 1 > 5 and 2 > 5 are FALSE and NOT FALSE is TRUE. The common mistake is to read NOT (x > 5) as x <= 5, which would include NULL under an invalid two-valued reading.

questions.prompt: Tables a(id) and b(id) have no NULL ids. Which query returns exactly the ids that appear in one table but not the other?
questions.explanation: A FULL JOIN emits matched rows plus one NULL-extended row for each unmatched row on either side. After USING (id) the join column is merged, but a.id and b.id still reveal which side was NULL-extended. Keeping rows where exactly one side is NULL therefore returns the symmetric difference. Option A keeps only matched rows, and options C and D are inner joins.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: The statement SELECT region_id, count(*) AS n FROM sale GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((region_id), ()) ORDER BY region_id NULLS LAST is executed on a non-empty table. What does it return?
questions.explanation: A grouping set is the set of columns a single aggregate pass groups by. GROUPING SETS ((region_id), ()) runs two passes: one grouped by region_id and one over the whole table. The grand total therefore appears as an extra row, and columns that are not part of that grouping set are reported as NULL. The empty set is meaningful, not ignored, and GROUP BY does accept grouping sets in PostgreSQL.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: The table sale is currently empty. The statement SELECT count(*) AS n FROM sale HAVING count(*) > 0 is executed. What is the result?
questions.explanation: When a query has HAVING but no GROUP BY, the entire table is treated as a single group, so exactly one candidate row is produced before HAVING runs. count(*) on an empty table is 0, so the condition 0 > 0 is false and the group is discarded, leaving an empty result. PostgreSQL permits HAVING without GROUP BY; it is not a syntax error.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: customer(customer_id) has one row per customer, while orders may contain several rows per customer. Which query returns each customer with at least one order exactly once?
questions.explanation: EXISTS is a semi-join: it answers a yes/no question per outer row and never duplicates that row, so several orders still produce one customer row. The plain JOIN multiplies the customer once per order. The uncorrelated EXISTS in option C is true for every customer as soon as orders is non-empty, and option D uses a scalar subquery that raises an error when the customer has more than one order.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Table score(player TEXT, points INT) contains ('a',100), ('b',100) and ('c',90). The statement SELECT player, points, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS rn, rank() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS rk, dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS dr FROM score is executed. Which pattern of values is produced?
questions.explanation: row_number always assigns distinct integers, so the two tied rows get 1 and 2, but which player receives 1 is not defined because ORDER BY points DESC is not a total order. rank leaves a gap after ties and continues at 3, while dense_rank continues at 2. Options A and B wrongly give row_number a duplicate value, and option D wrongly assumes all three functions behave alike.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the LATERAL key word is correct?
questions.explanation: A FROM subquery is normally evaluated independently and cannot see other FROM items. LATERAL lifts that restriction, allowing the subquery to refer to columns of preceding items, which is how a per-row top-N lookup is expressed. LATERAL is valid in FROM, it is not a SELECT-list feature, and it has nothing to do with the number of rows returned.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Table emp(dept_id INT, salary INT) has a nullable salary column. The query SELECT dept_id, count(*) AS all_rows, count(*) FILTER (WHERE salary > 5000) AS high FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id returns one row per department. What does the high column contain?
questions.explanation: FILTER restricts the rows fed to one aggregate inside the current group. Comparing NULL salary with 5000 yields UNKNOWN, and only TRUE rows are fed to the aggregate, so NULL salaries are skipped while count(*) still counts them in all_rows. FILTER is general: it applies to any aggregate, including count.

questions.prompt: Table sale(region_id INT, amount INT) stores rows whose region_id may be NULL. The query SELECT region_id, GROUPING(region_id) AS g, count(*) AS n FROM sale GROUP BY ROLLUP (region_id) ORDER BY g, region_id is executed. How can the grand-total row be distinguished from the group formed by the rows whose region_id is NULL?
questions.explanation: ROLLUP (region_id) is shorthand for GROUPING SETS ((region_id), ()), so it produces per-region rows plus one grand total. Both can show NULL in region_id, which is why the GROUPING function exists: it returns 1 when the column was supplied by the grouping-set machinery rather than read from the data, and 0 when it is a real value. NULL regions are grouped normally, they are not discarded.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Table sale(sale_id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount INT) records sales; amount is nullable and a region can have several sales. Return one row per region with the columns region_id (INT), sale_id (INT) and amount (INT): the sale with the greatest amount in that region, breaking ties by the lower sale_id. A region whose sales all have a NULL amount still gets a row, choosing the sale with the lowest sale_id. Order by region_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT DISTINCT ON (region_id) region_id, sale_id, amount FROM sale ORDER BY region_id, amount DESC NULLS LAST, sale_id
questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row per region in ORDER BY order. Within a region, amount DESC NULLS LAST ranks the largest amount first while placing NULL amounts last, and sale_id breaks the 500/500 tie in favour of sale 1. For region 3, where every amount is NULL, the sale_id key decides and sale 4 is chosen. The empty dataset correctly returns no rows.

questions.prompt:
A reporting team writes:
SELECT order_id FROM orders o
WHERE amount <> 0
  AND customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked)
Table orders has nullable amount and customer_id columns, and the blocked table may contain NULL.
(a) Explain which rows the WHERE clause keeps and why NULL amounts or a NULL in the subquery silently remove rows.
(b) Rewrite the exclusion so it is NULL-safe, using NOT EXISTS, and state which rows the rewrite now includes that the original dropped.
(c) Explain how the same reasoning applies to HAVING with sum(amount) > 100 on a group whose amounts are all NULL, and state what you must decide explicitly.
questions.reference_answer:
(a) WHERE keeps only rows for which the whole predicate is TRUE. amount <> 0 evaluates to UNKNOWN when amount is NULL, so those rows are dropped even though the amount is not zero. NOT IN is a chain of <> comparisons: a NULL customer_id, or any NULL produced by the subquery, makes the comparison UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN AND anything is never TRUE. The row therefore disappears silently, and the report under-counts without raising an error.
(b) Rewrite: WHERE amount IS DISTINCT FROM 0 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.customer_id = o.customer_id). IS DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe inequality, returning TRUE for a NULL amount against 0. NOT EXISTS is TRUE when no row satisfies the inner predicate; a NULL customer_id simply matches nothing, so the order is included. The rewrite therefore keeps rows the original dropped: orders with NULL amount, and orders with NULL customer_id. Whether a NULL customer should count as unblocked is a business decision that must be stated, not left implicit.
(c) HAVING runs after aggregation and keeps groups whose predicate is TRUE. sum ignores NULL inputs, so a group whose amounts are all NULL produces NULL, sum(amount) > 100 is UNKNOWN, and the group is dropped. If the intended rule is that such a group counts as zero, write coalesce(sum(amount), 0) > 100; if it should be excluded, say so explicitly. count(*) is never NULL, so count-based HAVING conditions do not have this problem.
questions.explanation: The answer must tie the behaviour to three-valued logic rather than to a vague 'NULL is special' claim. Part (a) should show that UNKNOWN is neither TRUE nor FALSE and that WHERE/HAVING keep only TRUE. Part (b) must give the NOT EXISTS form and identify the rows it recovers. Part (c) must note that SUM over an all-NULL group is NULL and that coalesce or an explicit exclusion rule is needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an output alias introduced in the SELECT list is correct in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Logical evaluation reaches WHERE before SELECT computes output expressions, so the alias does not exist yet. ORDER BY runs after SELECT and may refer to an output name. HAVING runs before SELECT as well, so aliases are not generally available there. An alias changes only the output name; input columns remain accessible by their own names.

questions.prompt: Table orders has a nullable customer_id, and the subquery SELECT customer_id FROM orders currently returns at least one NULL. Which query reliably returns customers that have no orders?
questions.explanation: NOT IN is equivalent to a chain of <> comparisons. Comparing any value with NULL yields UNKNOWN, so a NULL in the subquery makes the predicate UNKNOWN for every customer and the query returns no rows. NOT EXISTS tests the absence of a matching row and is unaffected by NULL values. Option C has the same NULL sensitivity, and option D applies NOT to the same IN test, so it is also NULL-sensitive and returns no rows when the subquery yields NULL.

questions.prompt: Which query returns only customers that have at least one order, although it is written with a LEFT JOIN?
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN emits NULL-extended rows for unmatched customers. Filtering o.customer_id IS NOT NULL afterwards removes those rows, leaving only customers with at least one match. IS NULL is the anti-join and returns the opposite set. HAVING without GROUP BY does not filter per customer. Moving the condition into ON only restricts which orders match and still keeps unmatched customers.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Table customer has a nullable email column. What does SELECT count(*), count(email) FROM customer return?
questions.explanation: count(*) counts rows. count(expression) counts non-NULL values of that expression, so the two numbers can differ. The forms can be combined in one aggregate query without GROUP BY, which then produces exactly one row.

questions.prompt: Consider SELECT dept_id FROM emp WHERE salary > 1000 GROUP BY dept_id HAVING count(*) >= 2. What does the query return?
questions.explanation: WHERE removes employees with salary <= 1000 or NULL salary before grouping. GROUP BY then forms departments from the surviving rows, and HAVING keeps departments whose surviving row count is at least two. The filter is per employee before grouping, not a sum, and the result has one row per qualifying department.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Table dept has dept_id as its primary key and a dept_name column. Why does PostgreSQL accept SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, count(*) FROM dept d JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL permits an ungrouped column when it is functionally dependent on the grouped columns, and a primary key determines the other columns of its table. The join does not break that dependency because dept_name comes from dept. Without such a dependency, each group could contain several dept_name values and PostgreSQL rejects the query instead of inventing an answer.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Each order has three rows in orders and two rows in items per order. The query SELECT sum(o.amount) FROM orders o JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id returns a total much larger than the sum of order amounts. Why?
questions.explanation: A one-to-many join multiplies each order row by its number of item rows. SUM has no DISTINCT here, so the repeated amount contributes once per joined row. The repair is to aggregate items first or sum the order amounts in a separate subquery. SUM does not deduplicate on its own, NULLs are ignored rather than converted to zero, and removing rows cannot increase a sum of non-negative amounts.

questions.prompt: Which select-list expression returns one row per sale with the original id and a computed column labelled gross, equal to amount multiplied by 1.1?
questions.explanation: AS labels the computed expression gross without changing the row count. Option B is a boolean comparison with an undefined identifier; option C aliases the table rather than the output column and leaves the computed column unnamed; option A puts the gross label on id.

questions.prompt: Column status is nullable. Which rows does WHERE status <> 'cancelled' return?
questions.explanation: In three-valued logic, NULL <> 'cancelled' evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE. Rows with status NULL are therefore dropped. To include them, test status IS NULL OR status <> 'cancelled', or use IS DISTINCT FROM, which treats NULL as a comparable value. NULL is not an empty string.

questions.prompt: A scalar subquery appears in the SELECT list. What happens if that subquery returns more than one row at execution time?
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery is used where a single value is expected. Zero rows yield NULL, but more than one row is an error ('more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression'). PostgreSQL does not silently choose a row or aggregate; the query must guarantee cardinality with an aggregate, LIMIT 1, or a correlated condition.

questions.prompt: Table customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL) and table orders(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, amount NUMERIC(10,2)). Return customer_id, name and order_count (BIGINT) for every customer, including customers with no orders. Order by order_count descending, then customer_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, count(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name ORDER BY order_count DESC, c.customer_id
questions.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps customers without orders, and counting o.order_id rather than * turns the join's NULL placeholder into 0. Grouping by customer_id and name keeps the selected name valid. ORDER BY may use the output alias order_count; the tie-breaker on customer_id makes the result deterministic.

questions.prompt: Table customer(customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL) and table orders(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT). Return order_id (INT), name (TEXT) and has_customer (BOOLEAN) for every order. Orders with a customer_id that matches no customer are returned with NULL name and has_customer false; NULL customer_id is treated the same way. Order by order_id ascending.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT o.order_id, c.name, (c.customer_id IS NOT NULL) AS has_customer FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customer c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_id
questions.explanation: The LEFT JOIN preserves every order. c.customer_id IS NOT NULL is FALSE for both an orphan key and a NULL key, so the boolean flag distinguishes matched from unmatched orders without converting NULL to text. The edge dataset has no orders and correctly returns no rows.

questions.prompt: Explain how a SELECT statement that joins two tables and applies WHERE produces its result. Cover the select list, row filtering, bag semantics and duplicate multiplication. Give an example in which a one-to-many join changes the number of rows and explain when DISTINCT or pre-aggregation is the appropriate correction.
questions.reference_answer: FROM builds the joined table, applying the ON condition to form pairs. WHERE then keeps rows for which the predicate is TRUE. The SELECT list evaluates expressions for each surviving row and labels them. SQL tables are bags: a left row matching three right rows produces three output rows, and no automatic deduplication occurs. If a customer has three orders, joining customer to orders yields three rows for that customer. SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate whole result rows, which is appropriate when the question asks for distinct entities and the selected columns uniquely identify them. When the goal is one row per customer with an aggregate, pre-aggregating orders in a subquery and then joining is safer than DISTINCT, because DISTINCT would not repair an incorrect SUM inflated by fan-out.
questions.explanation: The essential points are logical clause order, bag semantics, one-to-many row multiplication, and the distinction between DISTINCT as duplicate-row removal and pre-aggregation as a way to fix incorrect aggregates.

source_refs.title: Table Expressions
source_refs.section: 7.2 Table Expressions (joined tables, GROUP BY, HAVING)

questions.prompt: Explain how INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN affect count and sum aggregates. Address unmatched rows, NULL amounts, count(*) versus count(column), and row multiplication when the joined table has several matches. Give the rule you would use to count customers with zero orders correctly.
questions.reference_answer: INNER JOIN keeps only matching pairs, so customers without orders disappear and cannot be counted as zero. LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and NULL-extends the right columns. count(*) counts the NULL-extended row as one, which is wrong for counting orders; count(o.order_id) counts only non-NULL matched keys and yields 0 for unmatched customers. sum ignores NULL amounts, so an unmatched customer or an order with NULL amount contributes nothing, which may be the desired numeric total but must be documented.
